entries.en: On bingyin in the sixth month of Qingtai 3 the Minister of Works Cui Jian presented the empress dowager's seals and patent; she was posthumously named Xuanxian.
entries.literal: On bingyin of the sixth month, Qingtai 3, Minister of Works Cui Jian was sent to present the empress dowager's seals and patent; her posthumous name was Xuanxian.

entries.zh: 明宗和武憲皇后曹氏昭懿皇后夏氏
entries.en: Mingzong; Empress Hewuxian, Lady Cao; and Empress Zhaoyi, Lady Xia
entries.literal: Mingzong and Empress Wuhe, Lady Cao; Empress Zhaoyi, Lady Xia

entries.zh: 廢帝入立，嘗置酒妃院，妃舉酒曰：「願辭皇帝為比丘尼。」
entries.en: When the Deposed Emperor seized the throne, he once feasted in the consort’s quarters; she lifted her cup and said: “I beg to leave the emperor’s household and take the tonsure.”
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor entered and took the throne, he once set wine in the consort’s compound; she raised her cup and said: “I wish to leave the emperor and become a Buddhist nun.”

entries.zh: 帝驚，問其故，曰「小兒處偶得命，若大人不容，則死之日，何面見先帝！」
entries.en: The emperor was startled and asked why. She said: “The boy barely kept his life; if Your Majesty will not spare us, when I die how shall I face the late emperor!”
entries.literal: The emperor was startled and asked why; she said: “The boy barely escaped with his life; if Your Majesty does not bear with us, when I die how can I face the late emperor!”

entries.zh: 因泣下。
entries.en: And she wept.
entries.literal: And she wept.

entries.zh: 廢帝亦為之淒然，待之頗厚。
entries.en: The Deposed Emperor was stricken too and treated her with new warmth.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor was moved as well and treated her rather generously.

entries.zh: 石敬瑭兵犯京師，廢帝聚族將自焚。
entries.en: When Shi Jingtang’s army closed on the capital, the Deposed Emperor gathered his kin to die by fire.
entries.literal: When Shi Jingtang’s troops threatened the capital, the Deposed Emperor gathered his clan and meant to burn themselves.

entries.zh: 妃謂太后曰：「事急矣，宜少回避，以俟姑夫。」
entries.en: The consort told the dowager: “All is lost—withdraw for now and wait for our uncle-by-marriage.”
entries.literal: The consort said to the dowager: “Matters are urgent; you should withdraw a little and wait for our uncle-by-marriage.”

entries.zh: 太后曰：「我家至此，何忍獨生，妹自勉之！」
entries.en: The dowager answered: “Our house has come to this—how could I live on alone? Sister, save yourself!”
entries.literal: The dowager said: “Our house has come to this—how can I bear to live alone? Sister, take care of yourself!”

entries.zh: 太后乃與帝俱燔死，而妃與許王從益及其妹匿於鞠院以免。
entries.en: The dowager burned with the emperor, while the consort hid with Congyi, Xu Wang, and his sister in the hospital ward and survived.
entries.literal: The dowager then burned to death with the emperor, while the consort with Xu Wang Congyi and his sister hid in the hospital ward and escaped.

entries.zh: 晉高祖立，妃自請為尼，不可，乃遷於至德宮。
entries.en: When Jin Gaozu rose, the consort begged to become a nun but was denied and sent to Zhide Palace.
entries.literal: When Jin Gaozu took the throne, the consort asked to become a nun but was refused; she was moved to Zhide Palace.

entries.zh: 晉遷都汴，以妃子母俱東，置於宮中，高祖皇后事妃如母。
entries.en: When Jin shifted the capital to Bian, the consort and the boy’s mother went east and were lodged in the palace; Gaozu’s empress honored the consort as a mother.
entries.literal: When Jin moved the capital to Bian, the consort and the boy’s mother went east together and were housed in the palace; Gaozu’s empress treated the consort as a mother.

entries.zh: 天福四年九月癸未，詔以郇國三千戶封唐許王從益為郇國公，以奉唐祀，服色、旌旗一依舊制。
entries.en: On guiwei in the ninth month of Tianfu 4, an edict made Congyi, Xu Wang of Tang, Duke of Xun with three thousand households to keep the Tang rites; robes and banners followed the old forms.
entries.literal: On guiwei, the ninth month of Tianfu 4, an edict enfeoffed Tang’s Xu Wang Congyi as Duke of Xun with three thousand households of Xun to maintain Tang sacrifices; dress and banners followed the old system.

entries.zh: 太常議立莊宗、明宗、湣帝三室，以至德宮為廟；
entries.en: The Ministry of Rites proposed three ancestral tablets—for Zhuangzong, Mingzong, and the Last Emperor—with Zhide Palace as the shrine;
entries.literal: The Ministry of Rites proposed establishing three spirit tablets—for Zhuangzong, Mingzong, and the Last Emperor—with Zhide Palace as the temple;

entries.zh: 詔立高祖、太宗，為五廟，使從益歲時主祠。
entries.en: an edict added Gaozu and Taizong for five shrines and put Congyi in charge of the seasonal offerings.
entries.literal: an edict added Gaozu and Taizong for five temples, with Congyi presiding at the seasonal rites.

entries.zh: 湣帝哀皇后孔氏，父循，橫海軍節度使。
entries.en: Empress Ai of the Last Emperor, Lady Kong, was daughter of Xun, military governor of Henghai.
entries.literal: The Last Emperor's Empress Ai, Lady Kong—her father Xun was military governor of the Henghai army.

entries.zh: 后有賢行，生四子。
entries.en: The empress was known for virtue and bore four sons.
entries.literal: The empress had virtuous conduct and bore four sons.

entries.zh: 湣帝即位，立為皇后，未及冊命而難作。
entries.en: When the Last Emperor succeeded she was named empress, but before the enthronement rites were finished disaster struck.
entries.literal: When the Last Emperor took the throne she was made empress, but before the enthronement rites could be completed calamity arose.

entries.zh: 湣帝出奔，后病子幼，皆不能從。
entries.en: The Last Emperor fled; the empress was sick and the children too young to follow.
entries.literal: The Last Emperor fled; the empress was ill and the children young—none could follow.

entries.zh: 廢帝入立，后及四子皆見殺。
entries.en: When the Deposed Emperor seized the throne, the empress and all four sons were put to death.
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor entered and took the throne, the empress and all four sons were killed.

entries.zh: 晉高祖立，追謚曰哀。
entries.en: When Jin Gaozu rose he posthumously named her Ai.
entries.literal: When Jin Gaozu took the throne he posthumously gave her the name Ai.

entries.zh: 明宗子
entries.en: Mingzong's Sons
entries.literal: Mingzong's Sons

entries.zh: 淑妃王氏，邠州餅家子也，有美色，號「花見羞」。
entries.en: Chaste Consort Lady Wang came from a cake-selling family in Binzhou; famed for her beauty, she was called “Flowers Hide from Shame.”
entries.literal: Shufei Lady Wang was the daughter of a cake merchant in Binzhou; she had great beauty and was called “Flowers Hide from Shame.”

entries.zh: 少賣梁故將劉鄩為侍兒，鄩卒，王氏無所歸。
entries.en: Young, she was sold as a maid to Liu Yan, once a Liang general; when Yan died, she was left with nowhere to turn.
entries.literal: In her youth she was sold as a handmaid to Liu Yan, a former general of Liang; when Yan died, Wang had nowhere to go.

entries.zh: 是時，明宗夏夫人已卒，方求別室，有言王氏於安重誨者，重誨以告明宗而納之。
entries.en: Lady Xia had just died and Mingzong sought a new consort; word of Wang reached An Chonghui, who brought her to Mingzong’s notice, and he took her in.
entries.literal: At that time Lady Xia, Mingzong’s wife, had died and he was seeking another consort; someone spoke of Wang to An Chonghui, who told Mingzong and he took her in.

entries.zh: 王氏素得鄩金甚多，悉以遣明宗左右及諸子婦，人人皆為王氏稱譽，明宗益愛之。
entries.en: Wang had amassed a great fortune from Yan and lavished it on Mingzong’s staff and his daughters-in-law; praise for her spread, and Mingzong’s affection deepened.
entries.literal: Wang had received much gold from Yan and gave it all to Mingzong’s attendants and his sons’ wives; everyone praised Wang, and Mingzong loved her all the more.

entries.zh: 而夫人曹氏為人簡質，常避事，由是王氏專寵。
entries.en: Lady Cao was plain-spoken and unassuming and usually kept out of palace business, so Wang held favor alone.
entries.literal: Lady Cao was plain and modest in character and often stayed out of affairs, so Wang had the exclusive favor.

entries.zh: 明宗即位，議立皇后，而曹氏當立，曹氏謂王氏曰：「我素多病，而性不耐煩，妹當代我。」
entries.en: When Mingzong became emperor, the court debated the empress; Cao was the rightful choice. She told Wang: “I have been sick for years and cannot endure the burden—sister, you should take my place.”
entries.literal: When Mingzong took the throne they debated making an empress; Cao was the one to be enthroned. Cao said to Wang: “I have long been ill and cannot bear trouble—sister, you should stand in my place.”

entries.zh: 王氏曰：「后，帝匹也，至尊之位，誰敢幹之！」
entries.en: Wang replied: “The empress is the emperor’s match and the highest seat under Heaven—who would dare grasp at it!”
entries.literal: Wang said: “The empress is the emperor’s equal, the most exalted seat—who would dare seize it!”

entries.zh: 乃立曹氏為皇后，王氏為淑妃。
entries.en: Cao was enthroned as empress and Wang was made Chaste Consort.
entries.literal: So Cao was enthroned empress and Wang was made Shufei.

entries.zh: 妃事皇后亦甚謹，每帝晨起，盥櫛服御，皆妃執事左右，及罷朝，帝與皇后食，妃侍，食徹乃退，未嘗少懈，皇后心亦益愛之。
entries.en: The consort served the empress with equal devotion: each dawn she attended Mingzong’s washing, combing, and dressing; after court she waited at their meals and withdrew only when they finished—never once slackening—and the empress came to love her in return.
entries.literal: The consort also served the empress with great care: each morning when the emperor rose, washing, combing, and dressing were all tended by the consort at his side; after court, when emperor and empress ate, the consort waited on them and withdrew only after the meal—never slackening—and the empress’s heart grew fond of her as well.

entries.zh: 然宮中之事，皆主於妃。
entries.en: Yet within the palace, the consort held every thread of power.
entries.literal: Yet palace affairs were all directed by the consort.

entries.zh: 明宗病，妃與宦者孟漢瓊出納左右，遂專用事，殺安重誨、秦王從榮，皆與焉。
entries.en: When Mingzong sickened, the consort and the eunuch Meng Hanqiong controlled who saw him; she ruled alone thereafter, and had a hand in the deaths of An Chonghui and Congrong, Prince of Qin.
entries.literal: When Mingzong fell ill, the consort with the eunuch Meng Hanqiong managed his access; she then held sole power, and in killing An Chonghui and Prince of Qin Congrong she played a part.

entries.zh: 劉鄩諸子，皆以妃故封拜官爵。
entries.en: Liu Yan’s sons all received titles and posts through the consort’s favor.
entries.literal: Liu Yan’s sons were all enfeoffed and given offices because of the consort.

entries.zh: 湣帝即位，冊尊皇后為皇太后，妃為皇太妃。
entries.en: When the Last Emperor succeeded, the empress became empress dowager and the consort imperial consort dowager.
entries.literal: When the Last Emperor took the throne, the empress was elevated to empress dowager and the consort to imperial consort dowager.

entries.zh: 初，明宗後宮有生子者，命妃母之，是為許王從益。
entries.en: When a consort in Mingzong’s harem bore a son, he entrusted the boy to the consort to raise—this was Congyi, Xu Wang.
entries.literal: Earlier, when a woman in Mingzong’s rear palace bore a son, he had the consort serve as foster mother—this was Xu Wang Congyi.

entries.zh: 從益乳母司衣王氏，見明宗已老而秦王握兵，心欲自托為後計，乃曰：「兒思秦王。」
entries.en: Congyi’s wet nurse, wardrobe attendant Lady Wang, saw Mingzong aging and the Prince of Qin commanding troops; scheming for her own future, she said: “The child longs for the Prince of Qin.”
entries.literal: Congyi’s wet nurse, wardrobe attendant Lady Wang, saw Mingzong was old and the Prince of Qin held troops; intending to attach herself for the future, she said: “The boy misses the Prince of Qin.”

entries.zh: 是時從益已四歲，又數教從益自言求見秦王。
entries.en: Congyi was then four; she also drilled him to beg on his own to visit the Prince of Qin.
entries.literal: By then Congyi was four; she also repeatedly taught Congyi to ask on his own to see the Prince of Qin.

entries.zh: 明宗遣乳嫗將兒往來秦府，遂與從榮私通，從榮因使王氏伺察宮中動靜。
entries.en: Mingzong sent the nurse to bring the boy to and from the Prince of Qin’s residence; she then colluded with Congrong, who set her to watch the palace.
entries.literal: Mingzong sent the wet nurse to carry the child back and forth to the Prince of Qin’s mansion; she then had secret dealings with Congrong, and Congrong used Wang to spy on palace movements.

entries.zh: 從榮已死，司衣王氏以謂秦王實以兵入宮衛天子，而以反見誅，出怨言。
entries.en: After Congrong’s death, the wardrobe attendant insisted the Prince of Qin had marched in to protect the emperor and been killed as a traitor, and she began to complain aloud.
entries.literal: After Congrong died, wardrobe attendant Wang claimed the Prince of Qin had actually entered the palace with troops to guard the Son of Heaven but was executed as a rebel, and she voiced grievances.

entries.zh: 湣帝聞之，大怒，賜司衣王氏死，而事連太妃，由是心不悅，欲遷之至德宮，以太后素善妃，懼傷其意而止，然待之甚薄。
entries.en: The Last Emperor heard, flew into a rage, and ordered the wardrobe attendant’s death; the affair implicated the consort dowager, and he turned against her. He meant to banish her to Zhide Palace, but held back lest he wound the dowager, who had always favored the consort—still, his treatment grew harsh.
entries.literal: The Last Emperor heard, was furious, and granted wardrobe attendant Wang death; the matter touched the consort dowager, so his heart was ill pleased. He wished to move her to Zhide Palace, but stopped for fear of hurting the dowager, who had always been kind to the consort—yet he treated her very coldly.

entries.zh: 從敏字叔達，為人沉厚寡言，善騎射。
entries.en: Congmin, styled Shuda, was grave, quiet, and skilled in horsemanship and archery.
entries.literal: Congmin, styled Shuda, was deep, steady, and sparing of speech, skilled in horsemanship and archery.

entries.zh: 初從莊宗為馬步軍都指揮使兼行軍司馬，明宗入立，遷皇城使、保義軍節度使，與討王都。
entries.en: He first served Zhuangzong as commander of horse and foot and army marshal; when Mingzong succeeded he became imperial city envoy and governor of Baoyi and joined the campaign against Wang Du.
entries.literal: At first he followed Zhuangzong as commander of horse and foot armies and concurrent army marshal; when Mingzong took the throne he was made imperial city envoy and military governor of Baoyi and joined the campaign against Wang Du.

entries.zh: 歷鎮橫海、義武、成德、歸德、保義、昭義、河陽，封涇王。
entries.en: He governed Henghai, Yiwu, Chengde, Guide, Baoyi, Zhaoyi, and Heyang in turn and was enfeoffed Prince of Jing.
entries.literal: He governed in succession Henghai, Yiwu, Chengde, Guide, Baoyi, Zhaoyi, and Heyang, and was enfeoffed Prince of Jing.

entries.zh: 漢高祖時，為西京留守，封秦國公。
entries.en: Under Han Gaozu he was regent of the Western Capital and made Duke of Qin.
entries.literal: Under Han Gaozu he was Western Capital regent and enfeoffed Duke of Qin.

entries.zh: 周廣順元年卒，贈中書令，謚曰恭惠。
entries.en: He died in Zhou's first year Guangshun; posthumously made Director of the Secretariat and named Gonghui.
entries.literal: He died in Guangshun 1 of Zhou; posthumously made Director of the Secretariat with posthumous name Gonghui.

entries.zh: 廢帝皇后劉氏，父茂威，應州渾元人也。
entries.en: Empress Liu, wife of the deposed emperor, was the daughter of Maowei of Hunyuan in Ying Prefecture.
entries.literal: Empress Liu of the Deposed Emperor—her father was Maowei, a man of Hunyuan in Yingzhou.

entries.zh: 后為人彊悍，廢帝素憚之。
entries.en: She was fierce and domineering by nature, and the deposed emperor had always been afraid of her.
entries.literal: The empress was by nature fierce and overbearing, and the Deposed Emperor had long feared her.

entries.zh: 初封沛國夫人，廢帝即位，立為皇后。
entries.en: She was first created Lady of Pei; when the deposed emperor acceded, she was enthroned as empress.
entries.literal: At first she was enfeoffed as Lady of Pei; when the Deposed Emperor took the throne, she was made empress.

entries.zh: 其弟延皓，少事廢帝為牙將，廢帝即位，拜宮苑使、宣徽南院使。
entries.en: Her brother Yanhao had served the deposed emperor as a guards officer in his youth; on his accession Yanhao was made commissioner of the palace parks and of the southern court of the Bureau of Palace Attendants.
entries.literal: Her younger brother Yanhao had served the Deposed Emperor in youth as a guards officer; when the Deposed Emperor took the throne, Yanhao was appointed Commissioner of the Palace Parks and Commissioner of the Southern Court of the Bureau of Palace Attendants.

entries.zh: 清泰二年，為樞密使、天雄軍節度使。
entries.en: In Qingtai 2 he was appointed commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs and military governor of the Tianxiong Army.
entries.literal: In Qingtai 2 he became Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs and military governor of the Tianxiong Army.

entries.zh: 延皓為人素謹厚，及貴而改節，以后故用事，受賕，掠人園宅，在鄴下不恤軍士，軍士皆怨。
entries.en: Yanhao had been modest and honest, but once he rose in rank he changed his conduct; relying on his sister’s position he took power, accepted bribes, seized gardens and residences, and at Ye neglected the troops, who came to hate him.
entries.literal: Yanhao had been plain and honest in character, but once elevated he changed his ways; because of his sister he wielded power, accepted bribes, seized others’ gardens and houses, and at Ye showed no care for the soldiers, so the troops all resented him.

entries.zh: 捧聖都虞候張令昭以其屯駐兵逐延皓，延皓走相州。
entries.en: Zhang Lingzhao, chief inspector of the Pengsheng command, expelled Yanhao with the troops stationed under him, and Yanhao fled to Xiangzhou.
entries.literal: Zhang Lingzhao, chief inspector of the Pengsheng command, drove Yanhao out with the garrison troops under his command, and Yanhao fled to Xiangzhou.

entries.zh: 是時，石敬瑭已反，方用兵，而令昭之亂作。
entries.en: Shi Jingtang had already rebelled and fighting was under way when Lingzhao’s revolt erupted.
entries.literal: At that time Shi Jingtang had already rebelled and war was underway when Lingzhao’s mutiny broke out.

entries.zh: 令昭乃閉城，遣其副使邊仁嗣請己為節度使。
entries.en: Lingzhao closed the city and sent his deputy Bian Rensi to ask that he be appointed military governor.
entries.literal: Lingzhao then shut the city gates and sent his deputy Bian Rensi to request that he himself be made military governor.

entries.zh: 廢帝以令昭為右千牛衞將軍，權知天雄軍府事。
entries.en: The deposed emperor appointed Lingzhao general of the Right Thousand-Bull Guards and acting administrator of the Tianxiong headquarters.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor made Lingzhao General of the Right Thousand-Bull Guards and acting administrator of the Tianxiong headquarters.

entries.zh: 已而遣范延光討之，令昭敗走邢州，追至沙河，斬之，屯駐諸軍亂者三千餘人皆死。
entries.en: He then sent Fan Yanguang against him; Lingzhao was defeated, fled to Xingzhou, was pursued to Shahe and executed, and more than three thousand mutinous garrison soldiers were killed.
entries.literal: Soon afterward he sent Fan Yanguang to attack him; Lingzhao was defeated and fled to Xingzhou, was pursued to Shahe and beheaded, and more than three thousand mutinous garrison troops were put to death.

entries.zh: 有司請以延皓行軍法，廢帝以后故，削其官爵而已。
entries.en: Officials asked that Yanhao be punished under military law, but because of the empress the deposed emperor only removed his offices and titles.
entries.literal: The authorities asked that Yanhao be dealt with under military law, but because of the empress the Deposed Emperor merely stripped him of office and rank.

entries.zh: 廢帝二子，曰重吉、重美，一女為尼，號幼澄，皆不知其所生。
entries.en: His sons bore the names Chongji and Chongmei; a daughter took vows as a nun under the sobriquet Youcheng. History does not record who bore any of them.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor’s two sons were named Chongji and Chongmei; one daughter became a Buddhist nun, styled Youcheng; none of them is known by whom they were born.

entries.zh: 廢帝鎮鳳翔，重吉為控鶴指揮使，與尼俱留京師。
entries.en: While the deposed emperor governed Fengxiang, Chongji served as commander of the Crane-Controlled Guard and stayed in the capital with the nun.
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor held Fengxiang, Chongji was commander of the Crane-Controlled Guard and remained in the capital together with the nun.

entries.zh: 控鶴，親兵也。
entries.en: The Crane-Controlled were the sovereign’s personal guard.
entries.literal: The Crane-Controlled were the emperor’s personal troops.

entries.zh: 愍帝即位，不欲重吉掌親兵，乃出重吉為亳州團練使，居幼澄於禁中，又徙廢帝北京。
entries.en: When the Min emperor acceded, unwilling to let Chongji command the personal guard, he posted Chongji to Bozhou as regimental commissioner, kept Youcheng in the inner palace, and transferred the deposed emperor to the northern capital.
entries.literal: When the Min Emperor took the throne, he did not wish Chongji to command the personal guard, so he sent Chongji out as regimental commissioner of Bozhou, kept Youcheng within the palace, and also moved the Deposed Emperor to the northern capital.

entries.zh: 廢帝自疑，乃反。
entries.en: The deposed emperor grew suspicious and rose in revolt.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor grew suspicious and rebelled.

entries.zh: 愍帝遣人殺重吉于宋州，幼澄亦死。
entries.en: The Min emperor sent agents to kill Chongji at Songzhou, and Youcheng died as well.
entries.literal: The Min Emperor sent men to kill Chongji at Songzhou, and Youcheng also died.

entries.zh: 重美，幼而明敏如成人。
entries.en: Chongmei had been clever and quick-witted from childhood, like a grown man.
entries.literal: Chongmei from childhood was bright and keen like an adult.

entries.zh: 廢帝即位，自左衞上將軍領成德軍節度使、兼河南尹、判六軍諸衞事，改領天雄軍節度使、同中書門下平章事，封雍王。
entries.en: When the deposed emperor acceded, Chongmei advanced from general of the Left Guard to military governor of the Chengde Army, concurrently grand guardian of Henan and overseer of the Six Armies and all guards; he was then transferred to military governor of the Tianxiong Army, made grand councilor, and enfeoffed as Prince of Yong.
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, Chongmei rose from General of the Left Guard to military governor of the Chengde Army, concurrently Grand Guardian of Henan and overseer of the Six Armies and all guards; he was then transferred to military governor of the Tianxiong Army, made Grand Councilor of the Secretariat and Chancellery, and enfeoffed as Prince of Yong.

entries.zh: 石敬瑭反，廢帝欲北征，重美謂宜持重，固請毋行。
entries.en: When Shi Jingtang rebelled, the deposed emperor wanted to march north; Chongmei urged caution and firmly pleaded that he not go.
entries.literal: When Shi Jingtang rebelled, the Deposed Emperor wished to campaign north; Chongmei said he should act with restraint and firmly begged him not to go.

entries.zh: 廢帝心憚敬瑭，初不欲往，聞重美言，以為然，而劉延皓與劉延朗等迫之不已，廢帝遂如河陽，留重美守京師。
entries.en: The deposed emperor feared Jingtang and at first did not want to march; hearing Chongmei, he agreed, but Liu Yanhao, Liu Yanlang, and others kept pressing him, so he proceeded to Heyang and left Chongmei to hold the capital.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor inwardly feared Jingtang and at first did not wish to go; hearing Chongmei’s words, he thought them right, but Liu Yanhao, Liu Yanlang, and others pressed him without cease, so the Deposed Emperor went on to Heyang and left Chongmei to guard the capital.

entries.zh: 京師震恐，居民皆出城以藏竄，門者禁止之。
entries.en: The capital was gripped by panic; residents fled the city to hide, and gatekeepers tried to stop them.
entries.literal: The capital was shaken with terror; residents all left the city to hide, and the gatekeepers forbade it.

entries.zh: 重美曰：「國家多難，不能與民為主，而欲禁其避禍，可乎？」
entries.en: Chongmei said, “The realm is in grave trouble; we cannot protect the people, yet would forbid them to escape disaster—how can that be right?”
entries.literal: Chongmei said: “The state is in great difficulty; we cannot act as masters for the people, yet would forbid them to flee harm—can that be right?”

entries.zh: 因縱民出。
entries.en: He therefore allowed the people to go out.
entries.literal: He therefore let the people leave.

entries.zh: 及晉兵將至，劉皇后積薪于地，將焚其宮室，重美曰：「新天子至，必不露坐，但佗日重勞民力，取怨身後耳！」
entries.en: As the Jin army neared, Empress Liu heaped firewood to burn the palace. Chongmei said, “When the new emperor arrives he will not sit in the open air; this would only waste the people’s labor later and bring hatred after our deaths!”
entries.literal: When the Jin army was about to arrive, Empress Liu piled firewood on the ground and was about to burn the palace halls. Chongmei said: “When the new Son of Heaven comes, he will surely not sit in the open; this would only later overburden the people’s strength and win resentment after death!”

entries.zh: 后以為然。
entries.en: The empress agreed.
entries.literal: The empress thought him right.

entries.zh: 廢帝自焚，后及重美與俱死。
entries.en: The deposed emperor set himself afire; the empress and Chongmei perished with him.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor burned himself; the empress and Chongmei died with him.

entries.zh: 嗚呼！
entries.en: Alas!
entries.literal: Ah!

entries.zh: 家人之道，不可不正也。
entries.en: The norms that govern household and kin must be upheld.
entries.literal: The way of the "Family" cannot fail to be set right.

entries.zh: 夫禮者，所以別嫌而明微也。
entries.en: Ritual exists precisely to dispel doubt and bring fine distinctions to light.
entries.literal: Now ritual is that whereby one separates what is suspect and makes clear what is subtle.

entries.zh: 甚矣，五代之際，君君臣臣父父子子之道乖，而宗廟、朝廷，人鬼皆失其序，斯可謂亂世者歟！
entries.en: How far things had fallen! In the Five Dynasties the reciprocal duties of ruler and ruled, father and child, collapsed together; temple and palace alike were scenes where neither men nor shades kept their station—truly an era of disorder!
entries.literal: Extreme! At the time of the Five Dynasties, the way of lord and lord, minister and minister, father and father, son and son went awry; at the ancestral temple and at court, both the living and the dead lost their proper order—this may indeed be called an age of chaos!

entries.zh: 自古未之有也。
entries.en: Nothing like it appears in the earlier record.
entries.literal: From antiquity onward there has never been such a thing.

entries.zh: 唐一號而三姓，周一號而二姓。
entries.en: The house called Tang ruled under a single dynastic name yet passed through three clans; the house called Zhou did the same with two.
entries.literal: Tang bore one reign title but three surnames; Zhou bore one reign title but two surnames.

entries.zh: 唐太祖、莊宗為一家，明宗、湣帝為一家，廢帝為一家；
entries.en: Later Tang thus falls into three bloodlines: Taizu and Zhuangzong; Mingzong and the short-reigned Min emperor; and the deposed emperor alone.
entries.literal: Tang Taizu and Zhuangzong were one family; Mingzong and the Min Emperor were one family; the Deposed Emperor was one family;

entries.zh: 周太祖為一家，世宗為一家。
entries.en: Later Zhou likewise splits in two: the line of Taizu and that of Shizong.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu was one family, Shizong was one family.

entries.zh: 別其家而同其號者，何哉？
entries.en: Why, then, does the chronicle cleave the clans yet leave the dynastic label unchanged?
entries.literal: They distinguish their families yet share the same dynastic name—why is that?

entries.zh: 唐從其號，見其盜而有也；
entries.en: For Later Tang the shared name exposes naked usurpation: each claimant seized the throne from the last.
entries.literal: For Tang, following its name shows that they stole it yet came to possess it;

entries.zh: 周從其號，與之也。
entries.en: For Later Zhou the single title marks legitimate succession: the mandate was handed down within the alliance that founded the state.
entries.literal: for Zhou, following its name means it was given to them.

entries.zh: 而別其家者，昭穆親疏之不可亂也。
entries.en: The separate "families" preserve the temple order of fathers and sons, near kin and far—lines that must not be blurred.
entries.literal: But distinguishing their families is because senior and junior generations, close and distant kin, cannot be confused.

entries.zh: 號可同，家不可以不別，所以別嫌而明微也。
entries.en: Dynastic names may repeat; agnatic lines may not. That, again, is the work of ritual: clearing doubt and marking fine shades.
entries.literal: The name may be the same; families cannot fail to be distinguished—this is to separate suspicion and clarify the subtle.

entries.zh: 梁博王友文之不別，何哉？
entries.en: Why, then, does the Later Liang record leave Bo Prince You Wen outside the neat partition of "families" that I have just defended?
entries.literal: The Prince of Bo of Liang, You Wen—why was no family distinction drawn for him?

entries.zh: 著禍本也，梁太祖之禍，自友文始，存之所以戒也。
entries.en: Because the historian means to expose the taproot: the founder of Later Liang brought ruin on himself starting with You Wen, and the deliberate ambiguity in the record is itself the lesson for posterity.
entries.literal: It is to write down the root of calamity: the calamity of Liang Taizu began with You Wen; keeping this unresolved exists in order to warn.

entries.zh: 廢帝皇后劉氏
entries.en: Empress Liu, wife of the deposed Later Tang emperor.
entries.literal: Empress Liu of the Deposed Emperor

entries.zh: 高祖皇后李氏
entries.en: Empress Li, Consort of Gaozu
entries.literal: Empress Li, Consort of Gaozu

entries.zh: 高祖皇后李氏，唐明宗皇帝女也。
entries.en: Empress Li, Gaozu’s consort, was a daughter of Tang’s Emperor Mingzong.
entries.literal: Empress Li, consort of Gaozu, was a daughter of Emperor Mingzong of Tang.

entries.zh: 后初號永寧公主，清泰二年封魏國長公主。
entries.en: She was first styled Princess Yongning; in Qingtai 2 she was made Grand Princess of Wei.
entries.literal: She was first titled Princess Yongning; in the second year of Qingtai she was enfeoffed Grand Princess of Wei.

entries.zh: 自廢帝立，常疑高祖必反。
entries.en: Once the Deposed Emperor rose, he constantly feared Gaozu would rebel.
entries.literal: From the time the Deposed Emperor took the throne, he often suspected Gaozu would rebel.

entries.zh: 三年，公主自太原入朝千春節，辭歸，留之不得，廢帝醉，語公主曰：「爾歸何速，欲與石郎反邪？」
entries.en: In the third year the princess came from Taiyuan for the Qianchun Festival; when she asked leave to go home they could not hold her. The Deposed Emperor, drunk, told the princess: “Why leave so fast—do you plan to rebel with that Shi fellow?”
entries.literal: In the third year the princess came from Taiyuan to court for the Qianchun Festival; when she took leave to return they could not detain her. The Deposed Emperor, drunk, said to the princess: “Why return so soon—do you mean to rebel with that fellow Shi?”

entries.zh: 既醒，左右告之，廢帝大悔。
entries.en: When he woke, his attendants told him what he had said, and the Deposed Emperor was filled with remorse.
entries.literal: When he sobered, those around him told him, and the Deposed Emperor deeply regretted it.

entries.zh: 公主歸，以語高祖，高祖由是益不自安。
entries.en: The princess went home and told Gaozu; from then on he felt still less secure.
entries.literal: The princess returned and told Gaozu; Gaozu was therefore all the more ill at ease.

entries.zh: 高祖即位，公主當為皇后。
entries.en: When Gaozu succeeded, the princess was to be made empress.
entries.literal: When Gaozu took the throne, the princess was to become empress.

entries.zh: 天福二年三月，有司言：「皇太妃尊號已正，請上寶冊。」
entries.en: In the third month of Tianfu 2 the court said: “The Grand Consort’s title is now settled—we beg to invest her with seal and patent.”
entries.literal: In the third month of Tianfu 2 the responsible officials said: “The Grand Consort’s honorific title has been set—we ask to present the imperial seal and patent.”

entries.zh: 太妃，高祖庶母劉氏也。
entries.en: The Grand Consort was Liu, Gaozu’s stepmother.
entries.literal: The Grand Consort was Liu, Gaozu’s stepmother.

entries.zh: 高祖以宗廟未立，謙抑未皇。
entries.en: Gaozu, the ancestral temple not yet built, was humble and deferred.
entries.literal: Gaozu, since the ancestral temple had not yet been established, was modest and held back.

entries.zh: 七年夏五月，高祖已病，乃詔尊太妃為皇太后，然卒不奉冊而高祖崩，故后訖高祖世亦無冊命。
entries.en: In the fifth month of summer, Tianfu 7, Gaozu, already failing, decreed the Grand Consort empress dowager—but died before the patent could be given, and the empress received no investiture at all in Gaozu’s lifetime.
entries.literal: In the fifth month of summer, Tianfu 7, Gaozu already ill, issued an edict honoring the Grand Consort as empress dowager; yet the patent was never delivered before he died, so the empress too received no formal investiture throughout Gaozu’s reign.

entries.zh: 出帝天福八年七月，冊尊皇后為皇太后。
entries.en: In the seventh month of Tianfu 8, under the Deposed Emperor, the empress was invested as empress dowager.
entries.literal: In the seventh month of Tianfu 8 under the Deposed Emperor, the empress was formally invested as empress dowager.

entries.zh: 太后為人強敏，高祖常嚴憚之。
entries.en: The dowager was sharp and resolute; Gaozu often feared her.
entries.literal: The dowager was forceful and shrewd; Gaozu often stood in awe of her.

entries.zh: 出帝馮皇后用事，太后數訓戒之，出帝不從，乃及於敗。
entries.en: Empress Feng, the Deposed Emperor's consort, ran affairs; the dowager warned her again and again, but the Deposed Emperor would not heed her—and ruin followed.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor's wife Empress Feng held power; the dowager repeatedly admonished her, but the Deposed Emperor would not listen—and thus came ruin.

entries.zh: 孫男臣重貴言：頃者唐運告終，中原失馭，數窮否極，天缺地傾。
entries.en: Your Majesty’s grandson and subject Chonggui speaks: Lately the Tang mandate ended, the Central Plains lost their guide, number and fortune were spent and ruin complete—Heaven gaped and Earth gave way.
entries.literal: Your Majesty’s grandson and subject Chonggui speaks: Not long ago the mandate of Tang expired, the Central Plains lost their ruler, fortune ran to its end and misfortune reached its extreme—Heaven cracked and Earth tilted.

entries.zh: 先人有田一成，有眾一旅，兵連禍結，力屈勢孤。
entries.en: My forebear held one field and one band of men; battle piled on disaster until his strength failed and he stood alone.
entries.literal: My forebear held one patch of land and one company of men; war bred calamity after calamity until his strength was broken and he stood alone.

entries.zh: 翁皇帝救患摧剛，興利除害，躬擐甲胃，深入寇場。
entries.en: Honored Imperial Father, you rescued the afflicted and broke the hard-hearted, brought profit and cleared away harm, yourself donning armor and driving deep into the enemy’s ground.
entries.literal: Honored Imperial Father, you crushed misfortune and broke stubborn foes, you raised up good and swept away harm, yourself bearing armor and plunged deep into the field of battle.

entries.zh: 犯露蒙霜，度雁門之險；
entries.en: You faced dew and frost and crossed the danger of Yanmen Pass;
entries.literal: You braved dew and frost, crossed the peril of Yanmen Pass;

entries.zh: 馳風擊電，行中冀之誅。
entries.en: like wind and thunder you struck to punish the heart of Ji.
entries.literal: like wind and lightning you raced to execute judgment in central Ji.

entries.zh: 黃鉞一麾，天下大定，勢淩宇宙，義感神明。
entries.en: One sweep of the yellow axe and the realm was settled; your might rose above Heaven and Earth, your righteousness touched the spirits.
entries.literal: At one wave of the golden battle-axe the realm was pacified; your power towered over Heaven and Earth, your righteousness moved the gods.

entries.zh: 功成不居，遂興晉祚，則翁皇帝有大造於石氏也。
entries.en: You took no reward for victory but raised the Jin throne—thus the Honored Imperial Father gave the House of Shi a new life.
entries.literal: Having achieved success you did not keep it for yourself but raised the Jin dynasty—thus the Honored Imperial Father wrought great creation for the House of Shi.

entries.zh: 晉室皇太后新婦李氏妾言：張彥澤、傅住兒等至，伏蒙皇帝阿翁降書安撫者。
entries.en: The Empress Dowager of Jin, your daughter-in-law and subject Li, speaks: Zhang Yanze, Fu Zhuer, and others have come; we humbly received the reassuring letter from the Emperor Honored Father-in-Law.
entries.literal: The Empress Dowager of the Jin house, new wife and subject Li, speaks: Zhang Yanze, Fu Zhuer, and others have arrived; we humbly received the comforting letter from the Emperor Honored Father-in-Law.

entries.zh: 妾伏念先皇帝頃在並、汾，適逢屯難，危同累卵，急若倒懸，智勇俱窮，朝夕不保。
entries.en: I remember when my late husband was at Bing and Fen, sudden hardship fell; danger stacked like eggs, urgency like a man hung upside down; wit and courage were spent and each day and night held no promise.
entries.literal: I recall that my late husband the emperor, when he was in Bing and Fen, met sudden peril; danger piled like eggs in a stack, urgency like being hung upside down; wit and courage alike were exhausted and each day and night hung by a thread.

entries.zh: 皇帝阿翁發自冀北，親抵河東，跋履山川，逾越險阻。
entries.en: The Emperor Honored Father-in-Law set out from north of Ji, came himself to Hedong, tramped over mountains and rivers, and crossed every peril.
entries.literal: The Emperor Honored Father-in-Law marched from north of Ji, came in person to Hedong, crossed mountains and rivers, surmounted every barrier.

entries.zh: 立平巨孽，遂定中原，救石氏之覆亡，立晉朝之社稷。
entries.en: He quickly put down the great scourge and settled the Central Plains, saving the House of Shi from ruin and raising the altars of Jin.
entries.literal: He swiftly crushed the great evil and settled the Central Plains, saving the House of Shi from destruction and establishing the altars of Jin.

entries.zh: 不幸先帝厭代，嗣子承祧，不能繼好息民，而反虧恩辜義。
entries.en: Alas, my late husband died; the heir took the ancestral line but could not keep peace and renew friendship—instead he wronged kindness and broke faith.
entries.literal: Alas, my late husband passed from this world; the heir took up the ancestral line but could not continue friendship and give the people peace—instead he betrayed kindness and broke faith.

entries.zh: 兵戈屢動，駟馬難追，戚實自貽，咎將誰執！
entries.en: Arms moved again and again; even four horses could not chase back what was done—sorrow was truly self-made; on whom else can blame be laid?
entries.literal: Wars rose again and again; four-horse chariots could not overtake what was done—grief was truly self-wrought; on whom else can blame fall?

entries.zh: 今穹旻震怒，中外攜離，上將牽羊，六師解甲。
entries.en: Now Heaven rages; within and without all have parted; the lords come leading sheep and the six armies cast off their armor.
entries.literal: Now Heaven’s vault thunders in wrath; within and without all have turned away; the lords bring sheep in submission and the six armies lay down their arms.

entries.zh: 妾舉宗負釁，視景偷生，惶惑之中，撫問斯至，明宣恩旨，典示含容，慰諭丁寧，神爽飛越。
entries.en: I and my whole house bear fault; we clung to life while we could. In our confusion your inquiry came; your gracious will was declared, your tolerant example shown, your comforting words repeated—and our spirits lifted.
entries.literal: I and my whole clan bear guilt; we clung to life at the sight of the sun. In our bewilderment your inquiry arrived; your gracious intent was proclaimed, your tolerant decree displayed, your soothing words repeated—and our spirits soared.

entries.zh: 豈謂已垂之命，忽蒙更生之恩，省罪責躬，九死未報。
entries.en: Who could have thought lives already forfeit would suddenly receive the gift of life again? We review our crimes and blame ourselves; nine deaths would not repay this mercy.
entries.literal: Who would have thought that lives already forfeit should suddenly receive the mercy of rebirth? We examine our sins and blame ourselves; even nine deaths could not repay this grace.

entries.zh: 今遣孫男延煦、延寶，奉表請罪，陳謝以聞。
entries.en: Now I send my grandsons Yanxu and Yanbao with this memorial to beg forgiveness and report our shame.
entries.literal: Now I send my grandsons Yanxu and Yanbao to present this memorial begging pardon, that our repentance may be heard.

entries.zh: 開運三年十二月，耶律德光已降晉兵，遣張彥澤先犯京師，以書遺太后，具道已降晉軍，且曰：「吾有梳頭妮子竊一藥囊以奔於晉，今皆在否？
entries.en: In the twelfth month of Kaiyun 3 Yelü Deguang had already taken the surrender of the Jin armies and sent Zhang Yanze ahead against the capital; he wrote the dowager, setting out how the Jin had submitted, and asked: “I had a girl who combed my hair—she stole a medicine pouch and ran off to Jin. Are they all still there?
entries.literal: In the twelfth month of Kaiyun 3 Yelü Deguang had already received the surrender of Jin troops and sent Zhang Yanze ahead to strike the capital; he sent a letter to the dowager detailing the surrendered Jin army, and said: “I had a comb-girl who stole a medicine pouch and fled to Jin—are they all still there?

entries.zh: 吾戰陽城時，亡奚車一乘，在否？」
entries.en: When I fought at Yangcheng I lost a Xi carriage—is it still there?”
entries.literal: When I fought at Yangcheng I lost one Xi cart—is it still there?”

entries.zh: 又問契丹先為晉獲者及景延廣、桑維翰等所在。
entries.en: He also asked after Khitan taken earlier by Jin, and where Jing Yanguang, Sang Weihan, and the rest might be.
entries.literal: He also asked where those Khitan previously captured by Jin were, and where Jing Yanguang, Sang Weihan, and others were.

entries.zh: 太后與帝聞彥澤至，欲自焚，嬖臣薛超勸止之。
entries.en: When the dowager and the emperor heard Yanze was coming, they prepared to die by fire; the favorite Xue Chao persuaded them to hold back.
entries.literal: The dowager and the emperor, hearing Yanze had arrived, meant to burn themselves; the favorite minister Xue Chao urged them to stop.

entries.zh: 及得德光所與書，乃滅火，出上苑中。
entries.en: Once Deguang’s letter arrived, they put out the flames and went out into the upper garden.
entries.literal: When they received Deguang’s letter, they extinguished the fire and went out into the upper garden.

entries.zh: 帝召當直學士範質，謂曰：「杜郎一何相負！
entries.en: The emperor called the duty academician Fan Zhi and said: “How Du has failed us!
entries.literal: The emperor summoned the duty academician Fan Zhi and said: “How could Du have betrayed us so!

entries.zh: 昔先帝起太原時，欲擇一子留守，謀之北朝皇帝，皇帝以屬我，我素以為其所知，卿為我草奏具言之，庶幾活我子母。」
entries.en: When my late father first raised the banner at Taiyuan, he meant to leave one son behind and asked the Khitan emperor’s counsel; the emperor chose me—I always thought he understood. Draft a memorial for me and tell the whole story plainly; perhaps it will save my mother and me.”
entries.literal: When my late father rose at Taiyuan, he wished to choose a son to remain behind and consulted the Khitan emperor; the emperor entrusted the matter to me—I always believed he knew this. Draft a memorial for me setting out all of this in full, so perhaps my mother and I may yet live.”

entries.zh: 質為帝草降表曰：
entries.en: Fan Zhi drafted a surrender memorial for the emperor:
entries.literal: Fan Zhi drafted a surrender memorial for the emperor:

entries.zh: 旋屬天降鞠凶，先君即世，臣遵承遺旨，纂紹前基。
entries.en: Then Heaven sent down grief and my late father died; I obeyed his last charge and succeeded to carry on what he had built.
entries.literal: Soon Heaven sent down calamity and my late father passed; I followed his dying command and succeeded to carry on the former foundation.

entries.zh: 諒闇之初，荒迷失次，凡有軍國重事，皆委將相大臣。
entries.en: At the start of my mourning I was dazed and without bearing; every grave matter of army and state I left to my generals and ministers.
entries.literal: In the first days of mourning I was lost and out of order; all weighty matters of state and army I entrusted to my generals and ministers.

entries.zh: 至於擅繼宗祧，既非廩命；
entries.en: Yet to take the ancestral succession on my own was no mandate from Heaven;
entries.literal: Yet to seize the ancestral line of my own accord was never Heaven’s appointed decree;

entries.zh: 輕發文字，輒敢抗尊。
entries.en: I sent out words too lightly and again and again resisted Your Majesty’s supreme will.
entries.literal: I lightly issued writs and repeatedly dared to resist Your Majesty’s supreme authority.

entries.zh: 自啟釁端，果貽赫怒，禍至神惑，運盡天亡。
entries.en: I began the breach myself and brought down your thunder; disaster arrived, the gods were troubled, my luck ran out and Heaven pronounced my fall.
entries.literal: I opened the quarrel myself and truly earned your thunderous wrath; calamity came, the spirits were confounded, my fortune was spent and Heaven decreed my end.

entries.zh: 十萬師徒，望風束手；
entries.en: A hundred thousand troops waited with bound hands at the wind of your coming;
entries.literal: A hundred thousand soldiers stood with arms bound at the mere rumor of your approach;

entries.zh: 億兆黎庶，延頸歸心。
entries.en: millions of common people stretched their necks and gave you their hearts.
entries.literal: millions upon millions of common people craned their necks and turned their hearts to you.

entries.zh: 臣負義包羞，貪生忍恥，自貽顛覆，上累祖宗，偷度朝昏，茍存視息。
entries.en: I am guilty and shamed, greedy for life and swallowing humiliation, overthrowing myself and burdening my ancestors; I crawl through each dawn and dusk, barely drawing breath.
entries.literal: I bear guilt and wrap myself in shame, clinging to life and enduring disgrace, bringing on my own overthrow and heaping shame upon my ancestors; I steal through each day and night, barely keeping breath in my body.

entries.zh: 翁皇帝若惠顧疇昔，稍霽雷霆，未賜靈誅，不絕先祀，則百口荷更生之德，一門銜無報之恩，雖所願焉，非敢望也。
entries.en: Honored Imperial Father, if you would remember old kindness and soften your thunder, withhold the stroke of punishment, and not sever our ancestral rites, then our hundred mouths would owe the debt of rebirth and our whole house would carry a gratitude beyond repayment. That is our wish, though we dare not hope for it.
entries.literal: Honored Imperial Father, if you would look back upon old ties, let your thunder roll back a little, withhold the punishing blade, and do not cut off our ancestral sacrifices—then our hundred mouths would receive the grace of renewed life and our whole house would hold an unpayable debt of gratitude. That is our humble wish, though we dare not expect it.

entries.zh: 臣與太后、妻馮氏於郊野面縛俟罪次。
entries.en: I, with the Empress Dowager and my wife Lady Feng, wait in the open fields with faces and hands bound for judgment.
entries.literal: I, together with the Empress Dowager and my wife Lady Feng, await judgment in the open country with bound hands and faces.

entries.zh: 自幽州行十餘日，過平州，出榆關，行砂磧中，饑不得食，遣宮女、從官，采木實、野蔬而食。
entries.en: More than ten days out from Youzhou, through Pingzhou and Yugu Pass, they crossed sandy wastes, starving for food; palace women and attendants gathered tree fruit and wild herbs to eat.
entries.literal: After more than ten days from Youzhou, passing Pingzhou and out through Yugu Pass, they traveled through sandy desert, starving without food; palace women and attendants gathered tree fruit and wild greens to eat.

entries.zh: 又行七八日，至錦州，虜人迫帝與太后拜阿保機畫像。
entries.en: Seven or eight days later they reached Jin Prefecture; the Khitan forced the emperor and the dowager to bow before Abaoji’s portrait.
entries.literal: After another seven or eight days they reached Jin Prefecture; the barbarians forced the emperor and the dowager to bow before Abaoji’s portrait.

entries.zh: 帝不勝其辱，泣而呼曰：「薛超誤我，不令我死！」
entries.en: The emperor could not bear the shame and wept, crying: “Xue Chao misled me—he would not let me die!”
entries.literal: The emperor could not bear the humiliation and wept, crying: “Xue Chao misled me—he would not let me die!”

entries.zh: 又行五六日，過海北州，至東丹王墓，遣延煦拜之。
entries.en: Five or six days later they passed Haibei Prefecture, came to the Prince of Dongdan’s tomb, and sent Yanxu to bow there.
entries.literal: After another five or six days they passed Haibei Prefecture, reached the tomb of the Prince of Dongdan, and sent Yanxu to pay respects.

entries.zh: 又行十餘日，渡遼水，至渤海國鐵州。
entries.en: Ten-odd days later they crossed the Liao River and reached Tie Prefecture in Bohai.
entries.literal: After another ten-odd days they crossed the Liao River and reached Tie Prefecture in the Bohai state.

entries.zh: 又行七八日，過南海府，遂至黃龍府。
entries.en: Seven or eight days later they passed Nanhai Prefecture and finally reached Huanglong Prefecture.
entries.literal: After another seven or eight days they passed Nanhai Prefecture and at last reached Huanglong Prefecture.

entries.zh: 出帝皇后馮氏，定州人也。
entries.en: Empress Feng, consort of the Fleeing Emperor, came from Dingzhou.
entries.literal: Empress Feng of the Fleeing Emperor was a native of Dingzhou.

entries.zh: 父濛，為州進奏吏，居京師，以巧佞為安重誨所喜，以為鄴都副留守。
entries.en: Her father Meng was the circuit’s memorial courier in the capital; by smooth deceit he pleased An Chonghui and was made deputy regent at Ye.
entries.literal: Her father Meng served as the circuit’s memorial courier and lived in the capital; through crafty flattery he won An Chonghui’s favor and was made deputy regent of the Ye capital.

entries.zh: 高祖留守鄴都，得濛歡甚，乃為重胤娶濛女，後封吳國夫人。
entries.en: Gaozu, regent at Ye, grew fond of Meng and had Chongyin marry his daughter; later she was made Lady of Wu.
entries.literal: When Gaozu was regent at Ye he took a great liking to Meng and had Chongyin marry Meng’s daughter; she was later enfeoffed Lady of Wu.

entries.zh: 重胤早卒，后寡居，有色，出帝悅之。
entries.en: Chongyin died young. The widow was beautiful, and the Fleeing Emperor desired her.
entries.literal: Chongyin died young; the empress lived as a widow and was beautiful, and the Fleeing Emperor was taken with her.

entries.zh: 高祖崩，梓宮在殯，出帝居喪中，納之以為后。
entries.en: Gaozu had barely died—the coffin still in state—when the Fleeing Emperor, still in mourning, took her as empress.
entries.literal: When Gaozu died and the imperial coffin still lay in state, the Fleeing Emperor, while in mourning, took her in and made her empress.

entries.zh: 是日，以六軍仗衛、太常鼓吹，命后至西禦莊，見於高祖影殿。
entries.en: That same day he sent the empress, escorted by the Six Armies and imperial music, to the Western Imperial Manor to be presented at Gaozu’s spirit hall.
entries.literal: That day, with the Six Armies in arms and the Directorate of Ceremonies’ music, he ordered the empress to the Western Imperial Manor to be presented at Gaozu’s spirit hall.

entries.zh: 群臣皆賀。
entries.en: The ministers all offered congratulations.
entries.literal: The ministers all offered congratulations.

entries.zh: 帝顧謂馮道等曰：「皇太后之命，與卿等不任大慶。」
entries.en: The emperor turned to Feng Dao and the rest and said: “The empress dowager’s command forbids me to share this great rejoicing with you.”
entries.literal: The emperor turned to Feng Dao and the others and said: “By the empress dowager’s command, I cannot share your great rejoicing with you.”

entries.zh: 群臣出，帝與皇后酣飲歌舞，過梓宮前，酹而告曰：「皇太后之命，與先帝不任大慶。」
entries.en: After the ministers left, he and the empress drank and danced. Passing the coffin he poured wine and said: “By the empress dowager’s command, I cannot rejoice with the late emperor.”
entries.literal: When the ministers withdrew, the emperor and empress drank and danced in revelry; passing before the coffin he poured a libation and declared: “By the empress dowager’s command, I cannot share great rejoicing with the late emperor.”

entries.zh: 左右皆失笑，帝亦自絕倒，顧謂左右曰：「我今日作新女婿，何似？」
entries.en: His attendants burst out laughing; the emperor himself doubled over and asked them: “How do I look as a new bridegroom today?”
entries.literal: Those beside him all lost composure and laughed; the emperor himself collapsed in mirth and, turning to his attendants, said: “How do I look as a bridegroom today?”

entries.zh: 后與左右皆大笑，聲聞於外。
entries.en: The empress and the attendants roared with laughter until the sound carried beyond the hall.
entries.literal: The empress and the attendants all laughed loudly, and the sound carried outside.

entries.zh: 后既立，專內寵，封拜宮官尚宮、知客等皆為郡夫人，又用男子李彥弼為皇后宮都押衙。
entries.en: Once enthroned she monopolized favor within the palace; every officer she raised—Shanggong, Guest Manager, and the rest—became a Lady of Commandery, and she even set the man Li Yanbi over the empress’s household guard.
entries.literal: Once enthroned, the empress held exclusive favor within; palace officers she enfeoffed as Shanggong, Guest Manager, and the like all became Ladies of Commanderies, and she even appointed the man Li Yanbi chief steward of the empress’s palace.

entries.zh: 其兄玉執政，內外用事，晉遂以亂。
entries.en: Her brother Yu ran affairs inside and outside the court, and Jin slid into chaos.
entries.literal: Her elder brother Yu held power in and out of court, and Jin was thereby thrown into disorder.

entries.zh: 契丹犯京師，暴帝之惡於天下曰：「納叔母於中宮，亂人倫之大典。」
entries.en: When the Khitan took the capital they proclaimed the emperor’s crimes to the world: “He brought his uncle’s widow into the inner palace and violated the great canon of human relations.”
entries.literal: When the Khitan invaded the capital they broadcast the emperor’s crimes to the realm, saying: “He took his uncle’s widow into the inner palace and overturned the great canon of human relations.”

entries.zh: 後隨帝北遷，哀帝之辱，數求毒藥，欲與帝俱飲以死，而藥不可得。
entries.en: She followed him north. Grieving his disgrace, she begged again and again for poison so they might die together, but none could be found.
entries.literal: Later she followed the emperor north; grieving his humiliation, she repeatedly sought poison, wishing to drink it with him and die together, but no poison could be obtained.

entries.zh: 後不知其所終。
entries.en: After that no one knew her fate.
entries.literal: Afterward their end was unknown.

entries.zh: 高祖叔父兄弟
entries.en: Gaozu’s Paternal Uncles and Brothers
entries.literal: Gaozu’s paternal uncles and brothers

entries.zh: 高祖，孝元皇帝第二子也，而敬儒為兄，疑其長子也，則於高祖屬長而親，然贈官反最後於諸弟，而高祖世獨不得追封，此又可疑也。
entries.en: Gaozu was Emperor Xiaoyuan’s second son, yet Jingru is styled elder brother—as if he were the eldest—making him Gaozu’s senior close kin; yet posthumous honors came to him last among the brothers, and under Gaozu alone he received no princely enfeoffment. That too is suspect.
entries.literal: Gaozu was Emperor Xiaoyuan’s second son, yet Jingru is called elder brother—suggesting he was the eldest son—so in relation to Gaozu he would be the senior close kin; yet posthumous offices were granted him last among the brothers, and in Gaozu’s reign alone he received no posthumous enfeoffment. This too is doubtful.

entries.zh: 重胤，高祖弟也，亦不知其為親疏，然高祖愛之，養以為子，故於名加「重」而下齒諸子。
entries.en: Chongyin was Gaozu’s younger brother—again, near or distant kin is unclear—but Gaozu loved him, raised him as a son, gave him the “Chong” name, and ranked him with his sons.
entries.literal: Chongyin was Gaozu’s younger brother—again, whether close or distant kin is unknown—but Gaozu loved him and raised him as a son, so the name carries “Chong” and he ranks with the sons.

entries.zh: 高祖叔、兄與弟敬殷、子重進，皆前即位卒，而敬威、敬德、重胤、重英，高祖反時死。
entries.en: Gaozu’s paternal uncles, elder brother, younger brother Jingyin, and son Chongjin all died before his accession; Jingwei, Jingde, Chongyin, and Chongying died when Gaozu rose in rebellion.
entries.literal: Gaozu’s paternal uncles, elder brother, younger brother Jingyin, and son Chongjin all died before he took the throne; Jingwei, Jingde, Chongyin, and Chongying died when Gaozu rebelled.

entries.zh: 高祖少子曰馮六，未名而卒，而舊說以重睿為幼子者，非也。
entries.en: Gaozu’s youngest son was Feng Liu, unnamed when he died; the old story that Chongrui was the youngest is mistaken.
entries.literal: Gaozu’s youngest son was Feng Liu, who died before receiving a formal name; the old claim that Chongrui was the youngest son is wrong.

entries.zh: 晉氏始出夷狄而微，終為夷狄所滅，故其宗室次序本末不能究見。
entries.en: The Jin house rose from humble border barbarians and was destroyed by barbarians in the end, so the order and origins of its clan cannot be fully traced.
entries.literal: The Jin clan began as humble men of the barbarian borderlands and in the end was destroyed by barbarians, so the order and origins of its imperial house cannot be fully traced.

entries.zh: 其可見者，曰高祖二叔父，一兄六弟，七子二孫，而有略有詳，非惟禍亂多故而失其事實，抑亦無足稱焉者。
entries.en: What survives shows Gaozu had two paternal uncles, one elder brother, six younger brothers, seven sons, and two grandsons—some noted in passing, some at length. Facts were lost not only to war and disorder; little here merits praise.
entries.literal: What can be seen is this: Gaozu had two paternal uncles, one elder brother, six younger brothers, seven sons, and two grandsons—some noted briefly, some in detail. It is not only that turmoil and disorder caused the facts to be lost; little here is worth praising.

entries.zh: 然粗存其見者，以備其闕云。
entries.en: Still, I preserve what can be seen, however roughly, to fill the gaps.
entries.literal: Yet I roughly preserve what can be seen, to supply what is missing.

entries.zh: 二叔父曰萬友、萬詮，兄曰敬儒，弟曰敬威、敬德、敬殷、敬赟、敬暉、重胤，子曰重貴、重信、重乂、重英、重進、重睿、重杲，孫曰延煦、延寶。
entries.en: The two paternal uncles were Wanyou and Wanyuan; the elder brother, Jingru; the younger brothers Jingwei, Jingde, Jingyin, Jingyun, Jinghui, and Chongyin; the sons Chonggui, Chongxin, Chongyi, Chongying, Chongjin, Chongrui, and Chonggao; the grandsons Yanxu and Yanbao.
entries.literal: The two paternal uncles were Wanyou and Wanyuan; the elder brother was Jingru; the younger brothers were Jingwei, Jingde, Jingyin, Jingyun, Jinghui, and Chongyin; the sons were Chonggui, Chongxin, Chongyi, Chongying, Chongjin, Chongrui, and Chonggao; the grandsons were Yanxu and Yanbao.

entries.zh: 孝平皇帝生孝元皇帝、萬友、萬詮，孝元皇帝生高祖，萬友生敬威、敬赟，萬詮生敬暉，而敬儒、敬德、敬殷、重胤皆不知其於高祖為親疏也。
entries.en: Emperor Xiaoping fathered Emperor Xiaoyuan, Wanyou, and Wanyuan; Emperor Xiaoyuan fathered Gaozu; Wanyou fathered Jingwei and Jingyun; Wanyuan fathered Jinghui; but whether Jingru, Jingde, Jingyin, and Chongyin stood near or far from Gaozu in kinship is unknown.
entries.literal: Emperor Xiaoping begot Emperor Xiaoyuan, Wanyou, and Wanyuan; Emperor Xiaoyuan begot Gaozu; Wanyou begot Jingwei and Jingyun; Wanyuan begot Jinghui; while whether Jingru, Jingde, Jingyin, and Chongyin were close or distant kin to Gaozu is unknown.

entries.zh: 敬威字奉信，唐廢帝時為彰聖右第三都指揮使，領常州刺史。
entries.en: Jingwei, styled Fengxin, commanded the third division of the Right Zhangsheng Guard under Tang’s Deposed Emperor and served concurrently as prefect of Changzhou.
entries.literal: Jingwei, styled Fengxin, was third commander of the Right Wing of the Zhangsheng Guard under Tang’s Deposed Emperor and concurrently prefect of Changzhou.

entries.zh: 聞高祖舉兵太原，謂人曰「生而有死，人孰能免？
entries.en: Hearing Gaozu had risen at Taiyuan, he said: “Life ends in death—who escapes it?
entries.literal: When he heard that Gaozu had raised arms at Taiyuan, he told others: “Born, one must die—who can escape it?

entries.zh: 吾兄方舉大事，吾不可偷生取辱，見笑一時。」
entries.en: My brother is attempting a great thing; I will not cling to life and invite shame, to be mocked for a season.”
entries.literal: My elder brother is undertaking a great affair; I cannot cling to life and invite disgrace, becoming a laughingstock for a season.”

entries.zh: 遂自殺。
entries.en: He killed himself.
entries.literal: Thereupon he killed himself.

entries.zh: 敬德時為沂州馬步軍指揮使，以高祖反誅。
entries.en: Jingde, then commander of Yizhou’s horse and foot, was executed when Gaozu rebelled.
entries.literal: Jingde was then commander of the cavalry and infantry of Yizhou and was executed when Gaozu rebelled.

entries.zh: 天福二年正月，贈敬威、敬德皆為太傅，並贈敬殷以檢校太子賓客，亦贈太傅，而不及敬儒。
entries.en: In the first month of Tianfu 2, Jingwei and Jingde were both posthumously made Grand Tutor; Jingyin received the same with the acting post of Guest of the Heir Apparent—but Jingru was passed over.
entries.literal: In the first month of the second Tianfu year, Jingwei and Jingde were both posthumously granted Grand Tutor; Jingyin was also granted Grand Tutor with the post of Acting Guest of the Heir Apparent—but Jingru was not included.

entries.zh: 七年正月，追封敬威廣王，敬德福王，敬殷通王，皆贈太尉。
entries.en: In the first month of the seventh year, Jingwei was posthumously made Prince of Guang, Jingde Prince of Fu, and Jingyin Prince of Tong; each also received Grand Commandant.
entries.literal: In the first month of the seventh year, Jingwei was posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Guang, Jingde Prince of Fu, and Jingyin Prince of Tong; all were additionally granted Grand Commandant.

entries.zh: 敬儒始以故金紫光祿大夫、檢校尚書左僕射兼御史大夫、上柱國贈太傅，而獨不得封。
entries.en: Jingru alone was first granted Grand Tutor from former Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, acting Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, concurrent Grand Censor, and Pillar of the State—yet received no princely title.
entries.literal: Jingru was first granted Grand Tutor from former Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Grand Preceptor with the Staff, Concurrent Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Pillar of the State—yet alone received no enfeoffment.

entries.zh: 出帝天福八年五月，加贈三皇叔皆為太師，而皇伯敬儒始追封宋王，亦加贈太師。
entries.en: In the fifth month of Tianfu 8 under the Fleeing Emperor, all three imperial uncles received added grants of Grand Preceptor, and the imperial elder Jingru was at last posthumously made Prince of Song, likewise raised to Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: In the fifth month of the eighth Tianfu year under the Fleeing Emperor, the three imperial uncles were all additionally granted Grand Preceptor, and the imperial elder Jingru was at last posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Song, also with additional grant of Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 敬赟字德和，少無賴，竄身民間。
entries.en: Jingyun, styled Dehe, was unruly in youth and hid among the common people.
entries.literal: Jingyun, styled Dehe, was dissolute in youth and hid among the common people.

entries.zh: 高祖使人求得之，補太原牙將。
entries.en: Gaozu sent men to find him and appointed him a Taiyuan guards officer.
entries.literal: Gaozu sent men to find him and made him a Taiyuan guards officer.

entries.zh: 即位，以為飛龍皇城使，累遷曹州防禦使。
entries.en: On accession Gaozu made him Flying Dragon imperial-city commissioner and later raised him to defense commissioner of Caozhou.
entries.literal: On accession Gaozu made him Flying Dragon imperial-city commissioner; he rose to defense commissioner of Caozhou.

entries.zh: 天福五年冬，拜河陽三城節度使。
entries.en: In the winter of Tianfu 5 he was made military commissioner of the Three Cities of Heyang.
entries.literal: In the winter of the fifth Tianfu year he was appointed military commissioner of the Three Cities of Heyang.

entries.zh: 敬赟性貪暴，高祖為擇賢佐吏輔之，而敬赟亦憚高祖嚴，未嘗敢犯法。
entries.en: Jingyun was greedy and brutal; Gaozu chose worthy aides to assist him, and Jingyun also feared Gaozu's stern rule and never dared violate the law.
entries.literal: Jingyun was greedy and violent; Gaozu chose worthy assistants to aid him, and Jingyun also feared Gaozu's severity and never dared break the law.

entries.zh: 歲餘，徙鎮保義。
entries.en: After more than a year he was transferred to Baoyi.
entries.literal: After more than a year he was transferred to Baoyi.

entries.zh: 出帝時，加同中書門下平章事，始漸驕恣。
entries.en: Under the Fleeing Emperor he was made associate chief councilor and began to grow arrogant and unrestrained.
entries.literal: Under the Fleeing Emperor he was made Associate Chief Councilor of the Secretariat and Chancellery and began to grow arrogant.

entries.zh: 帝嘗遣使者至，必問曰：「小姪安否？」
entries.en: Whenever the emperor sent envoys, he always asked: "Is my little nephew well?"
entries.literal: When the emperor sent envoys, he always asked: "Is my little nephew well?"

entries.zh: 陝人苦其暴虐，召還京師，以其皇叔不能責也，斥其元從都押衙蘇彥存、鄭溫遇以警之。
entries.en: The people of Shaan suffered under his cruelty; he was recalled to the capital. Because he was an imperial uncle whom the emperor could not punish, his original followers Chief Custodian Su Yancun and Zheng Wenyun were demoted as a warning.
entries.literal: The people of Shaan suffered under his brutality; he was recalled to the capital. Because he was an imperial uncle whom the emperor could not hold accountable, his original followers Chief Custodian Su Yancun and Zheng Wenyun were demoted as a warning.

entries.zh: 契丹犯邊，敬赟從出帝幸澶淵，使以兵備汶陽，守麻家渡，未嘗見敵，皆無功。
entries.en: When the Khitan raided the frontier, Jingyun followed the Fleeing Emperor to Chanyuan and was ordered to secure Wenyang and hold Majia Ford; he never met the enemy and won no success.
entries.literal: When the Khitan raided the frontier, Jingyun followed the Fleeing Emperor to Chanyuan and was ordered to guard Wenyang and hold Majia Ford; he never met the enemy and achieved nothing.

entries.zh: 開運元年七月，復出為威勝軍節度使。
entries.en: In the seventh month of Kaiyun 1 he was again made military commissioner of Weisheng.
entries.literal: In the seventh month of the first Kaiyun year he was again made military commissioner of Weisheng.

entries.zh: 歲餘，出帝以曹州為威信軍，授敬赟節度使。
entries.en: After more than a year the Fleeing Emperor made Caozhou into Weixin Army and appointed Jingyun its commissioner.
entries.literal: After more than a year the Fleeing Emperor made Caozhou into Weixin Army and appointed Jingyun its commissioner.

entries.zh: 在曹貪暴尤甚，久之，召還。
entries.en: At Cao he was greedier and more brutal than ever; after a long while he was recalled.
entries.literal: At Cao he was greedier and crueler than ever; after a long while he was recalled.

entries.zh: 張彥澤兵犯京師，敬赟夜走，踰城東垣，墮沙濠溺死，時年四十九。
entries.en: When Zhang Yanze's troops invaded the capital, Jingyun fled by night, climbed the eastern wall, fell into the sand moat, and drowned at forty-nine.
entries.literal: When Zhang Yanze's troops invaded the capital, Jingyun fled by night, climbed the eastern wall, fell into the sand moat, and drowned—aged forty-nine.

entries.zh: 韓王敬暉字德昭，為人厚重剛直，勇而多智，高祖尤愛之。
entries.en: Prince of Han Jinghui, styled Dezhao, was steady, upright, brave, and shrewd; Gaozu loved him above the rest.
entries.literal: Prince of Han Jinghui, styled Dezhao, was grave, upright, brave, and resourceful; Gaozu loved him especially.

entries.zh: 高祖時為曹州防禦使，以廉儉見稱，卒於官，贈太傅。
entries.en: Under Gaozu he served as defense commissioner of Caozhou, praised for integrity and thrift; he died in office and received Grand Tutor.
entries.literal: Under Gaozu he was defense commissioner of Caozhou, famed for integrity and frugality; he died in office and was granted Grand Tutor.

entries.zh: 天福八年，加贈太師，追封韓王。
entries.en: In Tianfu 8 he was additionally made Grand Preceptor and posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Han.
entries.literal: In the eighth Tianfu year he was additionally granted Grand Preceptor and posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Han.

entries.zh: 子曦嗣。
entries.en: His son Xi succeeded him.
entries.literal: His son Xi succeeded.

entries.zh: 高祖諸子孫
entries.en: Gaozu’s Sons and Grandsons
entries.literal: Gaozu’s sons and grandsons

entries.zh: 高祖李皇后生楚王重信，其諸子皆不知其母。
entries.en: Gaozu’s Empress Li bore Prince of Chu Chongxin; the mothers of his other sons are unknown.
entries.literal: Empress Li of Gaozu bore Prince of Chu Chongxin; the mothers of his other sons are unknown.

entries.zh: 當高祖起太原，重英為右衛將軍，重胤為皇城副使，居京師。
entries.en: When Gaozu rose at Taiyuan, Chongying was Right Guard general and Chongyin deputy commissioner of the Imperial City—both in the capital.
entries.literal: When Gaozu rose at Taiyuan, Chongying was Right Guard general and Chongyin was deputy commissioner of the Imperial City; both were in the capital.

entries.zh: 聞高祖舉事，匿民家井中，捕得誅之，並族民家。
entries.en: Hearing of the rebellion, they hid in a commoner’s well; seized, they were put to death, and the host family was exterminated.
entries.literal: Hearing that Gaozu had launched his enterprise, they hid in a commoner’s well; captured, they were executed, and the commoner’s household was exterminated to the last.

entries.zh: 天福二年正月，高祖為二子發哀，皆贈為太保；
entries.en: In the first month of Tianfu 2, Gaozu mourned the two sons; both received posthumous rank as Grand Guardian.
entries.literal: In the first month of the second Tianfu year, Gaozu held mourning for the two sons; both were posthumously granted Grand Guardian.

entries.zh: 並贈重進以故左金吾衛將軍贈太保。
entries.en: Chongjin, former Left Golden Guard general, was likewise posthumously made Grand Guardian.
entries.literal: Chongjin was also granted Grand Guardian from his former post as Left Golden Guard general.

entries.zh: 七年正月，皆加贈太傅，追封重英虢王，重胤郯王，重進夔王。
entries.en: In the first month of the seventh year all were raised to Grand Tutor; Chongying was posthumously made Prince of Guo, Chongyin Prince of Tan, and Chongjin Prince of Kui.
entries.literal: In the first month of the seventh year all were additionally granted Grand Tutor; Chongying was posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Guo, Chongyin Prince of Tan, and Chongjin Prince of Kui.

entries.zh: 出帝天福八年五月，皆加贈太師。
entries.en: In the fifth month of Tianfu 8 under the Fleeing Emperor, all received additional grants of Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: In the fifth month of the eighth Tianfu year under the Fleeing Emperor, all were additionally granted Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 楚王重信字守孚，為人敏悟多智而好禮。
entries.en: Prince of Chu Chongxin, styled Shoufu, was sharp, clever, and devoted to ritual.
entries.literal: Prince of Chu Chongxin, styled Shoufu, was quick-witted, clever, and fond of ritual.

entries.zh: 天福二年二月，以左驍衛上將軍拜河陽三城節度使，有善政，高祖下詔褒之。
entries.en: In the second month of Tianfu 2 he was made military commissioner of the Three Cities of Heyang from senior general of the Left Flying Cavalry; Gaozu issued an edict praising his governance.
entries.literal: In the second month of the second Tianfu year he was appointed military commissioner of the Three Cities of Heyang from Left Flying Cavalry senior general; his good governance won Gaozu’s edict of praise.

entries.zh: 是歲範延光反，詔前靈武節度使張從賓發河陽兵討延光，從賓亦反，重信見殺，時年二十。
entries.en: That year Fan Yanguang rebelled; the court ordered former Lingwu commissioner Zhang Congbin to march Heyang troops against him. Congbin rebelled too, and Chongxin was killed at twenty.
entries.literal: That year Fan Yanguang rebelled; an edict ordered former Lingwu military commissioner Zhang Congbin to raise Heyang troops against Yanguang. Congbin also rebelled, and Chongxin was killed—aged twenty.

entries.zh: 高祖欲贈重信太尉，大臣引漢故事，皇子無為三公者。
entries.en: Gaozu wished to grant Chongxin Grand Commandant; the chief ministers cited Han precedent: no imperial son had ever held one of the Three Excellencies.
entries.literal: Gaozu wished to grant Chongxin Grand Commandant; the great ministers cited Han precedent that imperial sons were not made one of the Three Excellencies.

entries.zh: 高祖曰：「此兒為善被禍，吾哀之甚，自我而已，豈有例邪！」
entries.en: Gaozu said: “This boy did good and met calamity; my grief for him runs deep. Let the rule begin with me—what need of precedent!”
entries.literal: Gaozu said: “This boy did good and met disaster; I grieve for him deeply. Let it begin with me—what need is there for precedent!”

entries.zh: 乃贈太尉。
entries.en: He was granted Grand Commandant.
entries.literal: So he was granted Grand Commandant.

entries.zh: 七年正月，加贈太師，追封沂王。
entries.en: In the first month of the seventh year he was additionally made Grand Preceptor and posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Yi.
entries.literal: In the first month of the seventh year he was additionally granted Grand Preceptor and posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Yi.

entries.zh: 出帝天福八年五月，易封楚王。
entries.en: In the fifth month of Tianfu 8 under the Fleeing Emperor, his title was changed to Prince of Chu.
entries.literal: In the fifth month of the eighth Tianfu year under the Fleeing Emperor, his enfeoffment was changed to Prince of Chu.

entries.zh: 重睿為人貌類高祖。
entries.en: Chongrui resembled Gaozu in face.
entries.literal: Chongrui in appearance resembled Gaozu.

entries.zh: 高祖臥疾，宰相馮道入見臥內，重睿尚幼，高祖呼出使拜道於前，因以宦者抱持寘道懷中，高祖雖不言，左右皆知其以重睿托道也。
entries.en: Gaozu lay ill when Chancellor Feng Dao came to his bedside; Chongrui was still small. Gaozu had the boy brought forward to bow to Dao, then a eunuch lifted him into Dao’s arms. Gaozu never spoke, but everyone present knew he was entrusting Chongrui to Dao.
entries.literal: When Gaozu lay ill, Chancellor Feng Dao entered the sickroom; Chongrui was still young. Gaozu had him brought out to bow to Dao, then had a eunuch hold him and place him in Dao’s arms. Though Gaozu said nothing, all beside him knew he was entrusting Chongrui to Dao.

entries.zh: 高祖崩，晉大臣以國家多事，議立長君，而景延廣已陰許立出帝，重睿遂不得立。
entries.en: At Gaozu’s death the chief ministers, with the realm in turmoil, debated raising an elder prince; but Jing Yanguang had already secretly pledged the throne to the Fleeing Emperor, and Chongrui was passed over.
entries.literal: When Gaozu died, Jin’s great ministers, finding the state beset by troubles, debated enthroning an elder prince; but Jing Yanguang had already secretly promised the throne to the Fleeing Emperor, and Chongrui was not enthroned.

entries.zh: 出帝以重睿為檢校太保、開封尹，以左散騎常侍邊蔚權知開封府事。
entries.en: The Fleeing Emperor made Chongrui Acting Grand Guardian and prefect of Kaifeng, with Left Regular Attendant Bian Wei acting in his stead.
entries.literal: The Fleeing Emperor made Chongrui Acting Grand Guardian and metropolitan magistrate of Kaifeng, with Left Regular Attendant Bian Wei acting in charge of Kaifeng prefecture.

entries.zh: 開運二年五月，拜重睿雄武軍節度使，歲餘，徙鎮忠武，皆不之鎮。
entries.en: In the fifth month of Kaiyun 2 he was named commissioner of the Xiongwu Army; a year later he was shifted to Zhongwu, but never reported to either command.
entries.literal: In the fifth month of the second Kaiyun year he was appointed military commissioner of the Xiongwu Army; after more than a year he was transferred to the Zhongwu command, but never went to either post.

entries.zh: 契丹滅晉，重睿從出帝北遷，後不知其所終。
entries.en: When the Khitan destroyed Jin, Chongrui followed the Fleeing Emperor north; his fate afterward is unknown.
entries.literal: When the Khitan destroyed Jin, Chongrui followed the Fleeing Emperor north; later, what became of him is unknown.

entries.zh: 壽王重乂字弘理，為人好學，頗知兵法。
entries.en: Prince of Shou Chongyi, styled Hongli, loved learning and knew military affairs well.
entries.literal: Prince of Shou Chongyi, styled Hongli, loved learning and was well versed in military arts.

entries.zh: 高祖即位，拜左驍衛大將軍。
entries.en: When Gaozu took the throne, he was made grand general of the Left Flying Cavalry.
entries.literal: When Gaozu took the throne, he was appointed Grand General of the Left Flying Cavalry.

entries.zh: 高祖幸汴州，以為東都留守。
entries.en: When Gaozu visited Bianzhou, he was made regent of the Eastern Capital.
entries.literal: When Gaozu visited Bianzhou, he was made Eastern Capital stay-behind commissioner.

entries.zh: 張從賓反，攻河南，見殺，時年十九，贈太傅。
entries.en: Zhang Congbin rebelled and attacked Henan; Chongyi was killed at nineteen and posthumously granted Grand Tutor.
entries.literal: Zhang Congbin rebelled and attacked Henan; he was killed—aged nineteen—and granted Grand Tutor posthumously.

entries.zh: 天福七年正月，加贈太尉，追封壽王。
entries.en: In the first month of Tianfu 7 he was additionally made Grand Commandant and posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Shou.
entries.literal: In the first month of the seventh Tianfu year, he was additionally granted Grand Commandant and posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Shou.

entries.zh: 出帝天福八年五月，加贈太師。
entries.en: In the fifth month of Tianfu 8 under the Fleeing Emperor, he was additionally made Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: In the fifth month of the eighth Tianfu year under the Fleeing Emperor, he was additionally granted Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 皆無子。
entries.en: He had no sons.
entries.literal: He had no sons.

entries.zh: 子楚王重信
entries.en: The Son: Prince of Chu Chongxin
entries.literal: The son, Prince of Chu Chongxin

entries.zh: 子壽王重乂
entries.en: The Son: Prince of Shou Chongyi
entries.literal: The son, Prince of Shou Chongyi

entries.zh: 子重睿
entries.en: The Son Chongrui
entries.literal: The son Chongrui

entries.zh: 子重杲
entries.en: The Son Chonggao
entries.literal: The son Chonggao

entries.zh: 陳王重杲，高祖幼子也。
entries.en: Prince of Chen Chonggao was Gaozu’s youngest son.
entries.literal: Prince of Chen Chonggao was Gaozu’s youngest son.

entries.zh: 小字馮六，未名而卒，贈太傅，追封陳王，賜名重杲。
entries.en: His childhood name was Feng Liu; he died unnamed, received Grand Tutor, was posthumously made Prince of Chen, and granted the name Chonggao.
entries.literal: His childhood name was Feng Liu; he died before receiving a formal name, was granted Grand Tutor, posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Chen, and given the name Chonggao.

entries.zh: 出帝天福八年五月，加贈太師。
entries.en: In the fifth month of Tianfu 8 under the Fleeing Emperor, he was additionally made Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: In the fifth month of the eighth Tianfu year under the Fleeing Emperor, he was additionally granted Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 延煦、延寶，高祖諸孫也，出帝以為子。
entries.en: Yansxu and Yanbao, Gaozu’s grandsons, were adopted as sons by the Fleeing Emperor.
entries.literal: Yansxu and Yanbao, grandsons of Gaozu, were taken as sons by the Fleeing Emperor.

entries.zh: 嗚呼！
entries.en: Alas!
entries.literal: Alas!

entries.zh: 古之不幸無子，而以其同宗之子為後者，聖人許之，著之《禮》經而不諱也。
entries.en: In antiquity, when a man had no son and took a kinsman’s child as heir, the sages permitted it and set it down openly in the Book of Rites.
entries.literal: In antiquity, when men were unhappily without sons and took a son of the same clan as heir, the sages permitted it and recorded it in the Book of Rites without concealment.

entries.zh: 而後世閭閻鄙俚之人則諱之，諱則不勝其欺與偽也。
entries.en: Later generations of common folk hide the matter; and hiding it, they cannot escape fraud and pretense.
entries.literal: Later generations of common folk in lane and hamlet hide it; and in hiding it they cannot escape deceit and falsehood.

entries.zh: 故其茍偷竊取嬰孩繈褓，諱其父母，而自欺以為我生之子，曰：「不如此，則不能得其一誌盡愛於我，而其心必二也。」
entries.en: So they furtively seize an infant in swaddling clothes, conceal its parents, and persuade themselves it is their own, saying: “Otherwise I cannot win its whole heart—and its heart would be divided.”
entries.literal: So they furtively steal an infant in swaddling clothes, hide its parents, and fool themselves into thinking it their own child, saying: “If I do not do this, I cannot win its whole heart’s love for me—and its heart would surely be divided.”

entries.zh: 而為其子者，亦自諱其所生，而絕其天性之親，反視以為叔伯父，以此欺其九族，而亂其人鬼親疏之屬。
entries.en: The child, too, hides its birth and cuts natural ties, treating its own parents as uncles and aunts, deceiving the nine agnates and confounding kinship among the living and the dead.
entries.literal: And the child, too, hides its birth and severs natural kinship, instead treating its natural parents as uncles and aunts, thus deceiving the nine agnates and confounding the ranks of kin among the living and the dead.

entries.zh: 凡物生而有知，未有不愛其父母者。
entries.en: Every living thing that knows loves its parents—none fails to.
entries.literal: All things born with consciousness love their parents—none do not.

entries.zh: 使是子也，能忍而真絕其天性歟，曾禽獸之不若也。
entries.en: If such a son could truly endure and kill natural feeling, he would fall below birds and beasts.
entries.literal: If such a son could endure and truly sever his nature, he would be worse than birds and beasts.

entries.zh: 使其不忍而外陽絕之，是大偽也。
entries.en: If he cannot endure yet outwardly feigns severance, that is the deepest fraud.
entries.literal: If he cannot endure yet outwardly pretends severance, that is great falsehood.

entries.zh: 夫閭閻鄙俚之人之慮於事者，亦已深矣！
entries.en: Common folk calculate such matters very deeply indeed!
entries.literal: The common folk’s calculation in such matters runs very deep indeed!

entries.zh: 然而茍竊欺偽不可以為法者，小人之事也。
entries.en: Yet furtive fraud cannot be law—that is the petty man’s way.
entries.literal: Yet furtive theft and deceit cannot serve as law—that is the way of petty men.

entries.zh: 惟聖人則不然，以謂人道莫大於繼絕，此萬世之通制而天下之公行也，何必諱哉！
entries.en: The sages are otherwise. They hold that no human duty exceeds continuing a severed line—the universal rule for all ages and the open practice of the world. Why hide it!
entries.literal: The sages are not so. They hold that nothing in human relations exceeds continuing a severed line—this is the universal rule for ten thousand generations and the public practice under Heaven. Why must it be hidden!

entries.zh: 所謂子者，未有不由父母而生者也，故為人後者，必有所生之父，有所後之父，此理之自然也，何必諱哉！
entries.en: A son is never born except of parents; one who becomes another’s heir must have both a natural father and a successor father—that is reason’s natural order. Why hide it!
entries.literal: What is called a son is never born except of parents; therefore one who becomes another’s heir must have the father who begot him and the father he succeeds—this is the natural order of reason. Why must it be hidden!

entries.zh: 其簡易明白，不茍不竊，不欺不偽，可以為通制而公行者，聖人之法也。
entries.en: What is plain and simple—neither furtive nor stolen, neither deceitful nor false—and can serve as universal rule and public practice: that is the sages’ law.
entries.literal: What is plain and simple, neither furtive nor stolen, neither deceiving nor false, and can serve as universal rule and public practice—that is the sages’ law.

entries.zh: 又以謂為人之後者所承重，故加其服以斬。
entries.en: They also hold that one who becomes another’s heir bears the weight of succession, and so his mourning is raised to the highest grade of hemp.
