entries.literal: Zhu Youqian of Liang surrendered Hezhong and Tongzhou to Jin. Liang sent Liu Yan to attack Tongzhou; Youqian called for aid, and Cunshen was sent with Li Sizhao to the rescue.

entries.zh: 河中兵少而弱，梁人素易之，且不虞晉軍之速至也。
entries.en: Hezhong’s army was small and weak. Liang had always despised it and never dreamed Jin would come so fast.
entries.literal: Hezhong’s troops were few and weak; the Liang men had always looked down on them and did not expect Jin forces to arrive so quickly.

entries.zh: 存審選精騎二百雜河中兵出擊掞壘，陽敗而走，掞兵追之，晉騎反擊，獲其騎兵五十，梁人知其晉軍也，皆大驚。
entries.en: Cunshen picked two hundred elite riders, mingled them with Hezhong troops, and hit Liu Yan’s camp. They played at defeat and ran; Yan’s men chased, and the Jin horsemen turned and cut them down, taking fifty riders. Once Liang knew Jin had arrived, panic spread through the ranks.
entries.literal: Cunshen chose two hundred crack horsemen, mixed them with Hezhong troops, and struck Liu Yan’s camp. They feigned defeat and fled; Yan’s men pursued, and the Jin cavalry wheeled and counterattacked, taking fifty of his horsemen. The Liang men knew Jin had come and were all greatly alarmed.

entries.zh: 然河中糧少而新降，人心頗持兩端，晉軍屯朝邑，諸將皆欲速戰，存審曰：「使梁軍知吾利於速戰，則將夾渭而營，斷我餉道，以持久困我，則進退不可，敗之道也。
entries.en: Hezhong’s granaries were thin and the city had only just turned; loyalties still wavered. Jin encamped at Chaoyi, and every general wanted battle at once. Cunshen said: “Let Liang see we want a quick fight and they will fortify both banks of the Wei, sever our supplies, and grind us down. Then we cannot advance or retreat. That is how armies die.
entries.literal: Yet Hezhong had little grain and had only just submitted; hearts were divided. The Jin army encamped at Chaoyi, and the generals all wanted a quick fight. Cunshen said: “If Liang learns we favor speed, they will camp on both banks of the Wei, cut our supply line, and wear us down in a long stand—then advance and retreat alike become impossible. That is the road to defeat.

entries.zh: 不若緩師示弱，伺隙出奇，可以取勝。」
entries.en: Better to slow the march, look weak, wait for a gap, and strike from nowhere. That is how victory is won.”
entries.literal: Better to slacken the march, show weakness, watch for an opening, and strike with surprise—then victory can be taken.”

entries.zh: 乃按軍不動。
entries.en: He kept the army in place.
entries.literal: So he held the army still.

entries.zh: 居旬日，望氣者言：「有黑氣，狀如鬥雞。」
entries.en: Ten days passed. A reader of vapors said: “Black vapor rises, shaped like fighting cocks.”
entries.literal: After ten days a diviner of vapors said: “There is black vapor shaped like fighting cocks.”

entries.zh: 存審曰：「可以一戰矣！」
entries.en: Cunshen said: “The moment has come!”
entries.literal: Cunshen said: “We can fight now!”

entries.zh: 乃進軍擊掞，大敗之，掞閉壁不復出。
entries.en: He marched forward and smashed Liu Yan. Yan sealed himself in his walls and would not come out again.
entries.literal: He advanced and struck Liu Yan, defeating him greatly; Yan shut himself behind his walls and did not come out again.

entries.zh: 存審曰：「掞兵已敗，不如逸之。」
entries.en: Cunshen said: “Yan is already broken. Better to let him slip away.”
entries.literal: Cunshen said: “Yan’s army is already beaten—better to let him escape.”

entries.zh: 乃休士卒，遣裨將王建及牧馬於沙苑，掞以謂晉軍且懈，乃夜遁去，存審追擊於渭河，又大敗之。
entries.en: He rested the men and sent the deputy Wang Jianji to graze horses at Shayuan. Yan took it for slackness and bolted by night. Cunshen chased him to the Wei River and broke him again.
entries.literal: He rested the troops and sent the deputy Wang Jianji to graze horses at Shayuan. Yan thought the Jin army was slackening and fled by night; Cunshen pursued to the Wei River and again defeated him greatly.

entries.zh: 張文禮弒趙王王镕，晉遣閻寶、李嗣昭等攻之，至輒戰死，最後遣存審破之。
entries.en: Zhang Wenli murdered the Zhao king Wang Rong. Jin sent Yan Bao, Li Sizhao, and others against him; one after another they fell in battle, until Cunshen was sent and broke him at last.
entries.literal: Zhang Wenli murdered Zhao king Wang Rong. Jin sent Yan Bao, Li Sizhao, and others against him; they died in battle one after another, until at last Cunshen was sent and broke him.

entries.zh: 周德威
entries.en: Zhou Dewei
entries.literal: Zhou Dewei

entries.zh: 符習，趙州昭慶人也。
entries.en: Fu Xi came from Zhaqing in Zhao prefecture.
entries.literal: Fu Xi was a native of Zhaqing in Zhao prefecture.

entries.zh: 少事趙王王镕為軍校，自晉救趙，破梁軍柏鄉，趙常遣習將兵從晉。
entries.en: In youth he served Wang Rong of Zhao as a military officer. When Jin marched to save Zhao and broke Liang at Baixiang, Zhao often sent Xi with Jin’s host.
entries.literal: As a youth he served the Zhao king Wang Rong as a military officer; he joined Jin in rescuing Zhao, broke Liang forces at Baixiang, and Zhao often sent Xi leading troops to follow Jin.

entries.zh: 晉軍德勝，張文禮弒趙王王镕，上書莊宗，求習歸趙。
entries.en: After Jin’s victory at Desheng, Zhang Wenli murdered Wang Rong of Zhao and petitioned Zhuangzong to send Xi home to Zhao.
entries.literal: Jin’s army won at Desheng; Zhang Wenli assassinated the Zhao king Wang Rong and wrote to Zhuangzong requesting Xi be sent back to Zhao.

entries.zh: 莊宗遣之，習號泣曰：「臣世家趙，受趙王恩，王嘗以一劍與臣使自效，今聞王死，欲以劍自裁，念卒無益，請擊趙破賊，報王冤。」
entries.en: Zhuangzong sent him off. Xi wept and said: “My house has served Zhao for generations, and the king once gave me a sword to spend my life in his service. Now that he is dead I mean to fall on that sword—but what good would that do? Let me strike Zhao, break the rebels, and avenge my king.”
entries.literal: Zhuangzong sent him; Xi wept aloud and said: “My family has served Zhao for generations; I received the Zhao king’s grace. The king once gave me a sword to serve with my life. Now that I hear the king is dead, I wish to use that sword on myself—but that would serve nothing in the end. I ask to strike Zhao, break the rebels, and avenge the king.”

entries.zh: 莊宗壯之，乃遣閻寶、史建瑭等助習討文禮，以習為鎮州兵馬留後。
entries.en: Zhuangzong was moved. He sent Yan Bao and Shi Jiantan to help Xi crush Wenli and made Xi acting commander of Zhenzhou’s forces.
entries.literal: Zhuangzong was impressed, then sent Yan Bao, Shi Jiantan, and others to help Xi suppress Wenli, and made Xi acting regional commander of Zhenzhou horse and foot.

entries.zh: 習攻文禮不克，莊宗用佗將破之。
entries.en: Xi besieged Wenli without success; Zhuangzong sent other commanders and broke him.
entries.literal: Xi attacked Wenli but could not overcome him; Zhuangzong used other generals to break him.

entries.zh: 拜習成德軍節度使，習辭不敢受，乃以相、衛二州為義寧軍，以習為節度使，習辭曰：「魏博六州，霸王之府也，不宜分割以示弱，願授臣河南一鎮，得自攻取之。」
entries.en: They offered Xi the Chengde command; he refused. They carved Xiang and Wei into the Yining army and made him its governor. He refused again: “Weibo’s six prefectures are a hegemon’s seat—split them and you look weak. Give me one command south of the river and I will win it myself.”
entries.literal: Xi was appointed military governor of the Chengde army; Xi declined, not daring to accept. They then made Xiang and Wei prefectures into the Yining army and appointed Xi its military governor. Xi declined, saying: “The six prefectures of Weibo are the seat of a hegemon—they should not be carved up to show weakness. Grant me one command south of the Yellow River, and I will take it myself.”

entries.zh: 乃拜習天平軍節度使、東南面招討使，習亦未嘗攻取。
entries.en: They made him military governor of Tianping and southeast pacification commissioner—but he never took a command by force.
entries.literal: He was then appointed military governor of the Tianping army and southeast pacification commissioner; Xi also never actually attacked and seized territory.

entries.zh: 後徙鎮安國，又徙平盧。
entries.en: Later he moved to An’guo, then to Pinglu.
entries.literal: Later he was transferred to command An’guo, then transferred again to Pinglu.

entries.zh: 烏震，冀州信都人也。
entries.en: Wu Zhen came from Xindu in Ji prefecture.
entries.literal: Wu Zhen was a native of Xindu in Ji prefecture.

entries.zh: 少事趙王王镕為軍卒，稍以功遷裨校，隸符習軍。
entries.en: In youth he served Wang Rong of Zhao as a common soldier, won promotion to captain, and joined Fu Xi’s command.
entries.literal: As a youth he served the Zhao king Wang Rong as a soldier, was gradually promoted to captain through merit, and was attached to Fu Xi’s army.

entries.zh: 習從莊宗於河上，而镕為張文禮所弒，震從習討文禮，而家在趙，文禮執震母妻及子十餘人以招震，震不顧。
entries.en: Xi followed Zhuangzong on the river while Wenli murdered Wang Rong. Zhen marched with Xi against Wenli, but his kin were still in Zhao. Wenli seized Zhen’s mother, wife, and more than ten children to force him over. Zhen would not look.
entries.literal: Xi followed Zhuangzong on the river; Rong was assassinated by Zhang Wenli. Zhen followed Xi against Wenli, but his family was in Zhao. Wenli seized Zhen’s mother, wife, and more than ten children to lure Zhen; Zhen paid no attention.

entries.zh: 文禮乃皆斷其手鼻，割而不誅，縱至習軍，軍中皆不忍正視。
entries.en: Wenli cut off their hands and noses, maimed but did not kill them, and sent them to Xi’s camp. No soldier could meet their eyes.
entries.literal: Wenli then cut off all their hands and noses, mutilated but did not kill them, and released them to Xi’s army. Everyone in the army could not bear to look directly.

entries.zh: 震一慟而止，憤激自勵，身先士卒。
entries.en: Zhen wept once, then checked himself. Shame hardened him; he took the van and fought at the head of the line.
entries.literal: Zhen grieved once and stopped; stirred by indignation he steeled himself and led from the front among the soldiers.

entries.zh: 晉軍攻破鎮州，震以功拜刺史，歷深、趙二州。
entries.en: When Jin broke Zhenzhou, Zhen won a prefecture for his deeds and served at Deep and Zhao in turn.
entries.literal: Jin’s army broke Zhenzhou; Zhen through merit was appointed prefect and served successively at Deep and Zhao prefectures.

entries.zh: 震為人純質，少好學，通《左氏春秋》，喜作詩，善書。
entries.en: Zhen was plain and honest. As a young man he studied the Zuo Commentary, wrote verse, and practiced calligraphy.
entries.literal: Zhen as a person was plain and sincere; in youth he loved learning, mastered the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, enjoyed writing poetry, and was skilled at calligraphy.

entries.zh: 及為刺史，以廉平為政有聲，遷冀州刺史，兼北面水陸轉運使。
entries.en: As prefect he ruled with clean hands and a fair scale and won a name for it. He became prefect of Ji and north water-and-land transport commissioner.
entries.literal: When he became prefect he governed with integrity and fairness and won renown; he was transferred to Ji prefecture and concurrently made north water-and-land transport commissioner.

entries.zh: 明宗聞其名，擢拜河北道副招討使，領寧國軍節度使，代房知溫戍於盧臺軍。
entries.en: Mingzong heard of him, made him deputy Hebei pacification commissioner and military governor of Ningguo, and sent him to Lutai in Fang Zhiwen’s place.
entries.literal: Mingzong heard his name, promoted him to deputy Hebei pacification commissioner, made him military governor of the Ningguo army, and had him replace Fang Zhiwen garrisoning at Lutai.

entries.zh: 始至而戍兵龍至等作亂，見殺，贈太師。
entries.en: He had barely arrived when Long Zhi and other garrison troops mutinied and killed him. He was posthumously made Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: He had just arrived when garrison soldiers Long Zhi and others rebelled; he was killed. He was posthumously enfeoffed as Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 晉高祖有異志，三司財貨在太原者，延朗悉調取之，高祖深以為恨。
entries.en: Gaozu of Later Jin already nursed designs of his own. Yanlang seized every coin and store the Three Departments had at Taiyuan, and Gaozu never forgave him.
entries.literal: Gaozu of Later Jin harbored ambitions of his own; all the Three Departments’ goods stored at Taiyuan Yanlang requisitioned in full, and Gaozu deeply resented it.

entries.zh: 晉兵起，廢帝欲親征，而心畏高祖，遲疑不決，延朗與劉延朗等勸帝必行。
entries.en: When Jin’s armies rose, the deposed emperor meant to take the field himself—but he feared Gaozu and hung back. Yanlang, Liu Yanlang, and others pressed him to march.
entries.literal: When Jin troops rose, the deposed emperor wished to lead the campaign in person but feared Gaozu and hesitated; Yanlang together with Liu Yanlang and others urged the emperor that he must go.

entries.zh: 延朗籍諸道民為丁及括其馬，丁馬未至，晉兵入京師，高祖得延朗，殺之。
entries.en: Yanlang drafted men from every circuit and seized their horses. Before either men or mounts arrived, Jin troops were already in the capital. Gaozu took Yanlang and killed him.
entries.literal: Yanlang registered men from all circuits as conscripts and requisitioned their horses; before the conscripts and horses arrived, Jin troops entered the capital; Gaozu seized Yanlang and executed him.

entries.zh: 李嚴，幽州人也，初名讓坤。
entries.en: Li Yan came from Youzhou; he was first called Rangkun.
entries.literal: Li Yan was a man of Youzhou; his original name was Rangkun.

entries.zh: 事劉守光為刺史，後事莊宗為客省使。
entries.en: He served Liu Shouguang as regional inspector, then Zhuangzong as commissioner of the guest bureau.
entries.literal: He served Liu Shouguang as regional inspector, later served Zhuangzong as commissioner of the guest bureau.

entries.zh: 嚴為人明敏多藝能，習騎射，頗知書而辯。
entries.en: Bright and quick, he mastered many crafts, rode and shot well, read widely, and spoke with force.
entries.literal: Yan was bright and quick, skilled in many arts; he practiced mounted archery, knew books well, and was eloquent.

entries.zh: 同光三年，使於蜀，為王衍陳唐興復功德之盛，音辭清亮，蜀人聽之皆竦動。
entries.en: In Tongguang 3 (925) he went to Shu as envoy and before Wang Yan laid out the glory of Tang’s restoration. His voice rang clear; every Shu listener felt a shiver run through him.
entries.literal: In the third year of Tongguang he was sent as envoy to Shu; before Wang Yan he set forth the splendor of Tang’s restoration; his voice and words were clear and ringing, and Shu people who heard him were all stirred.

entries.zh: 衍樞密使宋光嗣召嚴置酒，從容問中國事。
entries.en: Wang Yan’s chief of military affairs, Song Guangsi, called Yan to wine and, at ease, asked how things stood in the Central Realm.
entries.literal: Wang Yan’s chief of military affairs Song Guangsi summoned Yan for wine and leisurely asked about affairs in the Central Realm.

entries.zh: 嚴對曰：「前年天子建大號於鄴宮，自鄆趨汴，定天下不旬日，而梁之降兵猶三十萬，東漸於海，西極甘涼，北懾幽陵，南逾閩嶺，四方萬里，莫不臣妾。
entries.en: Yan answered: “Two years ago the Son of Heaven took the great title at Ye. From Yunzhou he drove on to Bian and settled the realm in less than ten days—and Liang’s surrendered troops still numbered three hundred thousand. East to the sea, west to Gan and Liang, north to You and Ling, south beyond Min Ridge: for ten thousand li in every direction, all bowed as subjects.
entries.literal: Yan answered: “Two years ago the Son of Heaven raised the great title at the palace in Ye; from Yan he raced to Bian and settled the realm in less than ten days, and Liang’s surrendered troops still numbered three hundred thousand. East to the sea, west to Gan and Liang, north to You and Ling, south beyond Min Ridge—within ten thousand li on every side, none did not bow as subject.

entries.zh: 而淮南楊氏承累世之強，鳳翔李公恃先朝之舊，皆遣子入侍，稽首稱藩。
entries.en: The Yangs of Huainan, heirs to generations of power, and Lord Li of Fengxiang, leaning on old ties to the throne, both sent sons to court to serve and bowed as vassals.
entries.literal: Yet the Yang clan of Huainan, inheriting generations of strength, and Lord Li of Fengxiang, relying on ties from the former dynasty, both sent sons to court to serve and bowed as vassals.

entries.zh: 至荊、湖、吳越，修貢賦，效珍奇，願自比於列郡者，至無虛月。
entries.en: Jing, Hu, Wu, and Yue sent tribute and curiosities, asking to be counted no more than common prefectures—not a month passed without gifts.
entries.literal: As for Jing, Hu, Wu, and Yue, they sent tribute and rare goods, seeking to rank themselves with ordinary commanderies—not a month passed without it.

entries.zh: 天子方懷之以德，而震之以威，天下之勢，不得不一也。」
entries.en: The Son of Heaven now draws them with kindness and shakes them with force. The realm’s drift is toward unity, and nothing can turn it back.”
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven now treats them with virtue and awes them with might—the trend of the realm must inevitably become one.”

entries.zh: 光嗣曰：「荊、湖、吳越非吾所知，若鳳翔則蜀之姻親也，其人反覆，其可信乎？
entries.en: Guangsi said: “Jing, Hu, Wu, and Yue I cannot speak for. But Fengxiang is Shu’s kin by marriage—and kin who shift with every wind. Can you trust them?
entries.literal: Guangsi said: “Jing, Hu, Wu, and Yue I do not know; but Fengxiang is Shu’s kin by marriage—those people turn and turn again; can they be trusted?

entries.zh: 又聞契丹日益強盛，大國其可無慮乎？」
entries.en: And I hear the Khitan grow stronger every day. Should a great power not worry?”
entries.literal: I also hear the Khitan grow stronger day by day—can a great state have no concern?”

entries.zh: 嚴曰：「契丹之強，孰與偽梁？」
entries.en: Yan said: “Tell me—which is stronger, Khitan or false Liang?”
entries.literal: Yan said: “Which is stronger, the Khitan or the false Liang?”

entries.zh: 光嗣曰：「比梁差劣爾！」
entries.en: Guangsi said: “A little weaker than Liang, that is all!”
entries.literal: Guangsi said: “Compared to Liang they are somewhat weaker!”

entries.zh: 嚴曰：「唐滅梁如拉朽，況其不及乎！
entries.en: Yan said: “Tang broke Liang like pulling rotten timber. These are less still!
entries.literal: Yan said: “Tang destroyed Liang like pulling rotten wood—how much less these!

entries.zh: 唐兵布天下，發一鎮之眾，可以滅虜使無類。
entries.en: Tang soldiers cover the land. Raise one circuit’s host and you could wipe the barbarians from the earth.
entries.literal: Tang troops fill the realm; mobilize one circuit’s forces and you could wipe out the barbarians without leaving one alive.

entries.zh: 然而天生四夷，不在九州之內，自前古王者，皆存而不論，蓋不欲窮兵黷武也。」
entries.en: Yet Heaven set the Four Barbarians beyond the Nine Provinces. From the earliest kings, wise rulers let them be and never spoke of finishing them off—because no throne should drown the realm in endless war."
entries.literal: Yet the Four Barbarians were born by Heaven outside the Nine Provinces; from ancient kings onward all left them be and did not speak of conquering them—surely because they wished not to exhaust armies in endless war."

entries.zh: 蜀人聞嚴應對，愈益奇之。
entries.en: Shu listeners who heard Yan’s answers thought him stranger and more formidable than before.
entries.literal: Shu people who heard Yan’s replies found him even more extraordinary.

entries.zh: 冬，魏王繼岌西伐，以嚴為三川招討使，與康延孝以兵五千先行，所過州縣皆迎降。
entries.en: That winter the Prince of Wei marched west on Shu. Yan was named Three Rivers suppression commissioner and with Kang Yanxiao took five thousand men ahead. Every prefecture and county they reached opened its gates.
entries.literal: In winter the Prince of Wei marched west against Shu; Yan was made Three Rivers suppression commissioner and with Kang Yanxiao led five thousand men ahead; every prefecture and county they passed welcomed and surrendered.

entries.zh: 延孝至漢州，王衍告曰：「得李嚴來即降。」
entries.en: When Yanxiao reached Han prefecture, Wang Yan sent word: “Send Li Yan and I surrender at once.”
entries.literal: When Yanxiao reached Han prefecture, Wang Yan sent word: “If Li Yan comes, I will surrender at once.”

entries.zh: 眾皆以伐蜀之謀自嚴始，而衍怨嚴深，不宜往。
entries.en: Everyone said the war on Shu had begun with Yan, and Wang Yan hated him bitterly—he should not go.
entries.literal: All said the plan to attack Shu began with Yan, and Yan bore Wang Yan’s deep hatred—not fitting for him to go.

entries.zh: 嚴聞之喜，即馳騎入益州。
entries.en: Yan heard and was glad. He galloped straight into Yizhou.
entries.literal: Yan heard and rejoiced, immediately galloped into Yizhou.

entries.zh: 衍見嚴，以妻母為托，即日以蜀降。
entries.en: Wang Yan met Yan, entrusted wife and mother to his care, and that day Shu surrendered.
entries.literal: Wang Yan met Yan, entrusted wife and mother to him, and that same day Shu surrendered.

entries.zh: 嚴還，明宗以為泗州防禦使，客省使如故。
entries.en: When Yan returned, Mingzong made him defense commissioner of Sizhou and kept him as guest bureau commissioner.
entries.literal: When Yan returned, Mingzong made him defense commissioner of Sizhou, guest bureau commissioner as before.

entries.zh: 是時，蜀之君臣皆庸暗，而恃險自安，窮極奢僭。
entries.en: Shu’s court was dull and small-minded, trusting its mountains for safety while luxury ran to excess.
entries.literal: At that time Shu’s lord and ministers were all mediocre and dim, trusting in natural barriers for security, extravagance pushed to the utmost.

entries.zh: 嚴自蜀還，具言可取之狀。
entries.en: When Yan came back from Shu, he laid out in detail how the state could be taken.
entries.literal: When Yan returned from Shu, he fully described how Shu could be taken.

entries.zh: 初，莊宗遣嚴以名馬入蜀，市珍奇以充後宮，而蜀法嚴禁以奇貨出劍門，其非奇物而出者，名曰「入草物」，由是嚴無所得而還，惟得金二百兩、地衣、毛布之類。
entries.en: Zhuangzong had first sent Yan into Shu with fine horses to buy treasures for the inner palace. Shu forbade precious goods from passing Sword Gate; anything ordinary enough to leave was called “grass-bound goods.” Yan came back with almost nothing—two hundred taels of gold, moss cloth, hair-felt, and little else.
entries.literal: At first Zhuangzong had sent Yan into Shu with famous horses to buy rare goods for the inner palace; Shu law strictly forbade sending precious goods out through Sword Gate, and whatever was not precious enough to be barred was called “entering-the-grass goods”; thus Yan obtained nothing on the return journey save two hundred taels of gold, moss cloth, and hair-felt and the like.

entries.zh: 莊宗聞之，大怒曰：「物歸中國，謂之『入草』，王衍其能免為『入草人』乎？」
entries.en: Zhuangzong heard and raged: “Treasure bound for the Central Realm is ‘going into the grass.’ Can Wang Yan himself escape becoming grass-bound flesh?”
entries.literal: Zhuangzong heard and raged: “Goods returning to the Central Realm are called ‘going into the grass’—can Wang Yan escape becoming a ‘man who goes into the grass’?”

entries.zh: 於是決議伐蜀。
entries.en: And so they resolved to march on Shu.
entries.literal: Thus they resolved to campaign against Shu.

entries.zh: 毛璋，滄州人也。
entries.en: Mao Zhang came from Cangzhou.
entries.literal: Mao Zhang was a man of Cangzhou.

entries.zh: 梁末，戴思遠為橫海軍節度使，璋事思遠為軍校。
entries.en: At Liang’s end Dai Siyuan held Henghai. Zhang served him as a camp officer.
entries.literal: At the end of Liang, Dai Siyuan was military governor of the Henghai army; Zhang served Siyuan as a camp officer.

entries.zh: 晉已下魏博，思遠棄滄州出奔，璋以滄州降晉，以功為貝州刺史。
entries.en: After Jin took Weibo, Siyuan abandoned Cangzhou and fled. Zhang surrendered Cangzhou to Jin and for his deed was made prefect of Bei.
entries.literal: After Jin took Weibo, Siyuan abandoned Cangzhou and fled; Zhang surrendered Cangzhou to Jin and for merit was made prefect of Bei.

entries.zh: 璋為人有膽勇，自晉與梁相拒河上，璋累戰有功。
entries.en: Zhang was bold and brave. From the day Jin and Liang faced each other on the river he fought again and again with credit.
entries.literal: Zhang was bold and brave; from the time Jin and Liang faced each other on the river Zhang fought repeatedly with merit.

entries.zh: 莊宗滅梁，拜璋華州節度使。
entries.en: When Zhuangzong broke Liang, Zhang was made military governor of Hua.
entries.literal: When Zhuangzong destroyed Liang, Zhang was appointed military governor of Hua.

entries.zh: 在鎮多不法，議者疑其有異志，乃徙璋鎮昭義。
entries.en: In office he broke the law often. Critics suspected disloyalty, and he was moved to Zhaoyi.
entries.literal: At his post he committed many unlawful acts; critics suspected he harbored disloyal intent, and he was transferred to govern Zhaoyi.

entries.zh: 璋初欲拒命，其判官邊蔚切諫諭之，乃聽命。
entries.en: At first Zhang meant to refuse the transfer. His aide Bian Wei argued him down, and he obeyed.
entries.literal: At first Zhang wished to refuse the order; his aide Bian Wei urgently remonstrated and persuaded him, and he accepted.

entries.zh: 璋累歷藩鎮，又在華州得魏王繼岌伐蜀余貲，既富而驕，益為淫侈。
entries.en: Zhang had held one frontier post after another. At Hua he also took the Prince of Wei’s leftover spoils from the Shu campaign. Wealth made him proud, and his excess grew worse.
entries.literal: Zhang had served repeatedly as military governor; at Hua he also obtained the surplus funds from the Prince of Wei’s campaign against Shu; once rich he grew proud and more licentious and extravagant.

entries.zh: 嘗服赭袍飲酒，使其所得蜀奴為王衍宮中之戲於前。
entries.en: Once he drank in a vermilion robe and made his Shu slaves perform Wang Yan’s palace shows before him.
entries.literal: He once wore a vermilion robe while drinking wine and had the Shu slaves he had taken perform the palace entertainments of Wang Yan before him.

entries.zh: 明宗聞而惡之，召為金吾上將軍。
entries.en: Mingzong heard and loathed it. He recalled Zhang to be Grand General of the Golden Guard.
entries.literal: Mingzong heard and detested it; he summoned Zhang to be Grand General of the Golden Guard.

entries.zh: 東川董璋上書言璋遣子廷赟持書往西川，疑其有奸。
entries.en: Dong Zhang of Dongchuan wrote that Zhang had sent his son Tingyun west to Xichuan with a letter, and suspected treason.
entries.literal: Dong Zhang of Dongchuan memorialized that Zhang had sent his son Tingyun with a letter to Xichuan, suspecting treachery.

entries.zh: 明宗乃遣人追還廷赟，並璋下御史獄。
entries.en: Mingzong sent men to bring Tingyun back and threw Zhang into the censor’s prison.
entries.literal: Mingzong then sent men to bring Tingyun back and also cast Zhang into the censor’s prison.

entries.zh: 廷赟款稱實璋假子，有叔父在蜀，欲往省之，而無私書。
entries.en: Tingyun confessed he was Zhang’s adopted son. He had an uncle in Shu and meant only to visit him. There was no secret letter.
entries.literal: Tingyun confessed that he was in truth Zhang’s adopted son; he had an uncle in Shu and wished to visit him, and there was no private letter.

entries.zh: 璋無罪名，有司議：「璋前任藩鎮，陰畜異圖，及處班行，不慎行止。」
entries.en: No crime could be pinned on Zhang. The officials ruled: “As military governor he secretly nursed disloyal designs; in court rank he was careless in conduct.”
entries.literal: Zhang had no chargeable crime; the officials deliberated: “In his former military governorship Zhang secretly nourished disloyal designs; in court rank he was careless in conduct.”

entries.zh: 乃停璋見任官，勒還私第。
entries.en: He was removed from office and sent home.
entries.literal: He was stripped of his current office and ordered back to his private residence.

entries.zh: 朱弘昭，太原人也。
entries.en: Zhu Hongzhao came from Taiyuan.
entries.literal: Zhu Hongzhao was a native of Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 少事明宗為客將，明宗即位，為文思使。
entries.en: As a young man he served Mingzong as a guest officer. When Mingzong became emperor, he was made commissioner of the Bureau of Literary Thought.
entries.literal: In youth he served Mingzong as a guest officer; when Mingzong took the throne, he became commissioner of the Bureau of Literary Thought.

entries.zh: 與安重誨有隙，故常使於外。
entries.en: He feuded with An Chonghui and was therefore kept on duty outside the capital.
entries.literal: He was at odds with An Chonghui, so he was often sent on missions abroad.

entries.zh: 董璋為東川節度使，乃以弘昭為副使。
entries.en: Dong Zhang held Dongchuan as military governor; Hongzhao was appointed his deputy.
entries.literal: When Dong Zhang was military governor of Dongchuan, Hongzhao was made his deputy commissioner.

entries.zh: 西川孟知祥殺其監軍李嚴，弘昭大懼，求還京師，璋不許，遂相猜忌，弘昭益開懷待之不疑，璋頗重其為人。
entries.en: Meng Zhixiang of Xichuan killed the army supervisor Li Yan. Hongzhao was terrified and begged to return to court, but Dong Zhang refused. Suspicion grew between them—yet Hongzhao treated him openly and without mistrust, and Zhang came to respect him.
entries.literal: In Xichuan Meng Zhixiang killed the army supervisor Li Yan. Hongzhao was greatly afraid and asked to return to the capital, but Zhang would not allow it. They grew mutually suspicious. Hongzhao then opened his heart and treated Zhang without suspicion, and Zhang came to respect his character.

entries.zh: 後璋有軍事，遣弘昭入朝，弘昭乃免。
entries.en: Later Dong Zhang sent him to court on official business, and Hongzhao was able to leave.
entries.literal: Later, when Zhang had military affairs, he sent Hongzhao to court on tribute duty, and Hongzhao thus escaped.

entries.zh: 遷左衛大將軍內客省使、宣徽南院使、鳳翔節度使。
entries.en: He rose to Grand General of the Left Guard, commissioner of the Inner Service Bureau and of the Southern Palace Secretariat, and military governor of Fengxiang.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Grand General of the Left Guard, commissioner of the Inner Service Bureau, commissioner of the Southern Bureau of the Palace Secretariat, and military governor of Fengxiang.

entries.zh: 孟知祥反，石敬瑭伐蜀，久無功，明宗遣安重誨督軍。
entries.en: When Meng Zhixiang rebelled, Shi Jingtang’s campaign against Shu dragged on without success. Mingzong sent An Chonghui to take charge of the army.
entries.literal: Meng Zhixiang rebelled; Shi Jingtang campaigned against Shu without success for a long time. Mingzong sent An Chonghui to supervise the army.

entries.zh: 是時重誨已有間。
entries.en: By then Chonghui had already fallen from favor.
entries.literal: By then Chonghui was already estranged from the throne.

entries.zh: 重誨至鳳翔，弘昭迎謁，禮甚恭，延重誨於家，使其妻妾侍飲食。
entries.en: Chonghui reached Fengxiang. Hongzhao received him with elaborate courtesy, entertained him at home, and had his wife and concubines serve food and drink.
entries.literal: When Chonghui reached Fengxiang, Hongzhao went out to meet him with great courtesy, entertained him at home, and had his wife and concubines serve food and drink.

entries.zh: 重誨以弘昭厚己，酒酣，具言蒙天子厚恩，而所以讒間之端，因泣下。
entries.en: Hongzhao had been lavish toward him. Deep in wine, Chonghui spoke of the emperor’s kindness and of how slander had come between them—and wept.
entries.literal: Because Hongzhao had treated him generously, when the wine was deep Chonghui spoke at length of the emperor’s great grace toward him and of the origins of the slander that had set them at odds, and wept.

entries.zh: 弘昭即奏言重誨怨望，又陰遣人馳告敬瑭，使拒重誨。
entries.en: Hongzhao at once reported that Chonghui was disaffected, and secretly sent riders to urge Jingtang to defy him.
entries.literal: Hongzhao immediately memorialized that Chonghui harbored resentment, and also secretly sent men in haste to tell Jingtang to resist Chonghui.

entries.zh: 會敬瑭以糧餉不繼，遽燒營返軍。
entries.en: Jingtang’s supplies failed; he burned the camps and marched home.
entries.literal: Just then Jingtang, because provisions would not follow, suddenly burned the camps and turned the army back.

entries.zh: 重誨亦以被讒召還，過鳳翔，弘昭閉門不納，重誨由此得罪死。
entries.en: Chonghui was recalled on charges of disloyalty. At Fengxiang, Hongzhao shut him out. That was how Chonghui fell and died.
entries.literal: Chonghui too was recalled because of slander. Passing Fengxiang, Hongzhao shut his gates and would not admit him. From this Chonghui was condemned and died.

entries.zh: 樞密使範延光尤惡弘昭為人，罷為左武衛上將軍、宣徽南院使。
entries.en: Fan Yanguang, chief councillor, detested Hongzhao and had him reduced to Senior General of the Left Martial Guard and commissioner of the Southern Palace Secretariat.
entries.literal: Chief Councillor Fan Yanguang especially hated Hongzhao’s character and had him demoted to Senior General of the Left Martial Guard and commissioner of the Southern Palace Secretariat.

entries.zh: 久之，為山南東道節度使。
entries.en: In time he was made military governor of Shannan East Circuit.
entries.literal: After a long while he became military governor of Shannan East Circuit.

entries.zh: 是時，明宗已病，而秦王從榮禍起有端，唐諸大臣皆欲引去以避禍。
entries.en: Mingzong was ill, and the Prince of Qin Congrong’s rebellion was taking shape. Tang’s senior ministers all wanted to leave court to escape what was coming.
entries.literal: By then Mingzong was already ill, and trouble with the Prince of Qin, Congrong, was beginning to show. The great ministers of Tang all wished to withdraw to avoid disaster.

entries.zh: 樞密使範延光、趙延壽日夕更見，涕泣求去，明宗怒而不許。
entries.en: Fan Yanguang and Zhao Yanshou pleaded day and night, weeping to be released; Mingzong refused in anger.
entries.literal: Chief councillors Fan Yanguang and Zhao Yanshou saw the emperor day and night in turn, weeping and begging to go; Mingzong was angry and would not allow it.

entries.zh: 延壽使其妻興平公主入言於中，延光亦因孟漢瓊、王淑妃進說，故皆得罷。
entries.en: Yanshou’s wife, the Princess of Xingping, pleaded inside the palace; Yanguang won the same through Meng Hanqiong and Consort Wang. Both left office.
entries.literal: Yanshou had his wife, the Princess of Xingping, speak within the palace; Yanguang also advanced his case through Meng Hanqiong and Consort Wang. Thus both were dismissed.

entries.zh: 以弘昭及馮赟代延壽、延光，弘昭入見，辭曰：「臣廝養之才，不足當大任。」
entries.en: Hongzhao and Feng Yun took their places. Hongzhao appeared and declined: “I am only menial stock—unfit for such a post.”
entries.literal: Hongzhao and Feng Yun replaced Yanshou and Yanguang. When Hongzhao came to audience he declined, saying: “Your servant has only the talent of a menial—unfit for great responsibility.”

entries.zh: 明宗叱之曰：「公等皆不欲在吾目前邪？
entries.en: Mingzong snapped: “Do you all refuse to remain in my sight?
entries.literal: Mingzong rebuked him: “Do you gentlemen all refuse to stay before my eyes?

entries.zh: 吾養公等安用！」
entries.en: What use are you to me then!”
entries.literal: What use are you to me if I keep you!”

entries.zh: 弘昭惶恐，乃視事。
entries.en: Hongzhao, terrified, accepted the post.
entries.literal: Hongzhao was afraid and took up his duties.

entries.zh: 馮贇者，亦太原人也。
entries.en: Feng Yun too came from Taiyuan.
entries.literal: Feng Yun was also a native of Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 其父璋，事明宗為閽者。
entries.en: His father Zhang had been a gatekeeper in Mingzong’s service.
entries.literal: His father Zhang had served Mingzong as a gatekeeper.

entries.zh: 赟為兒時，以通黠為明宗所愛。
entries.en: As a boy Yun’s quick wit won Mingzong’s favor.
entries.literal: When Yun was a boy, his cleverness won Mingzong’s affection.

entries.zh: 明宗為節度使，以赟為進奏官。
entries.en: While Mingzong was still a military governor, he made Yun his memorial courier.
entries.literal: When Mingzong was military governor, he made Yun his memorial courier.

entries.zh: 明宗即位，即為客省使、宣徽北院使。
entries.en: At Mingzong’s accession Yun became commissioner of the Guest Bureau and of the Northern Palace Secretariat.
entries.literal: When Mingzong took the throne, Yun at once became commissioner of the Guest Bureau and of the Northern Palace Secretariat.

entries.zh: 歷河東忠武節度使、三司使。
entries.en: He later governed Hedong and Zhongwu and headed the Three Departments.
entries.literal: He served successively as military governor of Hedong and Zhongwu and as commissioner of the Three Departments.

entries.zh: 明宗病甚，大臣稀復進見，而孟漢瓊、王淑妃用事，弘昭及赟並掌機務於中，大事皆決此四人。
entries.en: Mingzong lay dying; ministers seldom gained audience. Meng Hanqiong and Consort Wang ran affairs. Hongzhao and Yun held the inner councils, and these four decided everything of weight.
entries.literal: When Mingzong was gravely ill, ministers rarely saw him again. Meng Hanqiong and Consort Wang held power. Hongzhao and Yun together handled affairs within the palace, and all great matters were decided by these four.

entries.zh: 及殺秦王而立湣帝，益自以為功。
entries.en: After killing the Prince of Qin and raising Emperor Min, they counted the deed their greatest triumph.
entries.literal: After they killed the Prince of Qin and enthroned Emperor Min, they thought their merit still greater.

entries.zh: 又其所用多非其人，給事中陳乂，為人險譎，好陰謀，嘗事梁張漢傑，又事郭崇韜，兩人皆輒敗死，弘昭乃引以為樞密直學士，而用其謀。
entries.en: They staffed posts with the wrong men. Chen Yi, a supervisory attendant, was devious and loved intrigue. He had served Zhang Hanjie of Liang and Guo Chongtao—both destroyed. Hongzhao still made him a direct academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs and followed his counsel.
entries.literal: Moreover, those they employed were often unworthy. The supervisory attendant Chen Yi was treacherous and fond of secret plots. He had served Zhang Hanjie of Liang and Guo Chongtao; both men had promptly met ruin and death. Hongzhao nevertheless brought him in as a direct academician of the Bureau of Military Affairs and used his schemes.

entries.zh: 是時，弘昭、赟遣漢瓊至魏，召湣帝入立，而留漢瓊權知後事。
entries.en: Hongzhao and Yun sent Hanqiong to Wei to bring Emperor Min to the throne, with Hanqiong left to govern in their absence.
entries.literal: At that time Hongzhao and Yun sent Hanqiong to Wei to summon Emperor Min to take the throne, leaving Hanqiong to manage affairs in the rear.

entries.zh: 明年正月，漢瓊請入朝，弘昭、赟乃議徙成德範延光代漢瓊，北京留守石敬瑭代延光，鳳翔潞王從珂代敬瑭。
entries.en: The next year’s first month, Hanqiong sought audience. Hongzhao and Yun proposed shifting Fan Yanguang from Chengde into Hanqiong’s post, Shi Jingtang from the northern capital into Fan’s, and the Prince of Lu Congke from Fengxiang into Jingtang’s.
entries.literal: In the first month of the following year Hanqiong asked to come to court. Hongzhao and Yun then planned to move Fan Yanguang of Chengde to replace Hanqiong, the northern capital’s regent Shi Jingtang to replace Yanguang, and the Prince of Lu Congke of Fengxiang to replace Jingtang.

entries.zh: 三人者皆唐大臣，以漢瓊故，輕易其地，又不降制書，第遣使者監其上道，從珂由此遂反。
entries.en: All three were senior Tang ministers. For Hanqiong’s sake their commands were swapped casually, without formal edicts—only escorts hurried them on the road. Congke rebelled because of it.
entries.literal: All three were great ministers of Tang. Because of Hanqiong they were moved lightly from their posts, and no imperial edict was issued—only envoys were sent to supervise their departure on the road. From this Congke rebelled.

entries.zh: 從珂兵已東，湣帝大懼，遣人召弘昭計事。
entries.en: Congke’s host was eastward bound. Emperor Min, terrified, sent for Hongzhao.
entries.literal: Congke’s army was already marching east. Emperor Min was greatly afraid and sent men to summon Hongzhao to counsel.

entries.zh: 弘昭謂其客穆延暉曰：「上召我急，將罪我也。
entries.en: Hongzhao told his client Mu Yanhui: “The emperor calls me urgently. He means to blame me.
entries.literal: Hongzhao told his retainer Mu Yanhui: “The emperor summons me in haste—he means to punish me.

entries.zh: 吾兒婦，君之女也，其以歸，無使及禍。」
entries.en: My daughter-in-law is your daughter. Take her away—do not let her be caught in this.”
entries.literal: My son’s wife is your daughter—take her home and do not let her share the disaster.”

entries.zh: 乃拔劍大哭，欲自裁，而家人止之。
entries.en: He drew his sword, wept, and tried to take his life; his family restrained him.
entries.literal: He drew his sword and wept aloud, wishing to kill himself, but his household stopped him.

entries.zh: 使者促弘昭入見甚急，弘昭呼曰：「窮至此邪！」
entries.en: The messenger hurried him to court. Hongzhao shouted: “Brought to this pass!”
entries.literal: The envoy pressed him to enter audience with great urgency. Hongzhao cried: “Driven to this extremity!”

entries.zh: 乃自投於井以死。
entries.en: He threw himself into a well and died.
entries.literal: Then he threw himself into a well and died.

entries.zh: 安從進聞之，亦殺赟於家，赟母新死，子母棄屍於道，妻子皆見殺。
entries.en: An Congjin heard and killed Yun at home. Yun’s mother had just died; their bodies were cast into the street. Wife and children perished with him.
entries.literal: When An Congjin heard of it, he also killed Yun at his home. Yun’s mother had just died; mother and son were left dead in the road. Wife and children were all killed.

entries.zh: 赟有子三歲，其故吏張守素匿之以免。
entries.en: Yun’s son was three. His old clerk Zhang Shousu hid the boy and spared him.
entries.literal: Yun had a three-year-old son; his former clerk Zhang Shousu hid the child and saved him.

entries.zh: 漢高祖即位，贈弘昭尚書令，赟中書令。
entries.en: Emperor Gaozu of Later Han posthumously made Hongzhao Grand Secretary and Yun Grand Councillor.
entries.literal: When Emperor Gaozu of Han took the throne, Hongzhao was posthumously made Grand Secretary and Yun made Grand Councillor.

entries.zh: 初，帝與晉高祖俱事明宗，而心不相悅。
entries.en: The emperor and the Jin High Ancestor had both served Mingzong, yet they never liked each other.
entries.literal: At first the emperor and the High Ancestor of Jin had both served Mingzong, but their hearts were not fond of each other.

entries.zh: 帝既入立，高祖不得已來朝，而心頗自疑，欲求歸鎮，且難言之，乃陽為羸疾，灸灼滿身，冀帝憐而遣之。
entries.en: Once enthroned, the emperor compelled the High Ancestor to attend court. Jingtang came, uneasy and eager to return to his post. Unable to speak plainly, he pretended grave illness and covered himself with moxa burns, hoping pity would send him home.
entries.literal: After the emperor entered the throne, the High Ancestor had no choice but to come to court, yet he was full of suspicion. He wished to return to his command but found it hard to say so. He feigned wasting illness and burned moxa over his whole body, hoping the emperor would pity him and send him away.

entries.zh: 延朗等多言敬瑭可留京師，昭胤、專美曰：「敬瑭與趙延壽皆尚唐公主，不可獨留。」
entries.en: Yanlang’s faction urged keeping Jingtang in the capital. Zhaoyin and Zhuanmei objected: “Jingtang and Zhao Yanshou both married Tang princesses. You cannot hold one and not the other.”
entries.literal: Yanlang and the others often said Jingtang could be kept in the capital. Zhaoyin and Zhuanmei said: “Jingtang and Zhao Yanshou have both married Tang princesses—they cannot be detained alone.”

entries.zh: 乃復授高祖河東而遣之。
entries.en: So the High Ancestor was sent back to Hedong.
entries.literal: They then reappointed the High Ancestor to Hedong and sent him off.

entries.zh: 是時，契丹數寇北邊，以高祖為大同、振武、威塞、彰國等軍蕃漢馬步軍都總管，屯於忻州。
entries.en: Khitan raids pressed the north. Jingtang was made overall commander of Tangut and Han forces of Datong, Zhenwu, Weisai, Zhangguo, and other commands, encamped at Xinzhou.
entries.literal: At that time the Khitan raided the northern border repeatedly. The High Ancestor was made overall commander of Tangut and Han horse and foot of the Datong, Zhenwu, Weisai, Zhangguo, and other armies, stationed at Xinzhou.

entries.zh: 而屯兵忽變，擁高祖呼「萬歲」，高祖懼，斬三十餘人而後止。
entries.en: His troops mutinied, surrounded him, and shouted “Long live!” He cut down thirty-odd men before order returned.
entries.literal: Suddenly the encamped troops mutinied, surrounded the High Ancestor, and shouted “Long live!” He was afraid and beheaded more than thirty men before they stopped.

entries.zh: 於是帝益疑之。
entries.en: The emperor’s suspicion deepened.
entries.literal: The emperor therefore suspected him all the more.

entries.zh: 延朗等請帝親征，帝心憂懼，常惡言敬瑭事，每戒人曰：「爾無說石郎，令我心膽墮地！」
entries.en: Yanlang urged a personal campaign. The emperor was sick with fear, could not bear talk of Jingtang, and warned his court: “Do not mention Lord Stone—I feel my heart fall through the floor!”
entries.literal: Yanlang and the others asked the emperor to campaign in person. The emperor’s heart was anxious and afraid; he often spoke harshly of Jingtang’s affair and would warn people: “Do not speak of Lord Stone to me—my heart and guts drop to the ground!”

entries.zh: 由此不欲行。
entries.en: He did not want to march.
entries.literal: From this he did not wish to go.

entries.zh: 而延朗等屢迫之，乃行。
entries.en: Yanlang pressed him until he went.
entries.literal: But Yanlang and the others pressed him again and again, and he went.

entries.zh: 至懷州，帝夜召李崧問以計策。
entries.en: At Huaizhou he called Li Song at night for counsel.
entries.literal: Reaching Huaizhou, the emperor summoned Li Song at night to ask his strategy.

entries.zh: 文遇不知而繼至，帝見之色變，崧躡其足，文遇乃出。
entries.en: Wenyu came in unaware. The emperor’s face changed. Song stepped on his foot; Wenyu withdrew.
entries.literal: Wenyu did not know and followed in; when the emperor saw him his color changed. Song trod on his foot, and Wenyu went out.

entries.zh: 帝曰：「我見文遇肉顫，欲抽刀刺之。」
entries.en: The emperor said: “I see Wenyu and my flesh crawls—I want to stab him.”
entries.literal: The emperor said: “When I see Wenyu my flesh trembles—I want to draw a knife and stab him.”

entries.zh: 崧曰：「文遇小人，致誤大事，刺之益醜。」
entries.en: Song said: “Wenyu is a petty man who has ruined everything. Stabbing him would only shame the throne.”
entries.literal: Song said: “Wenyu is a petty man who has ruined a great affair. To stab him would only add ugliness.”

entries.zh: 乃已。
entries.en: He let it go.
entries.literal: He desisted.

entries.zh: 是時，契丹已立敬瑭為天子，以兵而南，帝惶惑不知所之。
entries.en: The Khitan had made Jingtang emperor and marched south. The emperor panicked, without a plan.
entries.literal: By then the Khitan had already enthroned Jingtang as Son of Heaven and marched south with troops. The emperor was in panic and did not know where to turn.

entries.zh: 遣審虔將千騎至白馬坡踏戰地，審虔曰：「何地不堪戰？
entries.en: He sent Shenqian with a thousand horse to scout the White Horse Slope. Shenqian said: “What ground cannot be fought?
entries.literal: He sent Shenqian with a thousand horsemen to the White Horse Slope to reconnoiter the battlefield. Shenqian said: “What ground is not fit for battle?

entries.zh: 雖有其地，何人肯立於此？
entries.en: Even if there were, who would stand here?
entries.literal: Even if there is such ground, who would stand here?

entries.zh: 不如還也。」
entries.en: Better turn back.”
entries.literal: Better to turn back.”

entries.zh: 帝遂還，自焚。
entries.en: The emperor turned back and burned himself alive.
entries.literal: The emperor then returned and burned himself to death.

entries.zh: 高祖入京師，延朗等六人皆除名為民。
entries.en: Jingtang entered the capital. Yanlang and five others were demoted to commoners.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor entered the capital, Yanlang and the other six men were all stripped of office and made commoners.

entries.zh: 後月余，文遇獨直，帝夜召之，語罷敬瑭事，文遇曰：「臣聞『作舍道邊，三年不成』。
entries.en: A month later Wenyu held night watch alone. The emperor called him at night. When they came to Jingtang, Wenyu said: “They say, ‘Build a house beside the road and in three years it is still unfinished.’
entries.literal: More than a month later Wenyu alone was on night duty. The emperor summoned him at night and, when talk ended on Jingtang’s affair, Wenyu said: “I have heard, ‘Build a house beside the road and in three years it is not finished.’

entries.zh: 國家之事，斷在陛下。
entries.en: State affairs belong to Your Majesty alone.
entries.literal: The affairs of the state are decided by Your Majesty alone.

entries.zh: 且敬瑭徙亦反，不徙亦反，遲速爾，不如先事圖之。」
entries.en: Move Jingtang and he rebels; leave him and he rebels—only the timing differs. Strike first.”
entries.literal: Moreover, if Jingtang is moved he will rebel; if he is not moved he will rebel—the only question is sooner or later. Better to strike first.”

entries.zh: 帝大喜曰：「術者言朕今年當得一賢佐以定天下，卿其是邪！」
entries.en: The emperor rejoiced: “Soothsayers said I would gain one worthy man this year to settle the realm—is it you!”
entries.literal: The emperor was greatly pleased and said: “The diviners said that this year I would gain one worthy assistant to settle the realm—is it you!”

entries.zh: 乃令文遇手書除目，夜半下學士院草制。
entries.en: He had Wenyu write the appointment order himself and at midnight sent it to the Hanlin to draft the edict.
entries.literal: He had Wenyu write out the appointment order by hand, and at midnight sent it to the Academy to draft the edict.

entries.zh: 明日宣制，文武兩班皆失色。
entries.en: Next day the edict was read. Civil and military officials alike went white.
entries.literal: The next day the edict was proclaimed; both civil and military ranks turned pale.

entries.zh: 居五六日，敬瑭以反聞。
entries.en: Within a week came word that Jingtang had rebelled.
entries.literal: Within five or six days word came that Jingtang had rebelled.

entries.zh: 敬瑭上書，言帝非明宗子，而許王從益次當立。
entries.en: Jingtang’s memorial claimed the emperor was not Mingzong’s son and that Prince Xu Congyi should reign.
entries.literal: Jingtang sent up a memorial saying the emperor was not Mingzong’s son and that Prince Xu Congyi was next in line for the throne.

entries.zh: 帝得書大怒，手壞而投之，召學士馬胤孫為答詔，曰：「宜以惡語詆之。」
entries.en: The emperor read it, flew into a rage, tore the letter apart, and summoned Ma Yinsun to answer: “Revile him in the vilest terms.”
entries.literal: The emperor received the letter, was furious, tore it apart with his hands and cast it away, and summoned the academician Ma Yinsun to draft a reply, saying: “Use harsh words to revile him.”

entries.zh: 劉延朗，宋州虞城人也。
entries.en: Liu Yanlang came from Yucheng in Songzhou.
entries.literal: Liu Yanlang was a native of Yucheng in Songzhou.

entries.zh: 初，廢帝起於鳳翔，與共事者五人：節度判官韓昭胤，掌書記李專美，牙將宋審虔，客將房暠，而延朗為孔目官。
entries.en: When the Deposed Emperor first rose at Fengxiang, five men shared his cause: Han Zhaoyin as military aide, Li Zhuanmei as chief clerk, Song Shenqian as guard officer, Fang Hao as guest officer, and Yanlang as records clerk.
entries.literal: At first, when the Deposed Emperor rose at Fengxiang, five men worked with him: the military governor’s aide Han Zhaoyin, chief clerk Li Zhuanmei, guard officer Song Shenqian, guest officer Fang Hao, and Yanlang as records clerk.

entries.zh: 初，湣帝即位，徙廢帝為北京留守，不降制書，遣供奉官趙處愿促帝上道。
entries.en: When Emperor Min took the throne, he made the Deposed Emperor Defender of the Northern Capital without a formal edict and sent palace attendant Zhao Chuyuan to hurry him on his way.
entries.literal: When Emperor Min first took the throne, he transferred the Deposed Emperor to serve as Defender of the Northern Capital without issuing an edict, and sent palace attendant Zhao Chuyuan to hurry him on the road.

entries.zh: 帝疑惑，召昭胤等計議，昭胤等皆勸帝反，由是事無大小，皆此五人謀之。
entries.en: Uncertain, the emperor called Zhaoyin and the others; all urged revolt, and from then on these five decided every matter.
entries.literal: The emperor hesitated and summoned Zhaoyin and the others to counsel; they all urged rebellion, and thereafter matters great and small were plotted by these five.

entries.zh: 而暠又喜鬼神巫祝之說，有瞽者張濛，自言事太白山神，神，魏崔浩也，其言吉凶無不中，暠素信之。
entries.en: Hao also favored spirit worship. A blind man named Zhang Meng claimed to serve the god of Mount Taibai—said to be Cui Hao of Wei—and his omens never failed. Hao trusted him deeply.
entries.literal: Hao also delighted in spirits, ghosts, and shamanic rites. A blind man, Zhang Meng, claimed to serve the god of Mount Taibai—the god, he said, was Wei’s Cui Hao—and his words on fortune and disaster never missed. Hao had long trusted him.

entries.zh: 嘗引濛見帝，聞其語聲，驚曰：「此非人臣也！」
entries.en: He once presented Meng to the emperor, who started at his voice and cried: “This is no ordinary subject!”
entries.literal: Once he brought Meng before the emperor; hearing his voice, the emperor started and said: “This is no ordinary subject!”

entries.zh: 暠使濛問於神，神傳語曰：「三珠並一珠，驢馬沒人驅。歲月甲庚午，中興戊己土。」
entries.en: Hao had Meng ask the god, who answered: “Three pearls join into one; donkeys and horses sink while men drive on. In the year’s months, jia and gengwu; at Zhongxing, wu and jitu.”
entries.literal: Hao had Meng inquire of the god, and the god transmitted: “Three pearls join into one pearl; donkeys and horses sink, men drive on. In the year’s months, jia and gengwu; at Zhongxing, wu and jitu.”

entries.zh: 暠不曉其義，使問濛，濛曰：「神言如此，我能傳之，不能解也。」
entries.en: Hao could not grasp the meaning and asked Meng, who said: “The god spoke thus—I can relay it, but not explain it.”
entries.literal: Hao did not understand the meaning and had Meng asked; Meng said: “The god spoke thus—I can transmit it, but cannot explain it.”

entries.zh: 帝即以濛為館驛巡官。
entries.en: The emperor then made Meng touring officer of the post stations.
entries.literal: The emperor then made Meng touring officer of the post stations.

entries.zh: 帝將反，而兵少，又乏食，由此甚懼，使暠問濛，濛傳神語曰：「王當有天下，可無憂！」
entries.en: About to rebel but short of troops and food, the emperor was terrified and had Hao consult Meng, who relayed: “My lord shall rule the realm—fear nothing!”
entries.literal: The emperor was about to rebel, but his troops were few and food scarce; greatly afraid, he had Hao ask Meng, and Meng relayed the god’s words: “My lord shall possess the realm—have no fear!”

entries.zh: 於是決反，使專美作檄書，言：「朱弘昭、馮赟幸明宗病，殺秦王而立湣帝。帝年少，小人用事，離間骨肉，將問罪於朝！」
entries.en: He then rebelled and had Zhuanmei draft a proclamation: “Zhu Hongzhao and Feng Yun exploited Mingzong’s illness, killed the Prince of Qin, and enthroned Emperor Min. The boy emperor is ruled by petty men who divide the clan—they mean to bring us to court in chains!”
entries.literal: He then resolved on rebellion and had Zhuanmei draft a proclamation saying: “Zhu Hongzhao and Feng Yun took advantage of Mingzong’s illness, killed the Prince of Qin, and set up Emperor Min. The emperor is young; petty men hold power, estranging kin, and will bring charges in court!”

entries.zh: 遣使者馳告諸鎮，皆不應，獨隴州防禦使相里金遣其判官薛文遇計事。
entries.en: He sent envoys to the provinces; none answered except Longzhou commissioner Xiangli Jin, who sent his aide Xue Wenyu to counsel.
entries.literal: He sent envoys racing to notify the provinces; none answered save Xiangli Jin, commissioner of Longzhou, who sent his aide Xue Wenyu to consult.

entries.zh: 帝得文遇，大喜。
entries.en: The emperor welcomed Wenyu and rejoiced.
entries.literal: The emperor gained Wenyu and was greatly pleased.

entries.zh: 而延朗調率城中民財以給軍。
entries.en: Yanlang levied the city’s wealth to feed the army.
entries.literal: Yanlang levied the townspeople’s wealth to supply the army.

entries.zh: 王思同率諸鎮兵圍鳳翔，廢帝懼，又遣暠問神，神曰：「王兵少，東兵來，所以迎王也。」
entries.en: Wang Sitong besieged Fengxiang with provincial troops. The Deposed Emperor, afraid, again consulted the god through Hao, who answered: “Your troops are few—the eastern army comes to welcome you.”
entries.literal: Wang Sitong led provincial troops to besiege Fengxiang. The Deposed Emperor was afraid and again sent Hao to ask the god, who said: “My lord’s troops are few; the eastern troops come to welcome my lord.”

entries.zh: 已而東兵果叛降於帝。
entries.en: Soon the eastern troops mutinied and went over to him.
entries.literal: Before long the eastern troops indeed mutinied and surrendered to the emperor.

entries.zh: 帝入京師，即位之日，受冊明宗柩前。
entries.en: He entered the capital and, on his enthronement day, received investiture before Mingzong’s coffin.
entries.literal: The emperor entered the capital; on the day of enthronement he received investiture before Mingzong’s coffin.

entries.zh: 冊曰：「維應順元年，歲次甲午，四月庚午朔。」
entries.en: The investiture read: “In the first year of Yingshun, cyclical year jiawu, on gengwu the first day of the fourth month.”
entries.literal: The investiture read: “In the first year of Yingshun, the year jiawu, on gengwu the first day of the fourth month.”

entries.zh: 帝回顧暠曰：「張濛神言，豈不驗哉！」
entries.en: The emperor turned to Hao and said: “Zhang Meng’s oracle—was it not fulfilled!”
entries.literal: The emperor turned to Hao and said: “Zhang Meng’s spirit words—were they not fulfilled!”

entries.zh: 由是暠益見親信，而專以巫祝用事。
entries.en: Hao grew still more trusted, and shamanic rites alone governed affairs.
entries.literal: From this Hao was all the more trusted and favored, and shamanic rites alone governed affairs.

entries.zh: 是時，高祖悉握精兵在北，饋運芻糧，遠近勞弊。
entries.en: Jingtang held the best troops in the north; supply lines stretched far and exhausted the country.
entries.literal: At that time the High Ancestor held elite troops in the north in his grasp; fodder and grain were transported from afar, and the realm was worn out.

entries.zh: 帝與延朗等日夕謀議，而專美、文遇叠宿中興殿盧，召見訪問，常至夜分而罷。
entries.en: The emperor plotted with Yanlang day and night. Zhuanmei and Wenyu slept in the Zhongxing Hall and were called in for counsel, often until midnight.
entries.literal: The emperor and Yanlang and the others plotted day and night, while Zhuanmei and Wenyu lodged night after night in the Zhongxing Hall chambers and were summoned for counsel, often not dismissed until deep in the night.

entries.zh: 是時，高祖弟重胤為皇城副使，而石氏公主母曹太后居中，因得伺帝動靜言語以報高祖，高祖益自危懼。
entries.en: Jingtang’s brother Chongyin was deputy commissioner of the Imperial City. The Stone princess’s mother, Dowager Cao, was inside the palace. They watched the emperor’s every move and word and reported to Jingtang, who grew more fearful still.
entries.literal: The High Ancestor’s younger brother Chongyin was deputy commissioner of the Imperial City. The Stone princess’s mother, Empress Dowager Cao, was within the palace. Thus they could watch the emperor’s movements and words and report to the High Ancestor, who grew still more afraid.

entries.zh: 每帝遣使者勞軍，即陽為羸疾不自堪，因數求解總管以探帝心。
entries.en: Whenever the emperor sent envoys to the army, Jingtang played at collapse and begged again and again to be relieved of command—testing the throne’s intent.
entries.literal: Whenever the emperor sent envoys to comfort the army, he would feign wasting illness beyond endurance and repeatedly ask to be relieved of overall command to probe the emperor’s mind.

entries.zh: 是時，帝母魏氏追封宣憲皇太后，而墓在太原，有司議立寢宮。
entries.en: The emperor’s mother, Lady Wei, was posthumously made Empress Dowager Xuanxian. Her tomb lay at Taiyuan, and the ministries debated building a palace there.
entries.literal: At that time the emperor’s mother, the Wei clan, was posthumously titled Empress Dowager Xuanxian, and her tomb was at Taiyuan. The offices debated erecting a resting palace.

entries.zh: 高祖建言陵與民家墓相雜，不可立宮。
entries.en: Jingtang argued the tomb lay among commoners’ graves and that no palace should be raised.
entries.literal: The High Ancestor argued that the tomb was mixed among common graves and that no palace should be built.

entries.zh: 帝疑高祖欲毀民墓，為國取怨，帝由此發怒，罷高祖總管，徙鄆州。
entries.en: The emperor thought Jingtang meant to raze common graves and earn the realm’s hatred. Enraged, he stripped him of command and moved him to Yunzhou.
entries.literal: The emperor suspected the High Ancestor wished to destroy commoners’ graves and win the people’s hatred for the state. The emperor was enraged by this, removed the High Ancestor from overall command, and transferred him to Yunzhou.

entries.zh: 延朗等多言不可，而司天趙延義亦言天象失度，宜安靜以弭災，其事遂止。
entries.en: Yanlang’s party objected; the Director of Astronomy Zhao Yanyi said the heavens were disturbed and the court should keep still. The transfer was dropped.
entries.literal: Yanlang and the others often said it could not be done, and the Director of Astronomy Zhao Yanyi also said the heavens were out of measure and that quiet was needed to quell disaster. The matter then stopped.

entries.zh: 康思立，本山陰諸部人也。
entries.en: Kang Sili came from the Shanyin tribal confederations.
entries.literal: Kang Sili was originally a man of the Shanyin tribal groups.

entries.zh: 少為騎將，從莊宗破梁夾城，戰柏鄉，累以功遷突騎指揮使。
entries.en: As a young cavalry officer he followed Zhuangzong at Jia City and Baxiang and rose for merit to command the Vanguard Cavalry.
entries.literal: In youth he was a cavalry officer. He followed Zhuangzong in breaking Liang’s Jia City and fighting at Baxiang, and was repeatedly promoted for merit to commander of the Vanguard Cavalry.

entries.zh: 明宗即位，歷應嵐二州刺史、宿州團練使、昭武軍節度使，徙鎮保義，皆有善政。
entries.en: Under Mingzong he governed Ying and Lan, commanded Suzhou’s regiments, and held Zhaowu and Baoyi with a reputation for good rule.
entries.literal: When Mingzong took the throne, he served successively as prefect of Ying and Lan prefectures, regimental commissioner of Suzhou, and military governor of Zhaowu, then was transferred to govern Baoyi—all with good administration.

entries.zh: 潞王從珂反於鳳翔，湣帝遣王思同等討之，思立有捧聖、羽林屯兵千五百人，乃以羽林千人屬思同。
entries.en: When the Prince of Lu Congke rebelled at Fengxiang, Emperor Min sent Wang Sitong against him. Sili had fifteen hundred Sacred Support and Feathered Forest troops and lent Sitong a thousand of the Feathered Forest.
entries.literal: When the Prince of Lu Congke rebelled at Fengxiang, Emperor Min sent Wang Sitong to suppress him. Sili had fifteen hundred men of the Sacred Support and Feathered Forest encampments and gave a thousand of the Feathered Forest to Sitong.

entries.zh: 思同至鳳翔，軍叛，降於從珂。
entries.en: Sitong reached Fengxiang; his army mutinied and went over to Congke.
entries.literal: Sitong reached Fengxiang; the army mutinied and surrendered to Congke.

entries.zh: 思立聞之，欲盡誅羽林千人家屬，未及，而從珂兵已至，思立乃以捧聖兵城守，從珂兵傅其城，呼曰：「西兵七萬策新天子，爾五百人其能拒邪？
entries.en: Sili meant to slaughter the families of the thousand mutineers, but Congke’s host was already there. He held the walls with the Sacred Support. Congke’s men shouted: “Seventy thousand western troops have raised a new emperor—can five hundred of you stand against them?
entries.literal: Sili heard of it and wished to execute the families of the thousand Feathered Forest men, but before he could, Congke’s army arrived. Sili then held the city with the Sacred Support troops. Congke’s army pressed the walls and called: “Seventy thousand western soldiers have enthroned a new Son of Heaven—can your five hundred men resist?

entries.zh: 徒陷陜人於死耳！」
entries.en: You will only bury the people of Shaan in slaughter!”
entries.literal: You will only trap the people of Shaan into death!”

entries.zh: 捧聖兵聞之，皆解甲，思立遂開門迎從珂。
entries.en: The Sacred Support heard and threw down their arms. Sili opened the gates and welcomed Congke in.
entries.literal: When the Sacred Support troops heard this, they all laid down their armor. Sili then opened the gates and welcomed Congke.

entries.zh: 廢帝即位，以思立初無降意，頗不悅之，徙安遠，又徙安國，以年老罷為右神武統軍。
entries.en: The Deposed Emperor resented Sili’s first refusal to yield and moved him to Anyuan, then Anguo, then retired him as Senior Commander of the Right Divine Martial Guard.
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, because Sili at first had shown no intent to surrender, he was quite displeased and transferred him to Anyuan, then to Anguo, and finally dismissed him as Senior Commander of the Right Divine Martial Guard for old age.

entries.zh: 石敬瑭反太原，廢帝以思立為北面行營馬軍都指揮使。
entries.en: When Shi Jingtang rebelled at Taiyuan, the Deposed Emperor made Sili commander of the northern campaign’s cavalry.
entries.literal: When Shi Jingtang rebelled at Taiyuan, the Deposed Emperor made Sili overall commander of the northern campaign’s horse army.

entries.zh: 廢帝幸懷州，遣思立將從駕騎兵出團柏谷救張敬達，未至，而敬達死，楊光遠降晉，思立疾，卒於道。
entries.en: The emperor marched to Huaizhou and sent Sili with the imperial escort through Tuanbai Valley to relieve Zhang Jingda. Jingda died first; Yang Guangyuan surrendered to Jin. Sili fell ill and died on the march.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor went to Huaizhou and sent Sili with the accompanying cavalry out through Tuanbai Valley to rescue Zhang Jingda, but before he arrived Jingda was dead and Yang Guangyuan surrendered to Jin. Sili fell ill and died on the road.

entries.zh: 晉高祖入立，贈太子少師。
entries.en: Jingtang posthumously made him Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
entries.literal: When the Jin High Ancestor entered and took the throne, Sili was posthumously made Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent.

entries.zh: 潞王從珂反，彥稠為招討副使。
entries.en: When Congke rebelled, Yanchou was deputy pacification commissioner.
entries.literal: When the Prince of Lu Congke rebelled, Yanchou was deputy pacification commissioner.

entries.zh: 王思同兵潰，彥稠與思同俱東走，為潞王兵所得，囚之華州獄，已而殺之。
entries.en: Sitong’s army broke; Yanchou fled east with him, was caught, jailed at Hua, and killed.
entries.literal: Wang Sitong’s army collapsed; Yanchou fled east with Sitong, was taken by Congke’s troops, imprisoned in Hua prefecture, and later killed.

entries.zh: 晉高祖立，贈侍中。
entries.en: Jingtang posthumously made him Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: When the Jin High Ancestor took the throne, Yanchou was posthumously made Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 初，延朗與暠並掌機密，延朗專任事，諸將當得州者，不以功次為先後，納賂多者得善州，少及無賂者得惡州，或久而不得，由是人人皆怨。
entries.en: Yanlang and Hao had shared the secrets, but Yanlang ran everything. Generals awaiting commands bought their posts—heavy bribes won good provinces, light or none won bad ones, and some waited forever. Everyone hated him.
entries.literal: At first Yanlang and Hao together held the secrets, but Yanlang monopolized affairs. Of the generals due to receive prefectures, merit was not the order of precedence—those who paid larger bribes received good prefectures; those who paid little or none received bad ones, or sometimes waited long without receiving any. From this everyone resented him.

entries.zh: 暠心患之，而不能爭也，但日飽食高枕而已。
entries.en: Hao was uneasy but could not fight him. He ate well and slept with a high pillow.
entries.literal: Hao was troubled in heart but could not contend; he only ate his fill each day and slept with a high pillow.

entries.zh: 每延朗議事，則垂頭陽睡不省。
entries.en: Whenever Yanlang met to discuss policy, Hao hung his head and pretended to sleep.
entries.literal: Whenever Yanlang discussed affairs, he would hang his head and feign sleep, paying no attention.

entries.zh: 及晉兵入，延朗以一騎走南山，過其家，指而嘆曰：「吾積錢三十萬於此，不知何人取之！」
entries.en: When Jin troops entered, Yanlang fled south alone. At his house he pointed and sighed: “I piled three hundred thousand strings of cash here—who will take it now!”
entries.literal: When the Jin army entered, Yanlang fled south on a single horse. Passing his house he pointed and sighed: “I stored three hundred thousand cash here—who knows who will take it!”

entries.zh: 遂為追兵所殺。
entries.en: Pursuers cut him down.
entries.literal: Pursuing troops killed him.

entries.zh: 晉高祖聞暠常不與延朗事，哀之，後復以為將。
entries.en: The Jin High Ancestor heard Hao had kept out of Yanlang’s plots and pitied him; later he was restored to command.
entries.literal: The Jin High Ancestor heard that Hao had often refused to join Yanlang’s schemes and pitied him; later he was again made a general.

entries.zh: 歲餘卒。
entries.en: A year later he died.
entries.literal: After a year more he died.

entries.zh: 專美事晉為大理卿，開運中卒。
entries.en: Zhuanmei served Jin as director of the Court of Judicial Review and died in the Kaiyun period.
entries.literal: Zhuanmei served Jin as director of the Court of Judicial Review and died in the Kaiyun era.

entries.zh: 當晉之將起，廢帝以昭胤為中書侍郎、同中書門下平章事，出為河陽節度使，與審虔、文遇皆不知其所終。
entries.en: As Jin rose, the Deposed Emperor made Zhaoyin Vice Grand Councillor and sent him to govern Heyang. He, Shenqian, and Wenyu vanish from the record.
entries.literal: When Jin was about to rise, the Deposed Emperor made Zhaoyin Vice Grand Councillor and co-signer of the Secretariat, then sent him out as military governor of Heyang. Together with Shenqian and Wenyu, their ends are unknown.

entries.zh: 朱弘昭
entries.en: Zhu Hongzhao
entries.literal: Zhu Hongzhao

entries.zh: 〈（馮赟附）〉
entries.en: (With Feng Yun appended)
entries.literal: (With Feng Yun appended)

entries.zh: 任圜，京兆三原人也。
entries.en: Ren Huan came from Sanyuan in Jingzhao.
entries.literal: Ren Huan was a native of Sanyuan in Jingzhao.

entries.zh: 為人明敏，善談辯，見者愛其容止，及聞其論議縱橫，益皆悚動。
entries.en: Bright and quick, skilled in debate, he won admiration for his bearing; his sweeping arguments left listeners shaken.
entries.literal: As a man he was bright and quick, skilled in discourse and debate. Those who saw him loved his bearing; when they heard his sweeping arguments, they were all the more shaken.

entries.zh: 李嗣昭節度昭義，辟圜觀察支使。
entries.en: When Li Sizhao held Zhaoyi, he took Huan on as observation aide.
entries.literal: When Li Sizhao governed Zhaoyi, he invited Huan as observation aide.

entries.zh: 梁兵築夾城圍潞州，踰年而晉王薨，晉兵救潞者皆解去。
entries.en: Liang troops built the encircled fort and besieged Luzhou. After a year the Prince of Jin died, and every Jin relief force pulled away.
entries.literal: Liang troops built the encircled fort and besieged Luzhou. After more than a year the Prince of Jin died, and the Jin forces sent to relieve Luzhou all withdrew.

entries.zh: 嗣昭危甚，問圜去就之計，圜勸嗣昭堅守以待，不可有二心。
entries.en: Sizhao was desperate and asked Huan whether to stay or go. Huan urged him to hold on and wait and never waver.
entries.literal: Sizhao was in grave peril and asked Huan whether to stay or leave. Huan urged Sizhao to hold firm and wait—he must not waver.

entries.zh: 已而莊宗攻破梁夾城，聞圜為嗣昭畫守計，甚嘉之，由是益知名。
entries.en: Zhuangzong soon broke the Liang encircled fort. Learning Huan had planned Sizhao’s defense, he praised him warmly, and Huan’s name spread.
entries.literal: Before long Zhuangzong broke the Liang encircled fort. Hearing that Huan had devised Sizhao’s defense plan, he greatly praised him, and from then on Huan grew more famous.

entries.zh: 其後嗣昭與莊宗有隙，圜數奉使往來，辨釋讒構，嗣昭卒免於禍，圜之力也。
entries.en: Later Sizhao and Zhuangzong quarreled. Huan shuttled between them, clearing away slander, and Sizhao at last escaped ruin—Huan’s work.
entries.literal: Later Sizhao and Zhuangzong fell out. Huan repeatedly went back and forth as envoy, explaining away slanders and intrigues, and Sizhao at last escaped disaster—this was Huan’s doing.

entries.zh: 嗣昭從莊宗戰胡柳，擊敗梁兵，圜頗有功，莊宗勞之曰：「儒士亦破體邪？
entries.en: Sizhao followed Zhuangzong to Huliu and routed the Liang army. Huan served well. Zhuangzong praised him: “Even a scholar casts off restraint?
entries.literal: Sizhao followed Zhuangzong to fight at Huliu and routed the Liang army. Huan did considerable service. Zhuangzong praised him: “A scholar too throws off restraint?

entries.zh: 仁者之勇，何其壯也！」
entries.en: The courage of the humane—how mighty!”
entries.literal: The courage of the humane—how mighty!”

entries.zh: 張文禮弒王镕，莊宗遣嗣昭討之。
entries.en: Zhang Wenli killed Wang Rong. Zhuangzong sent Sizhao against him.
entries.literal: Zhang Wenli murdered Wang Rong. Zhuangzong sent Sizhao to suppress him.

entries.zh: 嗣昭戰歿，圜代將其軍，號令嚴肅。
entries.en: Sizhao fell in battle. Huan took his army and kept iron discipline.
entries.literal: Sizhao died in battle. Huan took command of his army with strict discipline.

entries.zh: 既而文禮子處球等閉城堅守，不可下，圜數以禍福諭鎮人，鎮人信之。
entries.en: Wenli’s son Chuchiu and others barred the city and would not yield. Huan again and again spoke of reward and ruin to the townsmen, and they trusted him.
entries.literal: Wenli’s son Chuchiu and others shut the city and held firm—it could not be taken. Huan repeatedly explained fortune and disaster to the townspeople, and they believed him.

entries.zh: 圜嘗擁兵至城下，處球登城呼圜曰：「城中兵食俱盡，而久抗王師，若泥首自歸，懼無以塞責，幸公見哀，指其生路。」
entries.en: Huan once marched to the walls. Chuchiu climbed the ramparts and called: “Soldiers and grain are gone, yet we long resisted the throne. If we bow in submission we may not atone. Show us mercy—point us a path to live.”
entries.literal: Huan once brought troops to the city walls. Chuchiu mounted the wall and called to Huan: “The city has exhausted its soldiers and food yet long resisted the imperial army. If we bow and surrender, we fear we cannot answer for our guilt. We beg your mercy—show us a way to live.”

entries.zh: 圜告之曰：「以子先人，固難容貸，然罰不及嗣，子可從輕。
entries.en: Huan answered: “Your father’s crime is hard to forgive—but guilt does not pass to sons, so you may be treated lightly.
entries.literal: Huan told him: “For your father’s crime you can hardly expect full pardon—but punishment does not extend to successors, so you may receive lighter sentence.

entries.zh: 其如拒守經年，傷吾大將，一朝困竭，方布款誠，以此計之，子亦難免。
entries.en: Yet you held out a year, killed our commander, and only now, spent, offer loyalty—weigh that, and you too may not escape.
entries.literal: Yet you held out for years, killed our great general, and only now when exhausted do you show good faith—weighed this way, you too will be hard to spare.

entries.zh: 然坐而待斃，曷若伏而俟命？」
entries.en: Still, to sit and die—is that better than bowing and awaiting judgment?”
entries.literal: But to sit and await death—how is that better than bowing down and waiting for judgment?”

entries.zh: 處球流涕曰：「公言是也！」
entries.en: Chuchiu wept: “You speak truth!”
entries.literal: Chuchiu wept and said: “What you say is right!”

entries.zh: 乃遣子送狀乞降，人皆稱圜其言不欺。
entries.en: He sent his son with a surrender petition. All said Huan’s words were honest.
entries.literal: He sent his son with a surrender petition. Everyone praised Huan for speaking without deception.

entries.zh: 既而佗將攻破鎮州，處球雖見殺，而鎮之吏民以嘗乞降，故得保其家族者甚眾。
entries.en: Later another general took Zhenzhou. Chuchiu was killed, but many who had sought surrender kept their families.
entries.literal: Later another general broke Zhenzhou. Chuchiu was killed, but many town officials and commoners who had surrendered were able to preserve their clans.

entries.zh: 蕭希甫，宋州人也。
entries.en: Xiao Xifu came from Song Prefecture.
entries.literal: Xiao Xifu was a native of Song Prefecture.

entries.zh: 為人有機辯，多矯激，少舉進士，為梁開封尹袁象先掌書記。
entries.en: Quick-witted and disputatious, prone to extravagant provocation, he passed the jinshi in youth and served Liang’s Kaifeng governor Yuan Xiangxian as chief secretary.
entries.literal: As a man he was quick-witted and disputatious, given to extravagant provocation. In youth he passed the jinshi examination and served Liang’s Kaifeng governor Yuan Xiangxian as chief secretary.

entries.zh: 象先為青州節度使，以希甫為巡官。
entries.en: When Xiangxian became military governor of Qingzhou, he made Xifu a circuit inspector.
entries.literal: When Xiangxian became military governor of Qingzhou, he made Xifu a circuit inspector.

entries.zh: 希甫不樂，乃棄其母妻，變姓名，亡之鎮州，自稱青州掌書記，謁趙王王镕。
entries.en: Xifu was displeased. He abandoned mother and wife, changed his name, and fled to Zhen Prefecture, posing as Qingzhou’s chief secretary to gain audience with Wang Rong of Zhao.
entries.literal: Xifu was displeased. He abandoned his mother and wife, changed his name, and fled to Zhen Prefecture, calling himself chief secretary of Qingzhou and presenting himself to the Zhao king Wang Rong.

entries.zh: 镕以希甫為參軍，尤不樂，居歲餘，又亡之易州，削髮為僧，居百丈山。
entries.en: Rong made him a staff officer; he liked it even less. A year later he fled to Yi Prefecture, shaved his head, and became a monk on Mount Baizhang.
entries.literal: Rong made Xifu a staff officer; he was still more unhappy. After more than a year he fled again to Yi Prefecture, shaved his head, became a monk, and lived on Mount Baizhang.

entries.zh: 莊宗將建國於魏，置百官，求天下隱逸之士，幽州李紹宏薦希甫為魏州推官。
entries.en: As Zhuangzong prepared to found his state at Wei, fill the hundred offices, and seek hidden worthies, Li Shaohong of Youzhou recommended Xifu as legal officer at Wei.
entries.literal: When Zhuangzong was about to establish his state at Wei, set up the hundred offices, and seek hidden worthies throughout the realm, Youzhou’s Li Shaohong recommended Xifu as Wei Prefecture’s legal officer.

entries.zh: 豆盧革
entries.en: Dou Luge
entries.literal: Dou Luge

entries.zh: 桑维翰，字国侨，河南人也。
entries.en: Sang Weihan, styled Guoqiao, came from Henan.
entries.literal: Sang Weihan, styled Guoqiao, was a native of Henan.

entries.zh: 为人丑怪，身短而面长，常临鉴以自奇曰：「七尺之身，不如一尺之面。」
entries.en: He was homely and odd—short-bodied, long-faced. He would study himself in a mirror and say: “Seven feet of body cannot match one foot of face.”
entries.literal: His person was ugly and strange—short in stature and long in face. He often looked in a mirror and marveled at himself, saying: “A body of seven feet is not equal to a face of one foot.”

entries.zh: 慨然有志于公辅。
entries.en: He burned to reach the highest councils of state.
entries.literal: He harbored a grand ambition for high office.

entries.zh: 初举进士，主司恶其姓，以「桑」「丧」同音。
entries.en: At his first jinshi attempt the chief examiner disliked his surname—“Sang” echoed “funeral.”
entries.literal: When he first took the jinshi examination, the chief examiner disliked his surname, because “Sang” and “mourning” were homophones.

entries.zh: 人有劝其不必举进士，可以从佗求仕者，维翰慨然，乃著《日出扶桑赋》以见志。
entries.en: Friends said he need not sit the jinshi and could find office elsewhere. Weihan, stung, wrote “Rising Sun over the Mulberry” to show his resolve.
entries.literal: Someone urged him that he need not pursue the jinshi and could seek office by other paths. Weihan was indignant and wrote “Rising Sun over the Mulberry” to declare his intent.

entries.zh: 又铸铁砚以示人曰：「砚弊则改而佗仕。」
entries.en: He cast an iron inkstone and said: “When this wears through, I change course—but not before.”
entries.literal: He also cast an iron inkstone and told people: “When the stone wears out, I will change and seek another path.”

entries.zh: 卒以进士及第。
entries.en: He passed the jinshi in the end.
entries.literal: In the end he passed the jinshi.

entries.zh: 晋高祖辟为河阳节度掌书记，其后常以自从。
entries.en: The Jin High Ancestor made him chief secretary at Heyang and kept him close thereafter.
entries.literal: The Jin High Ancestor made him chief secretary to the Heyang military governor, and afterward often kept him at his side.

entries.zh: 高祖自太原徙天平，不受命，而有异谋，以问将佐，将佐皆恐惧不敢言，独维翰与刘知远赞成之，因使维翰为书求援于契丹。
entries.en: The High Ancestor refused transfer from Taiyuan to Tianping and plotted rebellion. He asked his staff; all feared and were silent. Only Weihan and Liu Zhiyuan urged him on. Weihan wrote to the Khitan for aid.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor moved from Taiyuan to Tianping and refused orders, already harboring rebellion, he asked his officers. They were all afraid and dared not speak. Only Weihan and Liu Zhiyuan approved. He therefore had Weihan write seeking aid from the Khitan.

entries.zh: 耶律德光已许诺，而赵德钧亦以重赂啖德光，求助己以篡唐。
entries.en: Yelü Deguang had promised—but Zhao Dejun bribed him to put himself on Tang’s throne instead.
entries.literal: Yelü Deguang had already promised, but Zhao Dejun also bribed Deguang heavily, asking him to help seize Tang for himself.

entries.zh: 高祖惧事不果，乃遣维翰往见德光，为陈利害甚辩，德光意乃决，卒以灭唐而兴晋，维翰之力也。
entries.en: Fearing failure, the High Ancestor sent Weihan to Deguang. Weihan argued the stakes so well that Deguang committed. Tang fell and Jin rose—chiefly through Weihan.
entries.literal: The High Ancestor feared the plan would fail and sent Weihan to see Deguang. He argued profit and harm with great eloquence; Deguang’s mind was settled. He at last destroyed Tang and raised Jin—Weihan’s power did this.

entries.zh: 高祖即位，以维翰为翰林学士、礼部侍郎、知枢密院事，迁中书侍郎、同中书门下平章事，兼枢密使。
entries.en: At enthronement Weihan became Hanlin academician, Vice Minister of Rites, and Military Affairs director, then Vice Grand Councillor, co-signer, and chief councillor of Military Affairs.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor took the throne, Weihan was made Hanlin academician, Vice Minister of Rites, and director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, then promoted to Vice Grand Councillor, co-signer of the Secretariat, and chief councillor of Military Affairs.

entries.zh: 天福四年，出为相州节度使，岁余，徙镇泰宁。
entries.en: Tianfu year four he governed Xiangzhou; a year later he moved to Taining.
entries.literal: In the fourth year of Tianfu he went out as military governor of Xiangzhou; after a year he was transferred to govern Taining.

entries.zh: 吐浑白承福为契丹所迫，附镇州安重荣以归晋，重荣因请与契丹绝好，用吐浑以攻之。
entries.en: Bai Chengfu of the Tuyuhun, harried by the Khitan, joined An Chongrong at Zhen and submitted to Jin. Chongrong asked to break with the Khitan and strike them with Tuyuhun allies.
entries.literal: The Tuyuhun Bai Chengfu, pressed by the Khitan, attached himself to An Chongrong of Zhenzhou and submitted to Jin. Chongrong therefore asked to break with the Khitan and use the Tuyuhun to attack them.

entries.zh: 高祖重违重荣，意未决。
entries.en: The High Ancestor hesitated to cross Chongrong.
entries.literal: The High Ancestor was loath to oppose Chongrong and had not decided.

entries.zh: 维翰上疏言契丹未可与争者七，高祖召维翰使者至卧内，谓曰：「北面之事，方挠吾胸中，得卿此疏，计已决矣，可无忧也。」
entries.en: Weihan listed seven reasons not to fight the Khitan. The High Ancestor called the messenger to his bedside: “The north has tormented me. This memorial settles it.”
entries.literal: Weihan memorialized seven reasons the Khitan could not be contested. The High Ancestor summoned Weihan’s messenger to his bedside and said: “The northern affair has been tangling my heart. With your master’s memorial the plan is settled—I need not worry.”

entries.zh: 维翰又劝高祖幸邺都。
entries.en: Weihan also urged a royal progress to Ye.
entries.literal: Weihan also urged the High Ancestor to visit the northern capital at Ye.

entries.zh: 七年，高祖在邺，维翰来朝，徙镇晋昌。
entries.en: Year seven the High Ancestor was at Ye. Weihan attended court and was sent to Jinchang.
entries.literal: In the seventh year the High Ancestor was at Ye; Weihan came to court and was transferred to govern Jinchang.

entries.zh: 出帝即位，召拜侍中。
entries.en: The Deposed Emperor made him Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, Weihan was summoned and made Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 而景延广用事，与契丹绝盟，维翰言不能入，乃阴使人说帝曰：「制契丹而安天下，非用维翰不可。」
entries.en: Yanguang ruled and broke the Khitan pact. Weihan’s voice was shut out. He secretly urged the throne: “Only Weihan can tame the Khitan and steady the realm.”
