entries.literal: Jing Yanguang held power and broke the Khitan alliance. Weihan’s counsel could not enter. He secretly had men tell the emperor: “To control the Khitan and secure the realm, none but Weihan will do.”

entries.zh: 乃出延广于河南，拜维翰中书令，复为枢密使，封魏国公，事无巨细，一以委之。
entries.en: Yanguang went to Henan; Weihan became Grand Secretary and Military Affairs chief, Duke of Wei. Every matter passed through his hands.
entries.literal: Yanguang was sent out to govern Henan; Weihan was made Grand Secretary and again chief councillor of Military Affairs, enfeoffed Duke of Wei. Great and small affairs were all entrusted to him.

entries.zh: 数月之间，百度浸理。
entries.en: Within months government found its rhythm again.
entries.literal: Within months the hundred offices were gradually set in order.

entries.zh: 初，李瀚为翰林学士，好饮而多酒过，高祖以为浮薄。
entries.en: Li Han of the Hanlin loved wine and drank too deep. The High Ancestor found him flighty.
entries.literal: At first Li Han was Hanlin academician, fond of drink and often drunk. The High Ancestor thought him frivolous.

entries.zh: 天福五年九月，诏废翰林学士，按《唐六典》归其职于中书舍人，而端明殿学士、枢密院学士皆废。
entries.en: Tianfu five, ninth month: Hanlin posts were abolished and their work returned to Secretariat drafters; Duanming and Military Affairs academics went too.
entries.literal: In the ninth month of Tianfu’s fifth year an edict abolished Hanlin academicians and, per the Tang Six Offices canon, returned their duties to Secretariat drafters; Duanming academics and Military Affairs academics were also abolished.

entries.zh: 及维翰为枢密使，复奏置学士，而悉用亲旧为之。
entries.en: As Military Affairs chief Weihan restored the academics—and stocked them with kin and cronies.
entries.literal: When Weihan became chief councillor of Military Affairs he memorialized to restore academics—and filled every seat with kin and old friends.

entries.zh: 明宗时，朱守殷以汴州反，晋高祖为六军副使，主诛从守殷反者。
entries.en: Under Mingzong, Zhu Shouyin rebelled at Bian. The Jin High Ancestor commanded punishment of the rebels.
entries.literal: Under Mingzong, Zhu Shouyin rebelled at Bianzhou. The Jin High Ancestor was deputy commander of the Six Armies and oversaw executing Shouyin’s followers.

entries.zh: 延广为汴州军校当诛，高祖惜其才，阴纵之使亡，后录以为客将。
entries.en: Yanguang was marked for death. The High Ancestor prized him, let him slip away, and later took him as a guest officer.
entries.literal: Yanguang was a Bianzhou officer due for execution. The High Ancestor prized his talent and secretly let him escape; later he enrolled him as a guest officer.

entries.zh: 高祖即位，以为侍卫步军都指挥使，领果州团练使，从领宁江军节度使。
entries.en: At enthronement Yanguang commanded the palace foot guard and governed Guo, then Ningjiang.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor took the throne, Yanguang was made commander of the palace foot guard and concurrent regimental commissioner of Guozhou, then military governor of Ningjiang.

entries.zh: 天福四年，出镇义成，又徙保义，复召为侍卫马步军都虞候，徙镇河阳三城，迁马步军都指挥使，领天平。
entries.en: Tianfu four he held Yicheng, then Baoyi; he returned as deputy commander of horse and foot, held Heyang’s three cities, then Tianping.
entries.literal: In Tianfu’s fourth year he went out to govern Yicheng, then was moved to Baoyi, recalled as deputy commander of palace horse and foot, transferred to the three cities of Heyang, promoted to commander of horse and foot, and given Tianping.

entries.zh: 高祖崩，出帝立，延广有力，颇伐其功。
entries.en: The High Ancestor died; the Deposed Emperor rose. Yanguang had clout and trumpeted his deeds.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor died and the Deposed Emperor rose, Yanguang had leverage and boasted of his merit.

entries.zh: 初，出帝立，晋大臣议告契丹，致表称臣，延广独不肯，但致书称孙而已，大臣皆知其不可而不能夺。
entries.en: At the new reign Jin’s ministers meant to notify the Khitan as subjects. Yanguang alone refused—he wrote as grandson, not vassal. Everyone knew disaster would follow; none could stop him.
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor first took the throne, Jin’s ministers debated notifying the Khitan with a memorial of subjection. Yanguang alone refused—he sent only a letter calling himself grandson. The ministers all knew it would not do but could not overrule him.

entries.zh: 契丹果怒，数以责晋，延广谓契丹使者乔莹曰：「先皇帝北朝所立，今卫子中国自册，可以为孙，而不可为臣。
entries.en: The Khitan raged and rebuked Jin again and again. Yanguang told envoy Qiao Ying: “Your court made our last emperor. Weizi’s Son of Heaven enthrones himself—we are grandson, not subject.
entries.literal: The Khitan were enraged and repeatedly reproached Jin. Yanguang told the Khitan envoy Qiao Ying: “The former emperor was enthroned by your court. Now the Son of Heaven of Weizi enthrones himself—we may be grandson, but not subject.

entries.zh: 且晋有横磨大剑十万口，翁要战则来，佗日不禁孙子，取笑天下。」
entries.en: Jin keeps a hundred thousand “horizontal-grinding” great swords. If you want war, come. One day you may fail to leash your grandson—and the world will laugh.”
entries.literal: Moreover Jin has a hundred thousand horizontal-grinding great swords. If the old man wants war, let him come. Another day he may not restrain his grandson—the realm will laugh.”

entries.zh: 莹知其言必起两国之争，惧后无以取信也，因请载于纸，以备遗忘。
entries.en: Ying knew this would kindle war and feared he would not be believed. He asked for it in writing.
entries.literal: Ying knew these words would surely raise strife between the two states and feared he could not be believed later. He asked that they be written down lest he forget.

entries.zh: 延广敕吏具载以授莹，莹藏其书衣领中以归，具以延广语告契丹，契丹益怒。
entries.en: Yanguang had it written and handed over. Ying hid it in his collar, repeated every word at home, and the Khitan fury doubled.
entries.literal: Yanguang ordered a clerk to record and give it to Ying. Ying hid the paper in his collar and returned, reporting Yanguang’s words in full. The Khitan grew still angrier.

entries.zh: 吴峦，字宝川，郓州卢县人也。
entries.en: Wu Luan, styled Baochuan, came from Lu County in Yun Prefecture.
entries.literal: Wu Luan, styled Baochuan, was a native of Lu County in Yun Prefecture.

entries.zh: 少举明经不中，清泰中为大同沙彦珣节度判官。
entries.en: He failed the Mingjing in youth. Under Qingtai he was chief secretary to Sha Yanxun of Datong.
entries.literal: In youth he took the Mingjing examination but did not pass. In the Qingtai era he was chief secretary to Sha Yanxun, military governor of Datong.

entries.zh: 晋高祖起太原，召契丹为援，契丹过云州，彦珣出城迎谒，为契丹所虏。
entries.en: The Jin High Ancestor rose at Taiyuan and called in the Khitan. They passed Yun; Yanxun went out to greet them and was captured.
entries.literal: When the Jin High Ancestor rose at Taiyuan and called the Khitan as allies, the Khitan passed Yun Prefecture. Yanxun went out to welcome them and was taken by the Khitan.

entries.zh: 城中推峦主州事，峦即闭门拒守，契丹以兵围之。
entries.en: The city made Luan governor. He shut the gates and held. The Khitan besieged him.
entries.literal: The city pushed Luan to manage affairs. Luan shut the gates and refused to yield. The Khitan besieged him.

entries.zh: 高祖入立，以云州入于契丹，而峦犹守城不下，契丹围之凡七月。
entries.en: The High Ancestor ceded Yun to the Khitan—but Luan still would not yield. The siege lasted seven months.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor took the throne he ceded Yun Prefecture to the Khitan, yet Luan still held the city and would not come down. The Khitan besieged it for seven months in all.

entries.zh: 高祖义峦所为，乃以书告契丹，使解兵去。
entries.en: The High Ancestor admired his stand and asked the Khitan to withdraw.
entries.literal: The High Ancestor honored Luan’s conduct and wrote the Khitan asking them to lift the siege.

entries.zh: 高祖召峦，以为武宁军节度副使、谏议大夫、复州防御使。
entries.en: He summoned Luan, made him deputy governor of Wuning, Remonstrating Censor, and defender of Fu.
entries.literal: The High Ancestor summoned Luan and made him deputy military governor of Wuning, Remonstrating Censor, and defender of Fu Prefecture.

entries.zh: 德光犯京师，行至相州，遣骑兵数千杂晋军渡河趋洛，以取延广，戒曰：「延广南奔吴，西走蜀，必追而取之。」
entries.en: Deguang marched on the capital. At Xiangzhou he sent thousands of horse with Jin units toward Luoyang for Yanguang: “If he flees to Wu or Shu, take him.”
entries.literal: Deguang entered the capital. Reaching Xiangzhou he sent several thousand cavalry mixed with Jin troops across the river toward Luoyang to seize Yanguang, warning: “If Yanguang flees south to Wu or west to Shu, pursue and take him.”

entries.zh: 而延广顾虑其家，未能引决，虏骑奄至，乃与从事阎丕驰骑见德光于封丘，并丕见锁。
entries.en: He could not leave his family. Khitan horse swept in. He and aide Yan Pi rode to Deguang at Fengqiu; Pi was chained too.
entries.literal: Yanguang, thinking of his family, could not resolve to die. Khitan riders suddenly arrived. He and his aide Yan Pi rode to see Deguang at Fengqiu; Pi was bound as well.

entries.zh: 延广曰：「丕，臣从事也，以职相随，何罪而见锁？」
entries.en: Yanguang said: “Pi serves by duty—why chain him?”
entries.literal: Yanguang said: “Pi is my staff officer and followed by duty—what crime warrants chains?”

entries.zh: 丕乃得释。
entries.en: Pi was freed.
entries.literal: Pi was then released.

entries.zh: 德光责延广曰：「南北失欢，皆因尔也。」
entries.en: Deguang rebuked him: “You broke north and south.”
entries.literal: Deguang reproached Yanguang: “North and south lost harmony—all because of you.”

entries.zh: 召乔莹质其前言，延广初不服，莹从衣领中出所藏书，延广乃服。
entries.en: He called Qiao Ying. Yanguang denied until Ying produced the paper from his collar. Then he yielded.
entries.literal: He summoned Qiao Ying to verify the earlier words. Yanguang at first denied; Ying drew the hidden paper from his collar. Yanguang then submitted.

entries.zh: 因以十事责延广，每服一事，授一牙筹，授至八筹，延广以面伏地，不能仰视，遂叱而锁之。
entries.en: Ten charges, one tally each confession. At eight Yanguang lay facedown, unable to look up. They bound him.
entries.literal: Deguang then charged him with ten counts; for each admission he gave one tally stick. At eight sticks Yanguang lay face down and could not look up. He was shouted at and bound.

entries.zh: 将送之北行，至陈桥，止民家。
entries.en: They were sending him north; at Chen Bridge he lodged in a common house.
entries.literal: About to send him north, at Chen Bridge they stopped at a commoner’s house.

entries.zh: 夜分，延广伺守者殆，引手扼吭而死，时年五十六。
entries.en: At night, guards slack, he seized his throat and died. He was fifty-six.
entries.literal: Deep in the night, when the guards slackened, Yanguang reached up and throttled himself to death. He was fifty-six.

entries.zh: 汉高祖时，赠侍中。
entries.en: Later Han posthumously made him Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: Under the Han High Ancestor he was posthumously made Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 景延广，字航川，陕州人也。
entries.en: Jing Yanguang, styled Hangchuan, came from Shaanzhou.
entries.literal: Jing Yanguang, styled Hangchuan, was a native of Shaanzhou.

entries.zh: 父建善射，尝教延广曰：「射不入铁，不如不发。」
entries.en: His father Jian was a master bowman and taught him: “If you cannot pierce iron, do not shoot.”
entries.literal: His father Jian was skilled at archery and once taught Yanguang: “If the shot does not pierce iron, better not to loose.”

entries.zh: 由是延广以挽强见称。
entries.en: He became famous for the heavy bow.
entries.literal: From this Yanguang was famed for drawing the heavy bow.

entries.zh: 事梁邵王友诲，友诲谋反被幽，延广亡去。
entries.en: He served Liang’s Prince of Shao Youhai; when Youhai rebelled and was jailed, Yanguang fled.
entries.literal: He served Liang’s Prince of Shao Youhai; when Youhai rebelled and was imprisoned, Yanguang fled.

entries.zh: 后从王彦章战中都，彦章败，延广身被数创，仅以身免。
entries.en: He followed Wang Yanzhang at Zhongdu; Yanzhang fell and Yanguang was riddled with wounds, barely alive.
entries.literal: Later he followed Wang Yanzhang in battle at Zhongdu; Yanzhang was defeated and Yanguang took many wounds, barely escaping with his life.

entries.zh: 桑维翰
entries.en: Sang Weihan
entries.literal: Sang Weihan

entries.zh: 周太祖鎮鄴，不落樞密使，逢吉以謂樞密之任，方鎮帶之非便，與史弘肇爭，於是卒如弘肇議。
entries.en: Zhou Taizu held Ye and kept the Privy Council. Fengji argued a frontier governor should not carry that post and fought Shi Hongzhao over it—in the end Hongzhao won.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu governed Ye but did not relinquish the Privy Council post. Fengji held that for a military commissioner to carry that office was unsuitable and contended with Shi Hongzhao—in the end it went as Hongzhao wished.

entries.zh: 弘肇怨逢吉異己，已而會飲王章第，使酒坐中，弘肇怒甚。
entries.en: Hongzhao resented Fengji’s opposition. At a drinking party at Wang Zhang’s house he drank hard and burned with anger.
entries.literal: Hongzhao resented Fengji for opposing him. Later they met for drink at Wang Zhang’s residence; Hongzhao drank heavily at table and was very angry.

entries.zh: 逢吉謀求出鎮以避之，既而中輟，人問其故，逢吉曰：「茍舍此而去，史公一處分，吾齏粉矣！」
entries.en: Fengji planned to take a provincial post and escape him—then changed his mind. Asked why, he said: “If I leave this seat, one word from Lord Shi and I am dust!”
entries.literal: Fengji planned to seek a posting outside the capital to avoid him; then he stopped halfway. When asked why, Fengji said: “If I should leave this post, one order from Lord Shi and I am powder!”

entries.zh: 是時，隱帝少年，小人在側。
entries.en: The Deposed Emperor was still a youth; petty men crowded his side.
entries.literal: At that time the Deposed Emperor was young; petty men were at his side.

entries.zh: 弘肇等威制人主，帝與左右李業、郭允明等皆患之。
entries.en: Hongzhao and his faction overawed the throne; the emperor and his intimates—Li Ye, Guo Yunming, and the rest—all hated it.
entries.literal: Hongzhao and the others overawed and controlled the sovereign; the emperor and those around him—Li Ye, Guo Yunming, and the rest—all chafed at it.

entries.zh: 逢吉每見業等，以言激之，業等卒殺弘肇，即以逢吉權知樞密院。
entries.en: Fengji goaded Ye and his circle whenever he saw them; they at last killed Hongzhao and made Fengji acting head of the Privy Council on the spot.
entries.literal: Whenever Fengji saw Ye and the others he goaded them with words; Ye and the others at last killed Hongzhao and immediately had Fengji serve as acting chief of the Privy Council.

entries.zh: 方命草麻，聞周太祖起兵，乃止。
entries.en: He was just drafting the appointment edict when word came that Zhou Taizu had risen in arms—and everything halted.
entries.literal: Just as he was ordered to draft the edict of appointment, they heard Zhou Taizu had raised troops—and stopped.

entries.zh: 逢吉夜宿金祥殿東閣，謂司天夏官正王處訥曰：「昨夕未暝，已見李崧在側，生人接死者，無吉事也。」
entries.en: Fengji spent the night in the eastern wing of the Jinxiang Hall and told Wang Chune, the Summer Office director of astronomy: “Last night, before dusk, I saw Li Song beside me—the living keeping company with the dead. Nothing good can come of that.”
entries.literal: Fengji lodged by night in the eastern wing of the Jinxiang Hall and said to Wang Chune, Director of the Directorate of Astronomy’s Summer Office: “Last night before dark I already saw Li Song at my side—the living meeting the dead: nothing auspicious.”

entries.zh: 周太祖至北郊，官軍敗於劉子陂。
entries.en: Zhou Taizu reached the northern suburbs; the imperial army broke at Liuzi Slope.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu reached the northern suburbs; the government army was defeated at Liuzi Slope.

entries.zh: 逢吉宿七里，夜與同舍酣飲，索刀將自殺，為左右所止。
entries.en: Fengji stopped at Qili. That night he drank deep with his companions, drew a knife to kill himself, and was restrained.
entries.literal: Fengji lodged at Qili. At night he drank heavily with his lodge-mates, took a knife intending suicide, and was stopped by attendants.

entries.zh: 明日與隱帝走趙村，自殺於民舍。
entries.en: The next day he fled with the Deposed Emperor to Zhao Village and took his life in a private house.
entries.literal: The next day he fled with the Deposed Emperor to Zhao Village and killed himself in a commoner’s dwelling.

entries.zh: 周太祖定京師，梟其首，適當李崧被刑之所。
entries.en: When Zhou Taizu took the capital, Fengji’s head was hung on a pole—exactly where Li Song had died.
entries.literal: When Zhou Taizu secured the capital, Fengji’s head was displayed on a pole—just where Li Song had been executed.

entries.zh: 廣順初，賜其子西京莊並宅一區。
entries.en: Early in Guangshun his son received a Western Capital estate and a mansion.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Guangshun, his son was granted an estate in the Western Capital and one mansion precinct.

entries.zh: 周太祖平李守貞，推功群臣，弘肇拜中書令。
entries.en: When Zhou Taizu crushed Li Shouzhen he shared credit among the ministers; Hongzhao was made Grand Secretary.
entries.literal: When Zhou Taizu pacified Li Shouzhen he spread credit among the ministers; Hongzhao was appointed Grand Secretary.

entries.zh: 隱帝自關西罷兵，漸近小人，與後贊、李業等嬉遊無度，而太后親族頗行幹托，弘肇與楊邠稍裁抑之。
entries.en: When the western war ended the Hidden Emperor drifted toward petty favorites—Hou Zan, Li Ye, and the rest—and played without restraint. The dowager’s kin peddled influence; Hongzhao and Yang Bin checked them where they could.
entries.literal: After the Deposed Emperor ended warfare in the western passes he drew gradually near petty men, sporting without measure with Hou Zan, Li Ye, and the rest; meanwhile the empress dowager’s kin often practiced influence-peddling. Hongzhao and Yang Bin somewhat checked and restrained this.

entries.zh: 太后有故人子求補軍職，弘肇輒斬之。
entries.en: The dowager’s old friend’s son sought a military post—Hongzhao had him beheaded on the spot.
entries.literal: The empress dowager had an old acquaintance’s son who sought to be appointed to a military post—Hongzhao instantly had him beheaded.

entries.zh: 帝始聽樂，賜教坊使等玉帶、錦袍，往謝弘肇，弘肇怒曰：「健兒為國征行者未有偏賜，爾曹何功，敢當此乎！」
entries.en: The emperor first heard music and gave the Music Bureau directors jade belts and brocade robes. They came to thank Hongzhao. He raged: “Hard soldiers on campaign get no such gifts—what have you done to deserve this!”
entries.literal: The emperor first listened to music and gave the directors of the Music Bureau jade belts and brocade robes. They went to thank Hongzhao. Hongzhao angrily said: “Stalwart soldiers campaigning for the state have received no special gifts—what merit have you people that you dare accept this!”

entries.zh: 悉取所賜還官。
entries.en: He stripped them of every gift and sent it all back to the treasury.
entries.literal: He took back everything they had been given and returned it to the government.

entries.zh: 周太祖出鎮魏州，弘肇議帶樞密行，蘇逢吉、楊邠以為不可，弘肇恨之。
entries.en: Zhou Taizu went out to govern Weizhou. Hongzhao wanted to keep the Privy Council and go; Su Fengji and Yang Bin refused—and Hongzhao hated them for it.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu went out to govern Weizhou. Hongzhao proposed carrying the Privy Council post with him; Su Fengji and Yang Bin thought it impossible—Hongzhao resented them.

entries.zh: 明日，會飲竇貞固第，弘肇厲聲舉爵屬太祖曰：「昨日廷論，何為異同？
entries.en: Next day they drank at Dou Zhengu’s house. Hongzhao lifted his cup toward Taizu and said in a hard voice: “Yesterday in court we split—why?
entries.literal: The next day they met for drink at Dou Zhengu’s residence. Hongzhao raised his cup in a loud voice and directed it at Taizu, saying: “Yesterday at court we argued—why the disagreement?

entries.zh: 今日與公飲此。」
entries.en: Today I drink with you, sir.”
entries.literal: Today I drink this with you, sir.”

entries.zh: 逢吉與邠亦舉大爵曰：「此國家事也，何必介意乎！」
entries.en: Fengji and Bin raised their cups too: “This is the realm’s business—why hold a grudge!”
entries.literal: Fengji and Bin also raised great cups and said: “This is state business—why take it to heart!”

entries.zh: 遂俱飲釂。
entries.en: They drained their cups together.
entries.literal: They then all drained their cups.

entries.zh: 弘肇曰：「安朝廷，定禍亂，直須長槍大劍，若『毛錐子』安足用哉？」
entries.en: Hongzhao said: “To settle the court and stop calamity you need long spears and great swords—what good are ‘hair awls’?”
entries.literal: Hongzhao said: “To secure the court and still chaos, one needs long spears and great swords—what use are ‘hair awls’?”

entries.zh: 三司使王章曰：「無『毛錐子』，軍賦何從集乎？」
entries.en: Wang Zhang, commissioner of the Three Departments, said: “Without ‘hair awls,’ where do military taxes come from?”
entries.literal: Three Departments commissioner Wang Zhang said: “Without ‘hair awls,’ whence come military taxes?”

entries.zh: 「毛錐子」，蓋言筆也。
entries.en: “Hair awls” meant writing brushes.
entries.literal: “Hair awls”—that is to say, writing brushes.

entries.zh: 弘肇默然。
entries.en: Hongzhao said nothing.
entries.literal: Hongzhao fell silent.

entries.zh: 他日，會飲章第，酒酣，為手勢令，弘肇不能為，客省使閻晉卿坐次弘肇，屢教之。
entries.en: Another day they drank at Zhang’s house. Wine deep, they played hand-gesture forfeits; Hongzhao could not manage. Yan Jinqing of the Guest Liaison Office sat below him and kept showing him how.
entries.literal: Another day they met for drink at Zhang’s residence. When the wine was deep they played hand-gesture forfeits; Hongzhao could not do it. The Guest Liaison Commissioner Yan Jinqing sat below Hongzhao and repeatedly taught him.

entries.zh: 蘇逢吉戲曰：「坐有姓閻人，何憂罰爵！」
entries.en: Su Fengji joked: “With a Yan at the table, who fears a penalty cup!”
entries.literal: Su Fengji jestingly said: “With someone surnamed Yan at the table, why worry about penalty cups!”

entries.zh: 弘肇妻閻氏，酒家倡，以為譏己，大怒，以醜語詬逢吉，逢吉不校。
entries.en: Hongzhao’s wife was Lady Yan, once a wine-shop singer; she took it as a jibe at her. She flew into a rage and cursed Fengji with foul words. Fengji did not reply.
entries.literal: Hongzhao’s wife was Lady Yan—a wine-shop singer—and she thought herself mocked. Greatly angered, she reviled Fengji with ugly words; Fengji did not answer.

entries.zh: 弘肇欲毆之，逢吉先出。
entries.en: Hongzhao meant to strike him; Fengji slipped out first.
entries.literal: Hongzhao wanted to beat him; Fengji left first.

entries.zh: 弘肇起索劍欲追之，楊邠泣曰：「蘇公，漢宰相，公若殺之，致天子何地乎？」
entries.en: Hongzhao rose for his sword to run him down. Yang Bin wept: “Su is Han’s chancellor. Kill him—and where does that leave the emperor?”
entries.literal: Hongzhao rose to seek a sword and chase him. Yang Bin wept and said: “Lord Su is Han’s chancellor. If you kill him, where will you leave the Son of Heaven?”

entries.zh: 弘肇馳馬去，邠送至第而還。
entries.en: Hongzhao galloped away. Bin saw Fengji home and came back.
entries.literal: Hongzhao rode off; Bin escorted him to his residence and returned.

entries.zh: 由是將相如水火。
entries.en: After that the ministers were fire and water.
entries.literal: From this the ministers were like fire and water.

entries.zh: 隱帝遣王峻置酒公子亭和解之。
entries.en: The Hidden Emperor sent Wang Jun to pour wine at the Prince’s Pavilion and force a truce.
entries.literal: The Hidden Emperor sent Wang Jun to set wine at the Prince’s Pavilion and reconcile them.

entries.zh: 弘肇已死，帝坐崇元殿召羣臣，告以弘肇等謀反，羣臣莫能對。
entries.en: Hongzhao was dead. The emperor sat in Chongyuan Hall, summoned the ministers, and charged that Hongzhao and his circle had rebelled. No minister could reply.
entries.literal: Hongzhao was already dead. The emperor took his seat in Chongyuan Hall, summoned the ministers, and told them that Hongzhao and the others had plotted rebellion. None of the ministers could answer.

entries.zh: 又召諸軍校見於萬歲殿，帝曰：「弘肇等專權，使汝曹常憂橫死，今日吾得為汝主矣！」
entries.en: He then summoned the army officers to Wansui Hall and said: “Hongzhao and his circle held all power and kept you fearing sudden death. Today I can be your master!”
entries.literal: He next summoned the army officers to appear before him in Wansui Hall. The emperor said: “Hongzhao and the others monopolized power and kept you in constant fear of sudden death. Today I am able to be your lord!”

entries.zh: 軍校皆拜。
entries.en: The officers all bowed.
entries.literal: The army officers all bowed.

entries.zh: 周太祖即位，追封弘肇鄭王，以禮歸葬。
entries.en: When Zhou Taizu took the throne, he posthumously made Hongzhao Prince of Zheng and buried him with full honors.
entries.literal: When Zhou Taizu took the throne, he posthumously enfeoffed Hongzhao as Prince of Zheng and had him buried with full rites.

entries.zh: 楊邠，魏州冠氏人也。
entries.en: Yang Bin came from Guanshi in Weizhou.
entries.literal: Yang Bin was a native of Guanshi in Weizhou.

entries.zh: 少為州掌籍吏，租庸使孔謙領度支，補邠勾押官，歷孟、華、鄆三州糧料院使。
entries.en: As a youth he kept the prefectural registers. Kong Qian of the Tax and Corvée Bureau made him auditing officer; he rose through grain commissions in Meng, Hua, and Yun.
entries.literal: In youth he was a clerk keeping registers for the prefecture. Kong Qian of the Tax and Corvée Bureau oversaw revenue and appointed Bin auditing officer; he served successively as grain commissioner for Meng, Hua, and Yun prefectures.

entries.zh: 事漢高祖為右都押衙，高祖即位，拜樞密使。
entries.en: Under Han’s High Ancestor he was right chief adjutant; at enthronement he became Privy Councilor.
entries.literal: Serving Han’s High Ancestor as right chief adjutant, when the High Ancestor took the throne he was made Privy Councilor.

entries.zh: 邠出於小吏，不喜文士，與蘇逢吉等內相排忌。
entries.en: A clerk by origin, he despised scholars; he and Su Fengji and their factions feuded in court.
entries.literal: Bin came from petty clerks and disliked men of letters; within the court he and Su Fengji and others mutually excluded and resented one another.

entries.zh: 逢吉諷李濤上疏罷邠與周太祖樞密使，邠泣訴李太后前，太后怒，罷濤相，加邠中書侍郎兼吏部尚書、同平章事。
entries.en: Fengji urged Li Tao to petition for Bin’s and Guo Wei’s removal from the Privy Council. Bin wept before Dowager Li; she raged, ousted Tao, and made Bin Vice Director, Minister of Personnel, and Associate Grand Councilor.
entries.literal: Fengji prompted Li Tao to memorial asking that Bin and Zhou Taizu be removed from the Privy Council. Bin wept and pleaded before Empress Dowager Li; the dowager was furious, dismissed Tao from the chancellorship, and made Bin Vice Director of the Secretariat, concurrent Minister of Personnel, and Associate Grand Councilor.

entries.zh: 是時，逢吉、禹珪頗以私賄除吏，多繆。
entries.en: Fengji and Yu Gui sold offices for bribes; appointments went wildly astray.
entries.literal: At that time Fengji and Yu Gui often appointed officials through private bribes, and many appointments were wrong.

entries.zh: 邠為相，事無大小，必先示邠，邠以為可，乃入白，而深革逢吉所為，凡門蔭出身，諸司補吏者，一切罷之。
entries.en: As chancellor, nothing passed until Bin approved—and he tore up Fengji’s work. Hereditary appointments and bureau supplements were all cancelled.
entries.literal: When Bin became chancellor, matters great and small were first shown to Bin; if Bin thought them acceptable, only then were they reported upward—and he deeply overturned what Fengji had done. Every appointment by hereditary privilege or bureau supplement was abolished.

entries.zh: 邠雖長於吏事，而不知大體，以謂為國家者，帑廩實、甲兵完而已，禮樂文物皆虛器也。
entries.en: Bin knew ledgers, not statecraft. A full treasury and sharp swords—that, he said, was government; rites, music, and culture were empty show.
entries.literal: Though Bin was skilled in clerical affairs, he did not grasp the larger pattern. He held that to govern a state one need only fill the treasury and complete the armor; rites, music, and cultural institutions were empty vessels.

entries.zh: 以故秉大政而務苛細，凡前資官不得居外，而天下行旅，皆給過所然後得行。
entries.en: In power he ruled by petty strictness. Former officials could not leave the capital; every traveler needed a pass.
entries.literal: Therefore, holding great power, he pursued petty strictness. Former officials could not serve outside the capital; travelers everywhere had to be given travel passes before they might go.

entries.zh: 旬日之間，人情大擾，邠度不可行而止。
entries.en: Within ten days the realm seethed; Bin saw it would not hold and backed off.
entries.literal: Within ten days popular feeling was greatly disturbed; Bin judged it could not be done and stopped.

entries.zh: 邠為人頗儉靜，四方之賂雖不卻，然往往以獻於帝。
entries.en: Bin lived frugally and quietly. He took bribes from every quarter—but often turned them over to the throne.
entries.literal: Bin was by nature rather frugal and quiet. Though he did not refuse bribes from the four directions, he often presented them to the emperor.

entries.zh: 居家謝絕賓客，晚節稍通縉紳，延客門下。
entries.en: At home he turned guests away; late in life he opened his gate a little to the gentry.
entries.literal: At home he shut out guests; in his later years he opened somewhat to gentry and kept guests at his gate.

entries.zh: 知史傳有用，乃課吏傳寫。
entries.en: He thought history worth keeping and set clerks to copying it.
entries.literal: Knowing history had use, he set clerks to copy it.

entries.zh: 未幾，及於禍。
entries.en: Soon after, disaster found him.
entries.literal: Before long he met disaster.

entries.zh: 周太祖即位，追封弘農王。
entries.en: Zhou Taizu posthumously made him Prince of Hongnong.
entries.literal: When Zhou Taizu took the throne, Bin was posthumously enfeoffed Prince of Hongnong.

entries.zh: 是時，李業、郭允明、後贊、聶文進等用事，不喜執政。
entries.en: Li Ye, Guo Yunming, Hou Zan, Nie Wenjin, and others held the court and hated the chief ministers.
entries.literal: At that time Li Ye, Guo Yunming, Hou Zan, Nie Wenjin, and others held sway and disliked the chief ministers.

entries.zh: 而隱帝春秋漸長，為大臣所制，數有忿言，業等乘間譖之，以謂弘肇威震人主，不除必為亂。
entries.en: The emperor was coming of age and chafed under his ministers; he muttered his anger. Ye and his circle whispered that Hongzhao overawed the throne and would bring rebellion if left alive.
entries.literal: The Hidden Emperor was gradually growing older and felt hemmed in by the great ministers; he often spoke in anger. Ye and the rest seized the moment to slander them, saying Hongzhao’s power overawed the ruler and that if he were not removed he would surely bring rebellion.

entries.zh: 隱帝頗欲除之。
entries.en: The emperor wanted them gone.
entries.literal: The Hidden Emperor very much wished to remove them.

entries.zh: 夜聞作坊鍛甲聲，以為兵至，達旦不寐。
entries.en: One night he heard armor being hammered in the workshops and thought the army was upon him. He lay awake until dawn.
entries.literal: At night he heard the sound of armor being forged in the workshops and thought troops had come; until dawn he could not sleep.

entries.zh: 由是與業等密謀禁中。
entries.en: He began to plot with Ye and the rest behind palace walls.
entries.literal: From this he secretly plotted with Ye and the rest within the palace.

entries.zh: 乾祐三年冬十月十三日，弘肇與楊邠、王章等入朝，坐廣政殿東廡，甲士數十人自內出，擒弘肇、邠、章斬之，並族其三家。
entries.en: On the thirteenth of the tenth month, Qianyou year three, Hongzhao came to court with Yang Bin and Wang Zhang and sat in the eastern gallery of Guangzheng Hall. Dozens of armored men burst from within, seized the three, and beheaded them—and wiped out every clan.
entries.literal: On the thirteenth day of the tenth month, winter, in the third year of Qianyou, Hongzhao entered court with Yang Bin and Wang Zhang and the rest. They sat in the eastern gallery of Guangzheng Hall. Several dozen armored soldiers came out from within, seized Hongzhao, Bin, and Zhang, and beheaded them—and exterminated all three clans.

entries.zh: 邠常與王章論事帝前，帝曰：「事行之後，勿使有言也！」
entries.en: Bin often debated policy with Wang Zhang before the throne. The emperor said: “Once a thing is done, let no one speak of it!”
entries.literal: Bin often discussed affairs with Wang Zhang before the emperor. The emperor said: “After a matter is done, let there be no talk of it!”

entries.zh: 邠遽曰：「陛下但禁聲，有臣在。」
entries.en: Bin snapped: “Your Majesty need only silence tongues. I am here.”
entries.literal: Bin blurted: “Your Majesty need only forbid talk—I am here.”

entries.zh: 聞者為之戰慄。
entries.en: Men who heard it shook.
entries.literal: Those who heard trembled.

entries.zh: 李太后弟業求為宣徽使，帝與太后私以問邠，邠止以為不可。
entries.en: The dowager’s brother Ye wanted the Palace Secretariat commission. Emperor and dowager asked Bin in private; he said no.
entries.literal: Empress Dowager Li’s younger brother Ye sought to be Commissioner of the Palace Secretariat. The emperor and the dowager privately asked Bin; Bin would only say it could not be done.

entries.zh: 帝欲立所愛耿夫人為後，邠又以為不可；
entries.en: The emperor meant to make his beloved Lady Geng empress; Bin again refused.
entries.literal: The emperor wished to make his beloved Lady Geng empress; Bin again thought it could not be done.

entries.zh: 夫人死，將以後禮葬之，邠又以為不可。
entries.en: When she died and he meant to bury her as empress, Bin refused once more.
entries.literal: When the lady died and he meant to bury her with empress rites, Bin again thought it could not be done.

entries.zh: 由是隱帝大怒，而左右乘間構之，與史弘肇等同日見殺。
entries.en: The emperor boiled with rage; courtiers drove the wedge deeper. He died the same day as Shi Hongzhao.
entries.literal: From this the Hidden Emperor was greatly enraged, and those around him seized the moment to set him against Bin; on the same day as Shi Hongzhao he was killed.

entries.zh: 王章，魏州南樂人也。
entries.en: Wang Zhang came from Nanle in Weizhou.
entries.literal: Wang Zhang was a native of Nanle in Weizhou.

entries.zh: 為州孔目官，張令昭逐節度使劉延皓，章事令昭。
entries.en: He was a prefectural clerk. When Zhang Lingzhao ousted Liu Yanhao, Zhang served him.
entries.literal: He was a prefectural clerk. When Zhang Lingzhao drove out military commissioner Liu Yanhao, Zhang served Lingzhao.

entries.zh: 令昭敗，章婦翁白文珂與副招討李周善，乃以章托周。
entries.en: Lingzhao fell; Zhang’s father-in-law Bai Wenke knew Deputy Pacification Commissioner Li Zhou and put Zhang in Zhou’s hands.
entries.literal: When Lingzhao was defeated, Zhang’s father-in-law Bai Wenke was on good terms with Deputy Pacification Commissioner Li Zhou; he entrusted Zhang to Zhou.

entries.zh: 周匿章褚中，以橐駝負之洛陽，藏周第。
entries.en: Zhou hid him in a leather sack, had a camel carry him to Luoyang, and kept him in his house.
entries.literal: Zhou hid Zhang in a leather bag and had a camel carry him to Luoyang, concealing him in Zhou’s residence.

entries.zh: 唐滅，章乃出，為河陽糧料使。
entries.en: When Tang fell he emerged and became Heyang grain commissioner.
entries.literal: When Tang fell, Zhang came out and became grain commissioner of Heyang.

entries.zh: 漢高祖典禁兵，補章孔目官，從之太原。
entries.en: When Han’s High Ancestor took the palace guard, Zhang became his clerk and followed him to Taiyuan.
entries.literal: When Han’s High Ancestor commanded the palace guard, Zhang was made clerk and followed him to Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 高祖即位，拜三司使、檢校太尉。
entries.en: At enthronement Zhang became Three Departments commissioner and Acting Grand Commandant.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor took the throne, Zhang was made commissioner of the Three Departments and Acting Grand General.

entries.zh: 高祖崩，隱帝即位，加太尉、同中書門下平章事。
entries.en: The High Ancestor died; the Hidden Emperor made Zhang Grand Commandant and Associate Grand Councilor.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor died and the Hidden Emperor succeeded, Zhang was made Grand General and Associate Grand Councilor.

entries.zh: 是時，漢方新造，承契丹之後，京師空乏，而關西三叛作，周太祖用兵西方，章供饋軍旅，未嘗乏絕。
entries.en: Han was newborn, the capital drained after the Khitan, and the west in revolt. Guo Wei marched west; Zhang fed the armies without fail.
entries.literal: At that time Han was newly founded, coming after the Khitan; the capital was empty and poor. The three western rebellions arose; Zhou Taizu campaigned in the west. Zhang supplied the armies and never fell short.

entries.zh: 然征利剝下，民甚苦之。
entries.en: Yet he squeezed the people, and they suffered.
entries.literal: Yet he squeezed profit from the people below, and the people suffered greatly.

entries.zh: 往時民租一石輸二升為「雀鼠耗」，章乃增一石輸二斗為「省耗」；
entries.en: Once two sheng per shi of rent was lost to “sparrow-and-rat wastage”; Zhang raised it to two dou and called it “provincial wastage.”
entries.literal: Formerly the people’s grain rent had two sheng per shi taken as “sparrow-and-rat wastage”; Zhang increased it to two dou per shi and called it “provincial wastage.”

entries.zh: 緡錢出入，皆以八十為陌，章減其出者陌三；
entries.en: Cash was counted eighty to the string; Zhang shaved three off every string paid out.
entries.literal: When cash went in and out, eighty counted as one string; Zhang reduced outgoing strings by three.

entries.zh: 州縣民訴田者，必全州縣覆之，以括其隱田。
entries.en: One field dispute and the whole county was resurveyed to flush out hidden acres.
entries.literal: When people in prefectures and counties sued over fields, the whole prefecture or county was re-surveyed to expose hidden land.

entries.zh: 天下由此重困。
entries.en: The realm groaned under the double weight.
entries.literal: Under heaven the people were thereby doubly burdened.

entries.zh: 然尤不喜文士，嘗語人曰：「此輩與一把算子，未知顛倒，何益於國邪！」
entries.en: He hated scholars above all. He said: “Hand these people an abacus and they cannot tell up from down—what use are they to the state?”
entries.literal: Yet he especially disliked men of letters. He once told people: “Give this lot an abacus and they still cannot tell which way is up—what good are they to the state?”

entries.zh: 百官俸廩，皆取供軍之余不堪者，命有司高估其價，估定又增，謂之「擡估」，章猶意不能滿，往往復增之。
entries.en: Officials were paid from army leftovers unfit for soldiers. Offices inflated the price, then inflated it again—“inflated appraisal.” Zhang still was not satisfied and raised it yet again.
entries.literal: The hundred offices’ salaries and grain allotments were all taken from what remained after supplying the army—what was unfit for use. He ordered the offices to appraise it high; after appraisal they raised it again—this was called “inflated appraisal.” Zhang still thought it insufficient and often raised it again.

entries.zh: 民有犯鹽、礬、酒曲者，無多少皆抵死，吏緣為奸，民莫堪命。
entries.en: Salt, alum, or yeast—any breach, any amount, meant death. Clerks turned the law to theft; life became unbearable.
entries.literal: People who violated salt, alum, or yeast laws, in whatever amount, all died for it. Clerks used this to commit fraud; the people could not bear life.

entries.zh: 已而與史弘肇等同日見殺。
entries.en: Soon he died the same day as Shi Hongzhao.
entries.literal: Before long he was killed on the same day as Shi Hongzhao.

entries.zh: 銖嘗切齒於史弘肇、楊邠等，已而弘肇等死，銖謂李業等曰：「諸君可謂僂儸兒矣。」
entries.en: Zhu had long ground his teeth at Shi Hongzhao and Yang Bin. When they fell, he told Li Ye’s circle: “You lot are spineless wretches.”
entries.literal: Zhu had often gnashed his teeth at Shi Hongzhao, Yang Bin, and the rest. After Hongzhao and the others died, Zhu told Li Ye and the rest: “You gentlemen may be called spineless wretches.”

entries.zh: 權知開封府，周太祖兵犯京師，銖悉誅太祖與王峻等家屬。
entries.en: As acting governor of Kaifeng, when Guo Wei’s army closed on the capital Zhu slaughtered Guo Wei’s and Wang Jun’s households.
entries.literal: Acting as governor of Kaifeng, when Zhou Taizu’s army threatened the capital Zhu executed the families of Taizu and Wang Jun and the rest.

entries.zh: 太祖入京師，銖妻裸露以席自蔽，與銖俱見執。
entries.en: Guo Wei entered the capital. Zhu’s wife stripped and hid behind a mat; both were taken.
entries.literal: When Taizu entered the capital, Zhu’s wife bared herself and covered herself with a mat; she and Zhu were both seized.

entries.zh: 銖謂其妻曰：「我則死矣，汝應與人為婢。」
entries.en: Zhu told his wife: “I die. You will be someone’s servant.”
entries.literal: Zhu told his wife: “I shall die; you will become someone’s servant girl.”

entries.zh: 太祖使人責銖曰：「與公共事先帝，獨無故人之情乎？
entries.en: Guo Wei sent word: “We served the late emperor together—where is old friendship?
entries.literal: Taizu sent a man to rebuke Zhu: “We served the late emperor together—have you no feeling for an old comrade?

entries.zh: 吾家屠滅，雖有君命，加之酷毒，一何忍也。
entries.en: My house was wiped out. An imperial order is one thing—your cruelty was another. How could you?
entries.literal: My household was wiped out. Though there was an imperial order, you added cruelty on top—how could you bear it?

entries.zh: 今公亦有妻子，獨念之乎？」
entries.en: You have wife and children too—do you think of them?”
entries.literal: Now you too have wife and children—do you not think of them?”

entries.zh: 銖曰：「為漢誅叛臣爾，豈知其佗。」
entries.en: Zhu said: “I killed Han’s rebels. Nothing more.”
entries.literal: Zhu said: “I executed Han’s rebel ministers—that is all. How should I know anything else?”

entries.zh: 是時，太祖方欲歸人心，乃與群臣議曰：「劉侍中墜馬傷甚，而軍士逼辱，迨有微生，吾欲奏太后，貸其家屬，何如？」
entries.en: Guo Wei meant to win hearts and asked his ministers: “Palace Attendant Liu fell hard from his horse; soldiers humiliated him, yet he lives. I would ask the dowager to spare his family—what say you?”
entries.literal: At that time Taizu wished to win hearts and discussed with his ministers: “Palace Attendant Liu fell from his horse and was badly hurt; soldiers pressed and humiliated him, yet he barely lives. I wish to memorialize the dowager and spare his household—what do you think?”

entries.zh: 群臣皆以為善。
entries.en: The ministers approved.
entries.literal: The ministers all thought it good.

entries.zh: 乃止殺銖，與李業等梟首於市，赦其妻子。
entries.en: He then killed only Zhu; Zhu, with Li Ye and the rest, had their heads exposed in the market, and their wives and children were pardoned.
entries.literal: He then limited the killing to Zhu and, with Li Ye and the rest, exposed their heads in the market; their wives and children were pardoned.

entries.zh: 太祖即位，賜陜州莊宅各一區。
entries.en: At enthronement Guo Wei granted each a Shaanzhou estate.
entries.literal: When Taizu took the throne, he granted one estate each in Shaanzhou.

entries.zh: 李業，高祖皇后之弟也。
entries.en: Li Ye was the younger brother of the High Ancestor’s empress.
entries.literal: Li Ye was the younger brother of the High Ancestor’s empress.

entries.zh: 後昆弟七人，業最幼，故尤憐之。
entries.en: Seven brothers she had; Ye was youngest and most favored.
entries.literal: The empress had seven brothers; Ye was the youngest, and therefore especially doted upon.

entries.zh: 高祖時，以為武德使。
entries.en: Under the High Ancestor he held the Martial Virtue commission.
entries.literal: Under the High Ancestor he was made Commissioner of Martial Virtue.

entries.zh: 隱帝即位，業以皇太后故，益用事，無顧憚。
entries.en: The Hidden Emperor’s reign let Ye rule through the dowager, without restraint.
entries.literal: When the Hidden Emperor succeeded, because of the empress dowager Ye wielded power still more and feared nothing.

entries.zh: 時天下旱、蝗，黃河決溢，京師大風拔木，壞城門，宮中數見怪物投瓦石、撼門扉。
entries.en: Drought and locusts scourged the land; the Yellow River broke; wind uprooted trees and smashed gates; in the palace things threw stones and rattled doors.
entries.literal: At that time drought and locusts afflicted the realm; the Yellow River burst its banks; a great wind in the capital uprooted trees and broke city gates; within the palace monsters were often seen throwing tiles and stones and shaking doors.

entries.zh: 隱帝召司天趙延乂問禳除之法，延乂對曰：「臣職天象日時，察其變動，以考順逆吉兇而已，禳除之事，非臣所知也。
entries.en: The emperor called Zhao Yanyi of the Astronomy Bureau and asked how to expiate the omens. Yanyi said: “I read heaven’s changes and judge fortune and ruin—that is my charge. Expiation is not mine to know.
entries.literal: The Hidden Emperor summoned the Director of Astronomy Zhao Yanyi and asked methods of expiation. Yanyi answered: “My office watches the heavens, day and time, observes their changes, and examines fortune and misfortune, compliance and rebellion—that is all. Matters of expiation are not within my knowledge.

entries.zh: 然臣所聞，殆山魈也。」
entries.en: What I have heard sounds like a mountain demon.”
entries.literal: Yet what I have heard—it is likely a mountain demon.”

entries.zh: 皇太后乃召尼誦佛書以禳之，一尼如廁，既還，悲泣不知人者數日，及醒訊之，莫知其然。
entries.en: The dowager sent nuns to chant sutras. One went to the privy; she returned weeping, lost to herself for days, and when she woke could explain nothing.
entries.literal: The empress dowager then summoned nuns to chant Buddhist scriptures for expiation. One nun went to the privy; when she returned she wept in grief and did not know herself for several days; when she woke and was questioned, no one knew why.

entries.zh: 而帝方與業及聶文進、後贊、郭允明等狎昵，多為廋語相誚戲，放紙鳶於宮中。
entries.en: The emperor meanwhile caroused with Ye, Nie Wenjin, Hou Zan, and Guo Yunming—veiled jests, mockery, paper kites in the palace.
entries.literal: Meanwhile the emperor was on intimate terms with Ye, Nie Wenjin, Hou Zan, Guo Yunming, and the rest, often trading veiled jests and mockery, flying paper kites in the palace.

entries.zh: 太后數以災異戒帝，不聽。
entries.en: The dowager warned him with every omen; he would not hear.
entries.literal: The empress dowager repeatedly warned the emperor with omens and disasters; he would not listen.

entries.zh: 時宣徽使闕，業欲得之，太后亦遣人諷大臣。
entries.en: The Palace Secretariat commission stood empty; Ye wanted it, and the dowager hinted the ministers.
entries.literal: At that time the Commissioner of the Palace Secretariat was vacant; Ye wished to obtain it, and the empress dowager also sent men to hint the great ministers.

entries.zh: 大臣楊邠、史弘肇等皆以為不可。
entries.en: Yang Bin, Shi Hongzhao, and the rest all refused.
entries.literal: The great ministers Yang Bin, Shi Hongzhao, and the rest all thought it could not be done.

entries.zh: 業由此怨望，謀殺邠等。
entries.en: Ye nursed the grudge and plotted their deaths.
entries.literal: From this Ye nursed resentment and plotted to kill Bin and the rest.

entries.zh: 邠等已死。
entries.en: Bin and the rest were dead.
entries.literal: Bin and the rest were already dead.

entries.zh: 又遣供奉官孟業以詔書殺郭威於魏州。
entries.en: He sent Palace Attendant Meng Ye with an edict to kill Guo Wei at Weizhou.
entries.literal: He again sent Palace Attendant Meng Ye with an edict to kill Guo Wei at Weizhou.

entries.zh: 威舉兵反，隱帝遣左神武統軍袁泬、侍衛馬軍都指揮使閻晉卿等率兵拒威於澶淵。
entries.en: Guo Wei rebelled. The emperor sent Yuan Xue and Yan Jinqing against him at Chanyuan.
entries.literal: Wei raised troops in rebellion. The Hidden Emperor sent Left Divine Martial Commander Yuan Xue, Palace Horse Guard Commander Yan Jinqing, and the rest to lead troops against Wei at Chanyuan.

entries.zh: 兵未出，威已至滑州，帝大懼，謂大臣曰：「昨太草草耳。」
entries.en: Before the army moved, Guo Wei was already at Huazhou. The emperor was terrified and told his ministers: “Yesterday we moved too rashly.”
entries.literal: Before the army marched out, Wei had already reached Huazhou. The emperor was greatly afraid and told the ministers: “Yesterday we were far too hasty.”

entries.zh: 業請出府庫以賚軍，宰相蘇禹珪以為未可，業拜禹珪於帝前曰：「相公且為官家勿惜府庫。」
entries.en: Ye asked to open the vaults and pay the troops. Su Yu Gui hesitated; Ye bowed to him before the throne: “Chancellor, for the emperor’s sake—do not hoard the treasury.”
entries.literal: Ye asked to open the treasury and reward the army. Chancellor Su Yu Gui thought it not yet permissible; Ye bowed to Yu Gui before the emperor and said: “Chancellor, for the ruler’s sake do not spare the treasury.”

entries.zh: 乃詔賜京師兵及魏兵從威南者錢人十千，督其子弟作書，以告北兵之來者。
entries.en: An edict paid ten thousand cash per man to capital troops and every soldier who had followed Guo Wei south, and pressed their kin to write north and summon more men.
entries.literal: An edict then granted ten thousand cash per man to capital troops and Wei troops south with Wei, urging their sons and younger brothers to write letters telling northern troops to come.

entries.zh: 及漢兵敗於北郊，業取內庫金寶，懷之以奔其兄保義軍節度使洪信，洪信拒而不納。
entries.en: When Han’s army was defeated at the northern suburb, Ye stuffed the inner treasury’s gold into his robes and fled to his brother Hongxin at Baoyi; Hongxin turned him away.
entries.literal: When Han’s army was defeated at the northern suburb, Ye took gold and jewels from the inner treasury, hid them on his person, and fled to his elder brother Hongxin, military commissioner of Baoyi; Hongxin refused him and would not admit him.

entries.zh: 業走至絳州，為人所殺。
entries.en: He ran to Jiangzhou and men there killed him.
entries.literal: Ye fled to Jiangzhou and was killed by men there.

entries.zh: 聶文進，并州人也。
entries.en: Nie Wenjin came from Bingzhou.
entries.literal: Nie Wenjin was a native of Bingzhou.

entries.zh: 少為軍卒，善書算，給事漢高祖帳中。
entries.en: As a youth he was a soldier, skilled at writing and reckoning, and served in the Han High Ancestor’s tent.
entries.literal: In youth he was a soldier, skilled at writing and reckoning, and served in the Han High Ancestor’s tent.

entries.zh: 高祖鎮太原，以為押司官。
entries.en: When the High Ancestor held Taiyuan, he made Wenjin auditing clerk.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor governed Taiyuan, he was made auditing clerk.

entries.zh: 高祖即位，歷拜領軍屯衞將軍、樞密院承旨。
entries.en: At the High Ancestor’s accession he rose to General of the Garrison Guard and Privy Council registrar.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor took the throne, Wenjin was promoted in succession to General of the Garrison Guard and registrar of the Privy Council.

entries.zh: 周太祖為樞密使，頗親信之，文進稍橫恣。
entries.en: Zhou Taizu, as chief of the Privy Council, trusted him deeply, and Wenjin grew arrogant.
entries.literal: When Zhou Taizu was chief of the Privy Council, he trusted Wenjin greatly, and Wenjin gradually grew arrogant and unrestrained.

entries.zh: 遷右領軍大將軍，入謝，召諸將軍設食朝堂，儀鸞、翰林、御廚供帳飲食，文進自如，有司不敢劾。
entries.en: Made Grand General of the Right Garrison Guard, he came to give thanks. The emperor summoned the generals and set a feast in the court hall; Ceremonial Escort, Hanlin, and Imperial Kitchen supplied the spread. Wenjin acted as he pleased, and no official dared object.
entries.literal: Promoted to Grand General of the Right Garrison Guard, he entered to give thanks. The emperor summoned the generals and set out food in the court hall; the Ceremonial Escort, Hanlin, and Imperial Kitchen supplied tents, food, and drink. Wenjin acted as he pleased, and the officials dared not impeach him.

entries.zh: 周太祖鎮鄴，文進等用事居中，及謀殺楊邠等，文進夜作詔書，制置中外。
entries.en: When Zhou Taizu held Ye, Wenjin and his circle ruled the court. When they plotted to kill Yang Bin and the rest, Wenjin drafted edicts by night and disposed affairs at home and abroad.
entries.literal: When Zhou Taizu governed Ye, Wenjin and the others held power at court. When they plotted to kill Yang Bin and the rest, Wenjin drafted edicts by night and disposed affairs within and without.

entries.zh: 邠等已死，文進點閱兵籍，指麾殺戮，以為己任。
entries.en: Once Bin and the rest were dead, Wenjin reviewed the rolls, directed the slaughter, and made it his personal task.
entries.literal: After Bin and the rest were dead, Wenjin reviewed the military registers, directed killings, and took this as his own charge.

entries.zh: 周太祖在鄴聞邠等遇害，初以為文進不與，及發詔書，皆文進手跡，乃大詬之。
entries.en: At Ye, Zhou Taizu heard Bin and the rest had been killed. At first he thought Wenjin was innocent, but when the edicts appeared, every line was Wenjin’s hand—and he cursed him bitterly.
entries.literal: Zhou Taizu at Ye heard that Bin and the rest had been killed. At first he thought Wenjin had not taken part, but when the edicts were issued, all were in Wenjin’s hand—and he cursed him bitterly.

entries.zh: 後贊，兗州瑕丘人。
entries.en: Hou Zan came from Xiqiu in Yan Prefecture.
entries.literal: Hou Zan was a native of Xiqiu in Yan Prefecture.

entries.zh: 其母，倡也。
entries.en: His mother was a singing girl.
entries.literal: His mother was a courtesan.

entries.zh: 贊幼善謳，事張延朗。
entries.en: Zan sang well from childhood and served Zhang Yanlang.
entries.literal: As a boy Zan was skilled at song and served Zhang Yanlang.

entries.zh: 延朗死，贊更事漢高祖，高祖愛之，以為牙將。
entries.en: Yanlang died; Zan entered the Han High Ancestor’s service. The High Ancestor favored him and made him a guard officer.
entries.literal: When Yanlang died, Zan entered the service of the Han High Ancestor, who favored him and made him a guard officer.

entries.zh: 高祖即位，拜飛龍使，隱帝尤愛幸之。
entries.en: At enthronement Zan became Dragon Flight Commissioner; the Hidden Emperor doted on him above all others.
entries.literal: When the High Ancestor took the throne, Zan was made Dragon Flight Commissioner; the Hidden Emperor cherished him above all.

entries.zh: 楊邠等執政，贊久不得遷，乃共謀殺邠等。
entries.en: Yang Bin and his faction ruled; Zan languished without promotion. He joined the plot to kill them.
entries.literal: Yang Bin and others held power, and Zan long went without promotion. He therefore joined in plotting to kill Bin and the rest.

entries.zh: 邠等死，隱帝悔之，贊與允明等番休侍帝，不欲左右言已短。
entries.en: Bin and the rest were dead; the Hidden Emperor repented. Zan and Yunming rotated attendance at his side so no courtier could whisper against them.
entries.literal: When Bin and the others were dead, the Hidden Emperor repented. Zan and Yunming took turns attending the emperor in rotation, lest anyone nearby speak ill of them.

entries.zh: 隱帝兵敗北郊，贊奔兗州，慕容彥超執送京師，梟首於市。
entries.en: The Hidden Emperor lost at the Northern Suburb. Zan fled to Yan; Murong Yanchao captured him, sent him to the capital, and had his head hung in the market.
entries.literal: When the Hidden Emperor’s army was defeated at the Northern Suburb, Zan fled to Yan Prefecture. Murong Yanchao seized him and sent him to the capital, where his head was displayed in the marketplace.

entries.zh: 周兵至京師，隱帝敗於北郊，太后懼，使謂文進善衛帝，對曰：「臣在此，百郭威何害！」
entries.en: Zhou troops reached the capital; the Hidden Emperor fell at the Northern Suburb. The empress dowager was terrified and asked Wenjin to guard the emperor. He replied: “While I stand here, what harm are a hundred Guo Weis?”
entries.literal: When Zhou’s troops reached the capital and the Hidden Emperor was defeated at the Northern Suburb, the empress dowager was afraid. She sent word asking Wenjin to guard the emperor well. He answered: “As long as I am here, what harm can a hundred Guo Weis do!”

entries.zh: 慕容彥超敗走，帝宿於七里，文進夜與其徒飲酒，歌呼自若。
entries.en: Murong Yanchao broke and fled. The emperor slept at Qili. Wenjin spent the night drinking with his men, singing and shouting as if the world were still whole.
entries.literal: Murong Yanchao was defeated and fled. The emperor lodged at Qili. That night Wenjin drank with his followers, singing and shouting as if nothing were amiss.

entries.zh: 明旦，隱帝遇弒，文進亦自殺。
entries.en: At dawn the Hidden Emperor was murdered. Wenjin took his own life.
entries.literal: At dawn the Hidden Emperor was assassinated. Wenjin killed himself as well.

entries.zh: 郭允明，少為漢高祖廝養，高祖愛之，以為翰林茶酒使。
entries.en: Guo Yunming had from youth been a steward in the Han High Ancestor’s household. The High Ancestor favored him and made him Hanlin Commissioner of Tea and Wine.
entries.literal: Guo Yunming had from youth been a steward in the Han High Ancestor’s household. The High Ancestor favored him and made him Hanlin Commissioner of Tea and Wine.

entries.zh: 隱帝尤狎愛之，允明益驕橫無顧避，大臣不能禁。
entries.en: The Hidden Emperor doted on him. Yunming grew brazen and unchecked; the great ministers could not stop him.
entries.literal: The Hidden Emperor was especially fond of him. Yunming grew ever more arrogant and reckless, and the great ministers could not restrain him.

entries.zh: 允明使荊南高保融，車服導從如節度使，保融待之甚厚。
entries.en: Yunming went as envoy to Gao Baorong of Jingnan with the carriage, robes, and escort of a military governor. Baorong treated him lavishly.
entries.literal: Yunming was sent as envoy to Gao Baorong of Jingnan, with carriage, robes, and retinue like a military governor. Baorong received him with great honor.

entries.zh: 允明乃陰使人步測其城池高下，若為攻取之計者以動之。
entries.en: Yunming secretly had men pace the walls and measure their height—as though planning conquest—to frighten him.
entries.literal: Yunming secretly sent men to pace and measure the height of the city walls, as if planning an attack, to intimidate him.

entries.zh: 荊人皆恐，保融厚賂以遺之。
entries.en: All Jingnan trembled. Baorong paid him off handsomely to see him gone.
entries.literal: The people of Jing were all afraid. Baorong gave him rich bribes to send him away.

entries.zh: 遷飛龍使。
entries.en: He was made Dragon Flight Commissioner.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Dragon Flight Commissioner.

entries.zh: 已而李業與允明謀殺楊邠等，是日無雲而昏，霧雨如泣，日中，載邠等十餘屍暴之市中。
entries.en: Li Ye and Yunming plotted to kill Yang Bin and the rest. That day the sky blackened though there were no clouds; misty rain fell like tears. At noon a dozen corpses were hauled into the market and left on display.
entries.literal: Soon Li Ye and Yunming plotted to kill Yang Bin and the others. That day, though cloudless, the sky darkened; misty rain fell like weeping. At noon more than ten corpses of Bin and the rest were loaded and exposed in the marketplace.

entries.zh: 允明手殺邠等諸子於朝堂西廡，王章婿張貽肅血流逆註。
entries.en: Yunming himself killed Bin’s sons and the others in the western corridor of the hall. Wang Zhang’s son-in-law Zhang Yisi bled upward in streams.
entries.literal: Yunming personally killed the sons of Bin and the others in the western corridor of the court hall. Wang Zhang’s son-in-law Zhang Yisi had blood flowing upward in streams.

entries.zh: 隱帝敗於北郊，還至封丘門，不得入，帝走趙村，允明從後追之，弒帝於民舍，乃自殺。
entries.en: Defeated at the Northern Suburb, the Hidden Emperor reached Fengqiu Gate but could not pass. He fled toward Zhao Village. Yunming ran him down, murdered him in a peasant house, and then took his own life.
entries.literal: The Hidden Emperor was defeated at the Northern Suburb. Returning to Fengqiu Gate, he could not enter. The emperor fled to Zhao Village. Yunming pursued from behind, assassinated the emperor in a commoner’s house, then killed himself.

entries.zh: 蘇逢吉
entries.en: Su Fengji
entries.literal: Su Fengji

entries.zh: 王朴，字文伯，東平人也。
entries.en: Wang Pu, styled Wenbo, came from Dongping.
entries.literal: Wang Pu, styled Wenbo, was a native of Dongping.

entries.zh: 少舉進士，為校書郎，依漢樞密使楊邠。
entries.en: He passed the jinshi while young, became a proofreader, and served under Yang Bin, Han’s Privy Council commissioner.
entries.literal: In youth he passed the jinshi examination, became proofreader, and attached himself to Yang Bin, Privy Council commissioner of Han.

entries.zh: 邠與王章、史弘肇等有隙，朴見漢興日淺，隱帝年少孱弱，任用小人，而邠為大臣，與將相交惡，知其必亂，乃去邠東歸。
entries.en: Bin feuded with Wang Zhang, Shi Hongzhao, and others. Pu saw Han still new, the Hidden Emperor young and frail, petty men in power—and Bin, a chief minister, at war with the generals. He knew ruin was coming and left Bin for the east.
entries.literal: Bin had a rift with Wang Zhang, Shi Hongzhao, and others. Pu saw that Han had risen only recently, that the Hidden Emperor was young and weak and employed petty men, and that Bin as a chief minister was at odds with the generals. Knowing chaos must follow, he left Bin and returned east.

entries.zh: 後李業等教隱帝誅權臣，邠與章、弘肇皆見殺，三家之客多及，而朴以故獨免。
entries.en: Later Li Ye and others persuaded the Hidden Emperor to purge the powerful ministers. Bin, Zhang, and Hongzhao were killed; clients of all three houses fell with them—Pu alone was spared, having left in time.
entries.literal: Later Li Ye and others urged the Hidden Emperor to execute the powerful ministers; Bin, Zhang, and Hongzhao were all killed, and many clients of the three households were implicated—yet Pu alone escaped because of his prior departure.

entries.zh: 周世宗鎮澶州，朴為節度掌書記。
entries.en: When Shizong of Zhou held Chanz, Pu was the military governor’s chief secretary.
entries.literal: When Zhou Shizong governed Chanz, Pu served as the military governor’s chief secretary.

entries.zh: 世宗為開封尹，拜朴右拾遺，為推官。
entries.en: When Shizong became Kaifeng Intendant, Pu was made Right Reminder and investigating officer.
entries.literal: When Shizong became Kaifeng Intendant, Pu was appointed Right Reminder and made investigating officer.

entries.zh: 世宗即位，遷比部郎中，獻《平邊策》，曰：
entries.en: At Shizong’s accession Pu rose to Director in the Ministry of Revenue and submitted his “Pacifying the Borderlands” memorial:
entries.literal: When Shizong took the throne, Pu was promoted to Director in the Ministry of Revenue and submitted the “Pacifying the Borderlands” memorial, saying:

entries.zh: 遷左諫議大夫，知開封府事。
entries.en: He rose to Left Remonstrance Councillor and took charge of Kaifeng.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Left Remonstrance Councillor and made administrator of Kaifeng.

entries.zh: 歲中，遷左散騎常侍，充端明殿學士。
entries.en: Within the year he became Left Regular Attendant and Academician of the Hall of Manifest Brightness.
entries.literal: Within the year he was promoted to Left Regular Attendant and made Academician of the Hall of Manifest Brightness.

entries.zh: 是時，世宗新即位，銳意征伐，已撓群議，親敗劉旻於高平，歸而益治兵，慨然有平一天下之志。
entries.en: Shizong had just taken the throne, hungry for war. He had already silenced the doubters, beaten Liu Min at Gaoping himself, and returned to drill the armies harder—suddenly burning to unite the realm.
entries.literal: At that time Shizong had newly acceded, was keen on campaigns, had already overborne collective opinion, had personally defeated Liu Min at Gaoping, and on returning further drilled the armies—suddenly possessed of the will to pacify all under Heaven.

entries.zh: 數顧大臣問治道，選文學之士徐臺符等二十人，使作《為君難為臣不易論》及《平邊策》，朴在選中。
entries.en: Again and again he asked his ministers how to rule. He picked twenty literary men, Xu Taifu among them, and set them to write “On the Difficulty of Being Ruler and the Difficulty of Being Minister” and “Pacifying the Borderlands”—Pu was chosen.
entries.literal: Repeatedly he turned to his ministers to ask the way of governance, selected twenty literary men including Xu Taifu, and had them compose “On the Difficulty of Being Ruler and the Difficulty of Being Minister” and “Pacifying the Borderlands”—Pu was among those chosen.

entries.zh: 而當時文士皆不欲上急於用武，以謂平定僭亂，在修文德以為先。
entries.en: Most literati of the day did not want the throne to hurry into war. Usurpation, they said, yields only to civil virtue first.
entries.literal: Yet the literati of the time did not wish the throne to rush into war, holding that to settle usurpation and disorder one must first cultivate civil virtue.

entries.zh: 惟翰林學士陶谷竇儀、御史中丞楊昭儉與朴皆言用兵之策，朴謂江淮為可先取。
entries.en: Only Hanlin Academician Tao Gu, Dou Yi, Censor-in-Chief Yang Zhaojian, and Pu argued for war—and Pu said take the Jianghuai first.
entries.literal: Only Hanlin Academician Tao Gu, Dou Yi, Censor-in-Chief Yang Zhaojian, and Pu all spoke of military strategy; Pu said the Jianghuai could be taken first.

entries.zh: 世宗雅已知朴，及見其議論偉然，益以為奇，引與計議天下事，無不合，遂決意用之。
entries.en: Shizong had known Pu for years; now his arguments struck like thunder, and Shizong found him even more extraordinary. He brought Pu into every plan for the realm. Nothing clashed. He decided to use him without reserve.
entries.literal: Shizong had long known Pu; when he saw his discourse so bold, he thought him even more remarkable, drew him into planning the realm’s affairs—nothing failed to agree—and resolved to employ him fully.

entries.zh: 顯德三年，征淮，以仆為東京副留守。
entries.en: Xiande year three, on the Huai campaign, Pu was made Deputy Commissioner of the Eastern Capital.
entries.literal: In the third year of Xiande, during the Huai campaign, Pu was made Deputy Commissioner of the Eastern Capital.

entries.zh: 還，拜戶部侍郎、樞密副使，遷樞密使。
entries.en: Back from the field he became Vice Minister of Revenue and Deputy Privy Council Commissioner, then Privy Council Commissioner.
entries.literal: On return he was appointed Vice Minister of Revenue and Deputy Privy Council Commissioner, then promoted to Privy Council Commissioner.

entries.zh: 四年，再征淮，以朴留守京師。
entries.en: Year four, on the second Huai campaign, Pu stayed behind to hold the capital.
entries.literal: In the fourth year, on the second Huai campaign, Pu was left to hold the capital.

entries.zh: 六年春，世宗遣朴行視汴口，作斗門，還，過故相李穀第，疾作，仆於坐上，舁歸而卒，年五十四。
entries.en: Spring of year six, Shizong sent Pu to inspect the Bian mouth and build sluice gates. On the way back he stopped at former chancellor Li Gu’s house; sickness took him, he fell from his seat, was carried home, and died at fifty-four.
entries.literal: In spring of the sixth year Shizong sent Pu to inspect the Bian mouth and build sluice gates. Returning, he passed the mansion of the former chancellor Li Gu; illness seized him, he collapsed in his seat, was carried home, and died—aged fifty-four.

entries.zh: 世宗臨其喪，以玉鉞叩地，大慟者數四。
entries.en: Shizong came to his funeral, struck the ground with the jade axe of mourning, and broke into great wailing four times.
entries.literal: Shizong attended his funeral, struck the ground with a jade axe-symbol, and wailed greatly four times.

entries.zh: 贈侍中。
entries.en: He was posthumously made Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: He was posthumously made Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 鄭仁誨，字日新，太原晉陽人也。
entries.en: Zheng Renhui, styled Rixin, came from Jinyang in Taiyuan.
entries.literal: Zheng Renhui, styled Rixin, was a native of Jinyang in Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 初，事唐將陳紹光。
entries.en: He first served the Tang general Chen Shaoguang.
entries.literal: At first he served the Tang general Chen Shaoguang.

entries.zh: 紹光為人驍勇而好使酒，嘗因醉怒仁誨，拔劍欲殺之，左右皆奔走，仁誨植立不動，無懼色，紹光擲劍於地，撫仁誨曰：「汝有器量，必富貴，非吾所及也。」
entries.en: Shaoguang was a fierce drinker. Once, drunk and furious at Renhui, he drew his sword to kill him. Everyone fled; Renhui stood still, unafraid. Shaoguang flung down his sword, clapped Renhui’s shoulder, and said: “You have the measure of a great man—you will rise high. That is beyond me.”
entries.literal: Shaoguang was fierce and brave and loved his wine. Once, drunk and angry at Renhui, he drew his sword to kill him. Those around all fled; Renhui stood rooted, unmoving, without fear. Shaoguang threw his sword to the ground, stroked Renhui, and said: “You have breadth of character—you will surely be rich and noble; that is not within my reach.”

entries.zh: 仁誨後棄紹光去，還鄉里，事母以孝聞。
entries.en: Renhui later left Shaoguang, went home, and became known for honoring his mother.
entries.literal: Renhui later abandoned Shaoguang, returned to his home district, and was known for filial service to his mother.

entries.zh: 漢高祖為河東節度使，周太祖居帳下，時時往過仁誨，與語甚歡。
entries.en: When Han Gaozu governed Hedong, Zhou Taizu served in his camp and often called on Renhui—they talked as old friends.
entries.literal: When Han Gaozu was military governor of Hedong, Zhou Taizu served under his banner and often visited Renhui; their talk was very pleasant.

entries.zh: 每事有疑，即從仁誨質問，仁誨所對不阿，周太祖益奇之。
entries.en: When Taizu was uncertain, he went to Renhui for plain answers. Renhui never flattered—and Taizu prized him the more.
entries.literal: Whenever Taizu doubted a matter he would go straight to Renhui to question him; Renhui’s answers did not flatter, and Taizu admired him all the more.

entries.zh: 漢興，周太祖為樞密使，乃召仁誨用之，累官至內客省使。
entries.en: When Han was established, Taizu became Privy Council Commissioner and brought Renhui in; he rose step by step to Commissioner of the Inner Clients Bureau.
entries.literal: When Han rose, Zhou Taizu became Privy Council Commissioner and summoned Renhui to serve; he rose by degrees to Commissioner of the Inner Clients Bureau.

entries.zh: 太祖破李守貞於河中，軍中機畫，仁誨多所參決。
entries.en: When Taizu broke Li Shouzhen at Hezhong, Renhui helped decide much of the army’s strategy.
entries.literal: When Taizu broke Li Shouzhen at Hezhong, Renhui took part in many of the army’s strategic decisions.

entries.zh: 太祖入立，以仁誨為大內都點檢、恩州團練使、樞密副使，累遷宣徽北院使，出為鎮寧軍節度使。
entries.en: When Taizu took the throne he made Renhui Grand Inspector of the Inner Palace, Military Training Commissioner of Enzhou, and Deputy Privy Council Commissioner; he rose to Commissioner of the Northern Hall of the Palace Secretariat, then went out to govern the Zhenning Army.
entries.literal: When Taizu entered and took the throne, he made Renhui Grand Inspector of the Inner Palace, Military Training Commissioner of Enzhou, and Deputy Privy Council Commissioner; he was promoted by degrees to Commissioner of the Northern Hall of the Palace Secretariat, then went out as military governor of the Zhenning Army.

entries.zh: 顯德元年，拜樞密使。
entries.en: Xiande year one, he became Privy Council Commissioner.
entries.literal: In the first year of Xiande he was made Privy Council Commissioner.

entries.zh: 世宗攻河東，仁誨留守東都。
entries.en: When Shizong attacked Hedong, Renhui stayed behind to hold the eastern capital.
entries.literal: When Shizong attacked Hedong, Renhui remained to hold the eastern capital.

entries.zh: 明年冬，以疾卒。
entries.en: The next winter he died of illness.
entries.literal: The next winter he died of illness.

entries.zh: 世宗將臨其喪，有司言歲不利臨喪，世宗不聽，乃先以桃荝而臨之。
entries.en: Shizong meant to attend his funeral; the officials warned that the year was ill-omened for mourning. Shizong refused to heed them, performed the peach-branch and reed exorcism, and went anyway.
entries.literal: Shizong meant to attend his funeral; the officials said the year was unfavorable for attending funerals. Shizong would not listen and first performed the peach-branch and reed rite before going to mourn.

entries.zh: 是時，天子英武，樂延天下奇才，而尤禮文士，載與張昭、竇儼、陶穀、徐臺符等俱被進用。
entries.en: The Son of Heaven was bold and martial, hungry for extraordinary men, and especially honored men of letters. Zai, with Zhang Zhao, Dou Yan, Tao Gu, Xu Taifu, and others, all rose into office.
entries.literal: At that time the Son of Heaven was heroic and martial, delighted to gather the realm’s extraordinary men, and especially honored literati. Zai, together with Zhang Zhao, Dou Yan, Tao Gu, Xu Taifu, and others, were all promoted and employed.

entries.zh: 穀居數人中，文辭最劣，尤無行。
entries.en: Among them Gu wrote worst—and behaved worst.
entries.literal: Among those several men, Gu’s literary skill was the worst—and his conduct especially lacking.

entries.zh: 昭、儼數與論議，其文粲然，而穀徒能先意所在，以進諛取合人主，事無大小，必稱美頌贊，至於廣京城，為木偶耕人、紫芝白兔之類，皆為頌以獻，其辭大抵類俳優。
entries.en: Zhao and Yan often argued with him; their prose shone. Gu could only read the ruler’s mood, flatter ahead of it, and praise every deed, great or small. Widening the capital, wooden farm figures, purple fungus, white hares—all won his hymns of praise, his words mostly fit for a clown.
entries.literal: Zhao and Yan often debated with him; their writing blazed—but Gu could only anticipate the ruler’s mind, advance flattery to win favor, and on matters large or small always offer praise and eulogy. Even widening the capital city, wooden farm figures, purple fungus, white hares—all received his celebratory odes, his words mostly like a jester’s.

entries.zh: 而載以不幸早卒，論議雖不及昭、儼，而不為穀之諛也。
entries.en: Zai, cut off young, never matched Zhao and Yan in argument—but he never flattered like Gu.
entries.literal: Zai, through misfortune, died young; in debate he did not reach Zhao and Yan—yet he did not flatter as Gu did.

entries.zh: 世宗之時，外事征伐，而內修法度。
entries.en: Under Shizong, war ran outward and law was rebuilt within.
entries.literal: In Shizong’s time, foreign affairs meant campaigns while domestic affairs meant repairing law.

entries.zh: 朴為人明敏多材智，非獨當世之務，至於陰陽律歷之法，莫不通焉。
entries.en: Pu was quick, brilliant, and many-sided—not only in the business of the day. Yin and yang, pitch pipes, calendrics: there was no art he did not command.
entries.literal: Pu was bright, keen, and rich in talent—not only in affairs of the age; in yin-yang, pitch pipes, and calendrics he had no branch he did not master.

entries.zh: 顯德二年，詔朴校定大歷，乃削去近世符天流俗不經之學，設通、經、統三法，以歲軌離交朔望周變率策之數，步日月五星，為《欽天曆》。
entries.en: Xiande year two, an edict put Pu to revising the Great Calendar. He stripped out recent Futian astrology and folk superstition, set up three methods—comprehensive, canonical, and systematic—and from the year’s track, lunar nodes, new and full moons, cyclical shifts, rates, and procedures calculated sun, moon, and the five planets, producing the Qintian Calendar.
entries.literal: In the second year of Xiande, an edict ordered Pu to revise the Great Calendar. He cut away recent Futian and vulgar, unorthodox learning, established three methods—comprehensive, canonical, and systematic—and from the numbers of the year’s track, lunar nodes, new and full moons, cyclical changes, rates, and procedures calculated sun, moon, and the five planets, producing the Qintian Calendar.

entries.zh: 六年，又詔朴考正雅樂，朴以謂十二律管互吹，難得其真，乃依京房為律準，以九尺之弦十三，依管長短寸分設柱，用七聲為均，樂成而和。
entries.en: Year six brought another edict: rectify court music. Pu argued that cross-blowing the twelve pitch pipes never yields true pitch. Following Jing Fang, he built a pitch standard, strung thirteen nine-foot strings, set bridges to each pipe’s length in inches and fractions, tuned to the seven-tone scale—and the music, finished, rang true.
entries.literal: In the sixth year another edict ordered Pu to rectify court music. Pu held that when the twelve pitch pipes blow against one another, the true pitch is hard to obtain; he therefore followed Jing Fang’s pitch standard, set thirteen strings of nine feet, placed bridges according to each pipe’s length in inches and fractions, used the seven tones as the mean—and the music, once complete, was harmonious.

entries.zh: 朴性剛果，又見信於世宗，凡其所為，當時無敢難者，然人亦莫能加也。
entries.en: Pu was hard and decisive, and Shizong believed in him. Whatever he undertook, no one dared stand in his way—nor could anyone outdo him.
entries.literal: Pu’s nature was firm and decisive, and Shizong trusted him; whatever he did, none in his day dared oppose him—yet none could surpass him either.

entries.zh: 世宗征淮，朴留京師，廣新城，通道路，莊偉宏闊，今京師之制，多其所規為。
entries.en: While Shizong fought on the Huai, Pu stayed in the capital, widened the new city, opened roads—monumental and vast. Much of today’s capital plan is his work.
entries.literal: When Shizong campaigned on the Huai, Pu remained at the capital, expanded the new city, opened roads—grand, vast, and broad. Much of the capital’s present layout was his design.

entries.zh: 其所作樂，至今用之不可變。
entries.en: The music he made is still used today—and cannot be altered.
entries.literal: The music he made is still used today and cannot be changed.

entries.zh: 其陳用兵之略，非特一時之策。
entries.en: The strategy he laid out was not a plan for one season alone.
entries.literal: The military strategy he laid out was not a plan for one season only.

entries.zh: 至言諸國興滅次第云：「淮南可最先取，並必死之寇，最後亡。」
entries.en: He even named the order of rise and fall: “Take Huainan first. Bing—the enemy that dies fighting—falls last.”
entries.literal: He even spoke of the order in which states would rise and fall: “Huainan can be taken first; Bing, the foe that fights to the death, will perish last.”

entries.zh: 其後宋興，平定四方，惟並獨後服，皆如朴言。
entries.en: When Song rose and settled the four quarters, only Bing submitted last—exactly as Pu foretold.
entries.literal: Later when Song rose and pacified the four quarters, only Bing submitted last—all as Pu had said.

entries.zh: 仁誨自其微時，常為太祖謀畫，及居大位，未嘗有所聞，而太祖、世宗皆親重之，然亦能謙謹好禮，不自矜伐，為士大夫所稱。
entries.en: From humble days Renhui had advised Taizu; in high office he never traded on it—yet Taizu and Shizong both cherished him. He remained modest, courteous, and ritual-minded, never vaunting himself, and the literati spoke well of him.
entries.literal: From his humble days Renhui had often plotted for Taizu; once in high office nothing was ever heard of him—yet Taizu and Shizong both held him in personal esteem. He was also humble, courteous, and fond of ritual, never boasting of himself, and the literati praised him.

entries.zh: 贈中書令，追封韓國公，謚曰忠正。
entries.en: He was posthumously made Grand Councillor, enfeoffed as Duke of Han, and given the posthumous title Loyal and Upright.
entries.literal: He was posthumously made Grand Councillor, enfeoffed posthumously as Duke of Han, and given the posthumous title Loyal and Upright.

entries.zh: 扈載，字仲熙，北燕人也。
entries.en: Hu Zai, styled Zhongxi, came from Northern Yan.
entries.literal: Hu Zai, styled Zhongxi, was a native of Northern Yan.

entries.zh: 少好學，善屬文。
entries.en: As a youth he loved books and wrote well.
entries.literal: In youth he loved learning and was skilled at composition.

entries.zh: 廣順初，舉進士高第，拜校書郎，直史館。
entries.en: Early in Guangshun he took the jinshi with top honors, became proofreader, and served in the History Institute.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Guangshun he passed the jinshi with high rank, was appointed proofreader, and served directly in the History Institute.

entries.zh: 再遷監察御史。
entries.en: He was promoted again to Investigating Censor.
entries.literal: He was promoted again to Investigating Censor.

entries.zh: 其為文章，以辭多自喜。
entries.en: In his prose he took pride in rich language.
entries.literal: In his writing he took pride in ornate language.

entries.zh: 常次歷代有國廢興治亂之跡為《運源賦》，甚詳。
entries.en: He once compiled the rise, fall, order, and chaos of dynasties through the ages into “Origins of Fate”—a work of great detail.
entries.literal: He once compiled the traces of dynastic rise, fall, order, and disorder through the ages into “Origins of Fate,” in great detail.

entries.zh: 又因遊相國寺，見庭竹可愛，作《碧鮮賦》，題其壁，世宗聞之，遣小黃門就壁錄之，覽而稱善，因拜水部員外郎、知制誥。
entries.en: Visiting Xiangguo Temple, he fell in love with the courtyard bamboo and wrote “Fresh Green” on the wall. Shizong heard, sent a palace eunuch to copy it from the wall, read it with praise, and made him Vice Director of the Waterways Office and drafter of edicts.
entries.literal: Also, while visiting Xiangguo Temple he saw courtyard bamboo he loved and wrote “Fresh Green,” inscribing it on the wall. Shizong heard of it, sent a palace eunuch to copy it from the wall, read it and praised it, and therefore appointed him Vice Director of the Waterways Office and drafter of edicts.

entries.zh: 遷翰林學士，賜緋，而載已病，不能朝謝。
entries.en: He rose to Hanlin Academician and was granted crimson robes—but Zai was already ill and could not attend court to give thanks.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Hanlin Academician and granted crimson robes—but Zai was already ill and could not attend court to give thanks.

entries.zh: 居百餘日，乃力疾入直學士院。
entries.en: After more than a hundred days he dragged himself, sick, into duty at the Academy.
entries.literal: After more than a hundred days he forced himself, ill, to enter duty at the Academy.

entries.zh: 世宗憐之，賜告還第，遣太醫視疾。
entries.en: Shizong pitied him, granted leave to go home, and sent the imperial physician to treat him.
entries.literal: Shizong took pity on him, granted leave to return home, and sent the imperial physician to treat his illness.

entries.zh: 嗚呼！
entries.en: Alas!
entries.literal: Alas!

entries.zh: 作器者，無良材而有良匠；
entries.en: To shape a vessel you need no perfect timber—only a perfect craftsman;
entries.literal: To make vessels, one needs no fine timber but a fine craftsman;

entries.zh: 治國者，無能臣而有能君。
entries.en: to govern a state you need no perfect ministers—only a perfect ruler.
entries.literal: to govern a state, one needs no able ministers but an able ruler.

entries.zh: 蓋材待匠而成，臣待君而用。
entries.en: Timber waits for the craftsman; ministers wait for the ruler.
entries.literal: Timber waits on the craftsman to be made; ministers wait on the ruler to be used.

entries.zh: 故曰，治國譬之於奕，知其用而置得其處者勝，不知其用而置非其處者敗。
entries.en: So they say: governing a state is like Go—know your pieces and place each where it belongs, and you win; misplace them, and you lose.
entries.literal: Therefore it is said: governing the state is like a game of Go—knowing how to use men and placing each in his proper place wins; not knowing how to use men and placing each where he does not belong loses.

entries.zh: 敗者臨棋註目，終日而勞心，使善奕者視焉，為之易置其處則勝矣。
entries.en: The loser stares at the board all day, mind in knots; let a master look—and by moving each piece to its right square, the game turns.
entries.literal: The loser stares at the board all day, laboring in mind; let a skilled player look—and by rearranging the pieces to their proper places, victory follows.

entries.zh: 勝者所用，敗者之棋也；
entries.en: The stones the victor plays are the loser’s own pieces.
entries.literal: What the victor uses are the loser’s chess stones;

entries.zh: 興國所用，亡國之臣也。
entries.en: The men a rising realm employs are the ministers of a fallen one.
entries.literal: What a rising state uses are the ministers of a perished state.

entries.zh: 王朴之材，誠可謂能矣。
entries.en: Wang Pu’s talent was genuine—capable indeed.
entries.literal: Wang Pu’s talents may truly be called capable.

entries.zh: 不遇世宗，何所施哉？
entries.en: Without Shizong, where could he have shown it?
entries.literal: Had he not met Shizong, where would he have applied them?

entries.zh: 世宗之時，外事征伐，攻取戰勝；
entries.en: Under Shizong the realm campaigned abroad—attacking, conquering, winning in battle;
entries.literal: In Shizong’s time, outwardly there was campaigning—in attack and conquest, victory in battle;

entries.zh: 內修制度，議刑法，定律歷，講求禮樂之遺文，所用者五代之士也，豈皆愚怯於晉、漢，而材智於周哉？
entries.en: Within he refined institutions, debated law, fixed the calendar, and recovered lost rites and music—the men he used were veterans of the Five Dynasties. Were they fools and cowards under Jin and Han, yet sages under Zhou?
