entries.literal: inwardly he refined institutions, debated penal law, fixed calendar and statutes, and sought out surviving texts of rites and music—the men he employed were men of the Five Dynasties; were they all stupid and timid under Jin and Han, yet talented and wise under Zhou?

entries.zh: 惟知所用爾。
entries.en: It comes down to knowing whom to use.
entries.literal: It is only a matter of knowing whom to employ.

entries.zh: 夫亂國之君，常置愚不肖於上，而強其不能，以暴其短惡，置賢智於下，而泯沒其材能，使君子、小人皆失其所，而身蹈危亡。
entries.en: A ruler who brings ruin puts fools in high office and drives them beyond their strength until their flaws stand bare; puts the wise below and buries their gifts, so gentlemen and petty men alike lose their proper stations—and he himself walks into peril and extinction.
entries.literal: A ruler who disorders his state commonly sets the foolish and unworthy above, forcing them beyond what they can do to expose their faults and vices; sets the wise and talented below, burying their abilities, so that gentlemen and petty men alike lose their proper place—and he himself walks into danger and ruin.

entries.zh: 治國之君，能置賢智於近，而置愚不肖於遠，使君子、小人各適其分，而身享安榮。
entries.en: A ruler who brings order keeps the wise close and the unworthy far, so gentlemen and petty men each fill their proper roles—and he enjoys safety and honor himself.
entries.literal: A ruler who orders his state can set the wise and talented near and the foolish and unworthy far, so gentlemen and petty men each fit their rank—and he himself enjoys safety and glory.

entries.zh: 治亂相去雖遠甚，而其所以致之者不多也，反其所置而已。
entries.en: Order and disorder seem worlds apart, yet what makes them differ is small: simply reverse whom you place where.
entries.literal: Though order and disorder stand vastly far apart, the causes that lead to them are not many—it is simply reversing whom one places where.

entries.zh: 嗚呼，自古治君少而亂君多，況於五代，士之遇不遇者，可勝嘆哉！
entries.en: Alas! Through the ages worthy rulers have been rare and ruinous ones many—all the more in the Five Dynasties. How many scholars found a master, and how many did not—what sighs could count them all!
entries.literal: Alas! From antiquity there have been few ordering rulers and many disordered ones; how much the more in the Five Dynasties—the scholars who found favor and those who did not, what sighs could number them all!

entries.zh: 王彥章，字子明，鄆州壽張人也。
entries.en: Wang Yanzhang, styled Ziming, came from Shouzhang in Yun Prefecture.
entries.literal: Wang Yanzhang, styled Ziming, was a native of Shouzhang in Yun Prefecture.

entries.zh: 少為軍卒，事梁太祖，為開封府押衙、左親從指揮使、行營先鋒馬軍使。
entries.en: He began as a common soldier under Liang Taizu, rising to Kaifeng escort officer, commander of the Left Personal Followers, and vanguard cavalry commander on campaign.
entries.literal: In youth he was a common soldier. He served Liang Taizu as Kaifeng Intendant escort officer, Left Personal Followers commander, and vanguard cavalry commander on campaign.

entries.zh: 末帝即位，遷濮州刺史，又徙澶州刺史。
entries.en: When the Last Emperor took the throne, he became prefect of Pu, then of Chan.
entries.literal: When the Last Emperor acceded, he was moved to prefect of Pu, then transferred to prefect of Chan.

entries.zh: 彥章為人驍勇有力，能跣足履棘行百步。
entries.en: Yanzhang was fierce and strong enough to walk a hundred paces barefoot over thorns.
entries.literal: Yanzhang was fierce, brave, and strong; he could walk a hundred paces barefoot over thorns.

entries.zh: 持一鐵槍，騎而馳突，奮疾如飛，而佗人莫能舉也，軍中號王鐵槍。
entries.en: He wielded an iron spear no other man could lift. Mounted, he charged like a gale. The army called him Wang Iron Spear.
entries.literal: He carried an iron spear; mounted, he charged and broke through like a gale—yet no other man could lift it. The army called him Wang Iron Spear.

entries.zh: 自梁失魏、博，與晉夾河而軍，彥章常為先鋒。
entries.en: Once Liang lost Wei and Bo, the two powers faced each other across the Yellow River—and Yanzhang was always in the vanguard.
entries.literal: After Liang lost Wei and Bo, its armies faced Jin across the river; Yanzhang was always in the vanguard.

entries.zh: 遷汝鄭二州防禦使、匡國軍節度使、北面行營副招討使，又徙宣義軍節度使。
entries.en: He rose to defender of Ru and Zheng, governor of Kuangguo, deputy northern campaign commissioner, then governor of Xuanyi.
entries.literal: He was promoted to defender of Ru and Zheng, military governor of the Kuangguo Army, deputy northern campaign commissioner, then transferred to military governor of the Xuanyi Army.

entries.zh: 是時，晉已盡有河北，以鐵鎖斷德勝口，築河南、北為兩城，號「夾寨」。
entries.en: By then Jin held all Hebei. They chained off Desheng Crossing and built twin cities north and south of the river—the "Pincer Forts."
entries.literal: By then Jin held all of Hebei. They blocked Desheng Crossing with iron chains and built north and south cities on the river—called the "Twin Forts."

entries.zh: 而梁末帝昏亂，小人趙巖、張漢傑等用事，大臣宿將多被讒間，彥章雖為招討副使，而謀不見用。
entries.en: The Last Emperor was lost; Zhao Yan and Zhang Hanjie ran the court, and veteran ministers and generals were slandered aside. Yanzhang was deputy campaign commander, but no one listened.
entries.literal: The Last Emperor was muddled; petty men Zhao Yan and Zhang Hanjie held power, and veteran ministers and generals were slandered out of favor. Though Yanzhang was deputy campaign commissioner, his counsel went unused.

entries.zh: 龍德三年夏，晉取鄆州，梁人大恐，宰相敬翔顧事急，以繩內靴中，入見末帝，泣曰：「先帝取天下，不以臣為不肖，所謀無不用。
entries.en: Summer, Longde year three: Jin took Yun Prefecture and Liang panicked. Chancellor Jing Xiang, seeing ruin close, hid a rope in his boot, went before the Last Emperor, and wept: "The Founder took the realm and never thought me unworthy—every plan of mine was used.
entries.literal: In summer of Longde year three Jin took Yun Prefecture. Liang was terrified. Chancellor Jing Xiang, seeing affairs desperate, hid a rope in his boot, entered to see the Last Emperor, and wept: "The Founding Emperor took the realm and did not think me unworthy—none of my counsel went unused.

entries.zh: 今強敵未滅，陛下棄忽臣言，臣身不用，不如死！」
entries.en: The great enemy still stands, yet Your Majesty ignores me. If I am useless, I would rather die!"
entries.literal: Now the great foe is not destroyed, yet Your Majesty casts aside my words and will not employ me—I would rather die!"

entries.zh: 乃引繩將自經。
entries.en: He drew the rope to hang himself.
entries.literal: He then drew the rope to hang himself.

entries.zh: 末帝使人止之，問所欲言。
entries.en: The Last Emperor stopped him and asked what he had to say.
entries.literal: The Last Emperor sent men to stop him and asked what he wished to say.

entries.zh: 翔曰：「事急矣，非彥章不可！」
entries.en: Xiang said: "It is desperate—only Yanzhang can save us!"
entries.literal: Xiang said: "Affairs are desperate—only Yanzhang will do!"

entries.zh: 末帝乃召彥章為招討使，以段凝為副。
entries.en: The Last Emperor summoned Yanzhang as campaign commander and made Duan Ning his deputy.
entries.literal: The Last Emperor then summoned Yanzhang as campaign commissioner and made Duan Ning his deputy.

entries.zh: 末帝問破敵之期，彥章對曰：「三日。」
entries.en: The Last Emperor asked when he could break the enemy. Yanzhang said: "Three days."
entries.literal: The Last Emperor asked when the enemy could be broken; Yanzhang answered: "Three days."

entries.zh: 左右皆失笑。
entries.en: Everyone around him laughed out loud.
entries.literal: Those around all burst out laughing.

entries.zh: 唐兵攻兗州，末帝召彥章使守捉東路。
entries.en: Tang attacked Yan Prefecture; the Last Emperor called Yanzhang to hold the eastern road.
entries.literal: Tang troops attacked Yan Prefecture; the Last Emperor summoned Yanzhang to guard the eastern route.

entries.zh: 是時，梁之勝兵皆屬段凝，京師只有保鑾五百騎，皆新捉募之兵，不可用，乃以屬彥章，而以張漢傑監之。
entries.en: Liang’s best troops were all with Duan Ning. The capital had only five hundred Palace Guard cavalry—raw recruits, good for nothing. These were handed to Yanzhang, with Zhang Hanjie watching over him.
entries.literal: By then Liang’s best troops all belonged to Duan Ning; the capital had only five hundred Palace Guard cavalry—all newly drafted and useless. These were given to Yanzhang, with Zhang Hanjie to oversee him.

entries.zh: 彥章至遞坊，以兵少戰敗，退保中都；
entries.en: At Difang Yanzhang was too weak to win; he fell back on Zhongdu;
entries.literal: Yanzhang reached Difang. Too few to fight, he was beaten and fell back on Zhongdu;

entries.zh: 又敗，與其牙兵百餘騎死戰。
entries.en: beaten again, he and a little over a hundred of his personal troops fought to the death.
entries.literal: beaten again, he and a little over a hundred of his personal troops fought to the death.

entries.zh: 唐將夏魯奇素與彥章善，識其語音，曰：「王鐵槍也！」
entries.en: The Tang general Xia Luqi had served with Yanzhang and knew his voice. He shouted: "Wang Iron Spear!"
entries.literal: The Tang general Xia Luqi had long been on good terms with Yanzhang and knew his voice. He cried: "Wang Iron Spear!"

entries.zh: 舉槊刺之，彥章傷重，馬踣，被擒。
entries.en: He drove his spear into him. Yanzhang was gravely wounded, his horse went down, and he was taken.
entries.literal: He thrust with his spear; Yanzhang was gravely wounded, his horse collapsed, and he was captured.

entries.zh: 莊宗見之，曰：「爾常以孺子待我，今日服乎？」
entries.en: Zhuangzong looked at him and said: "You always called me a stripling—are you satisfied now?"
entries.literal: Zhuangzong saw him and said: "You always treated me as a stripling—are you satisfied today?"

entries.zh: 又曰：「爾善戰者，何不守兗州而守中都？
entries.en: He asked again: "They say you are a master of war—why hold Zhongdu instead of Yan Prefecture?
entries.literal: He said again: "They say you are skilled in war—why hold Zhongdu and not Yan Prefecture?

entries.zh: 中都無壁壘，何以自固？」
entries.en: Zhongdu has no walls. How could you hold it?"
entries.literal: Zhongdu has no walls—how could you make yourself secure?"

entries.zh: 彥章對曰：「大事已去，非人力可為！」
entries.en: Yanzhang said: "The cause is lost. No human strength can mend it!"
entries.literal: Yanzhang answered: "The great affair is already lost; it is not within human power to mend!"

entries.zh: 莊宗惻然，賜藥以封其創。
entries.en: Zhuangzong was moved and sent medicine to bind his wounds.
entries.literal: Zhuangzong was moved and sent medicine to dress his wound.

entries.zh: 彥章武人不知書，常為俚語謂人曰：「豹死留皮，人死留名。」
entries.en: Yanzhang could not read, but he had a saying: "The leopard dies and leaves its hide; the man dies and leaves his name."
entries.literal: Yanzhang was a soldier who did not know books; he often used a common saying: "When the leopard dies it leaves its pelt; when a man dies he leaves his name."

entries.zh: 其於忠義，蓋天性也。
entries.en: Loyalty and righteousness were in his bones.
entries.literal: In loyalty and righteousness, it was his nature.

entries.zh: 莊宗愛其驍勇，欲全活之，使人慰諭彥章，彥章謝曰：「臣與陛下血戰十餘年，今兵敗力窮，不死何待？
entries.en: Zhuangzong admired his valor and wanted to save him. He sent men to win him over. Yanzhang refused: "I fought you in blood for more than ten years. Now my army is broken and my strength spent—if I do not die, what am I waiting for?
entries.literal: Zhuangzong admired his fierceness and wished to spare him. He sent men to comfort and persuade Yanzhang. Yanzhang declined: "Your servant fought Your Majesty in blood for more than ten years. Now the army is broken and strength spent—if I do not die, what am I waiting for?

entries.zh: 且臣受梁恩，非死不能報，豈有朝事梁而暮事晉，生何面目見天下之人乎！」
entries.en: I owe Liang a debt only death can pay. Serve Liang at dawn and Jin at dusk? What face would I show the world!"
entries.literal: Moreover I received Liang’s grace; only death can repay it. How could I serve Liang at dawn and Jin at dusk—what face would I have before the men of the realm!"

entries.zh: 莊宗又遣明宗往諭之，彥章病創，臥不能起，仰顧明宗，呼其小字曰：「汝非邈佶烈乎？
entries.en: Zhuangzong sent Mingzong to persuade him. Yanzhang’s wounds were too grave to rise. He looked up at Mingzong and called his childhood name: "Are you not Miaojilie?
entries.literal: Zhuangzong again sent Mingzong to persuade him. Yanzhang’s wounds were grave; he could not rise. He looked up at Mingzong and called him by his childhood name: "Are you not Miaojilie?

entries.zh: 我豈茍活者？」
entries.en: Do you take me for a man who clings to life?"
entries.literal: Do you think I am a man who clings to life?"

entries.zh: 遂見殺，年六十一。
entries.en: He was then killed—sixty-one years old.
entries.literal: He was then executed—aged sixty-one.

entries.zh: 晉高祖時，追贈彥章太師。
entries.en: Under Jin Gaozu he was posthumously made Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: Under Jin Gaozu he was posthumously made Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 至周世宗時，又有劉仁贍者焉。
entries.en: By Shizong’s day there was Liu Renzhan.
entries.literal: By the time of Later Zhou Shizong there was also Liu Renzhan.

entries.zh: 仁贍字守惠，彭城人也。
entries.en: Renzhan, styled Shouhui, came from Pengcheng.
entries.literal: Renzhan, styled Shouhui, was a native of Pengcheng.

entries.zh: 父金，事楊行密，為濠、滁二州刺史，以驍勇知名。
entries.en: His father Jin served Yang Xingmi as prefect of Hao and Chu and was famed for courage.
entries.literal: His father Jin served Yang Xingmi as prefect of Hao and Chu and was known for fierceness and bravery.

entries.zh: 仁贍為將，輕財重士，法令嚴肅，少略通兵書。
entries.en: As a commander Renzhan was generous with his purse and loyal to his men, stern in discipline, and had read some military texts.
entries.literal: As a commander Renzhan was light with wealth and heavy toward his men, strict in law, and had some grasp of military books.

entries.zh: 事南唐，為左監門衛將軍、黃袁二州刺史，所至稱治。
entries.en: He served Southern Tang as Left Gate Guard general and prefect of Huang and Yuan; everywhere he went men praised his rule.
entries.literal: He served Southern Tang as Left Gate Guard general and prefect of Huang and Yuan; wherever he went he was praised for good governance.

entries.zh: 李景使掌親軍，以為武昌軍節度使。
entries.en: Li Jing put him in charge of the imperial guard and made him governor of Wuchang.
entries.literal: Li Jing put him in charge of the personal guard and made him military governor of the Wuchang Army.

entries.zh: 周師征淮，先遣李穀攻自壽春，景遣將劉彥貞拒周兵，以仁贍為清淮軍節度使，鎮壽州。
entries.en: When Zhou marched on the Huai, Li Gu struck first from Shouchun. Jing sent Liu Yanzhen to meet the Zhou army and made Renzhan governor of Qinghuai, stationed at Shou.
entries.literal: When Zhou troops marched on the Huai, they first sent Li Gu to attack from Shouchun. Jing dispatched General Liu Yanzhen to meet the Zhou army and made Renzhan military governor of the Qinghuai Army, stationed at Shou Prefecture.

entries.zh: 李穀退守正陽浮橋，彥貞見周兵之卻，意其怯，急追之。
entries.en: Li Gu fell back on the Zhengyang floating bridge. Yanzhen saw the Zhou retreat and took them for cowards; he chased hard.
entries.literal: Li Gu fell back to hold the Zhengyang floating bridge. Yanzhen saw the Zhou army retreat and thought them cowards; he pressed the pursuit hotly.

entries.zh: 仁贍以為不可，彥貞不聽，仁贍獨按兵城守。
entries.en: Renzhan said it was folly; Yanzhen would not hear him. Renzhan alone kept his troops in the city.
entries.literal: Renzhan thought it unwise; Yanzhen would not listen. Renzhan alone held his troops and guarded the city.

entries.zh: 彥貞果敗於正陽。
entries.en: Yanzhen was routed at Zhengyang.
entries.literal: Yanzhen was indeed defeated at Zhengyang.

entries.zh: 世宗攻壽州，圍之數重，以方舟載炮，自淝河中流擊其城；
entries.en: Shizong besieged Shou, ring upon ring. He mounted catapults on barges and hammered the walls from midstream on the Fei;
entries.literal: Shizong besieged Shou Prefecture, ring upon ring. He loaded catapults on barges and struck the city from midstream on the Fei River;

entries.zh: 又束巨竹數十萬竿，上施版屋，號為「竹龍」，載甲士以攻之，又決其水砦入於淝河。
entries.en: he bound hundreds of thousands of bamboo poles, roofed them with boards into "Bamboo Dragons," loaded armored men to assault the walls, and broke the water fortifications to flood the Fei.
entries.literal: he also bound hundreds of thousands of great bamboo poles, roofed them with planking, called them "Bamboo Dragons," loaded armored men aboard to attack, and broke the water fortifications to pour into the Fei.

entries.zh: 攻之百端，自正月至於四月不能下，而歲大暑，霖雨彌旬，周兵營寨水深數尺，淮、淝暴漲，炮舟竹龍皆飄南岸，為景兵所焚，周兵多死。
entries.en: Every assault failed from the first month to the fourth. Heat hammered the land; rain fell ten days straight. Zhou camps stood knee-deep in water; the Huai and Fei rose in flood. Catapult barges and Bamboo Dragons drifted south and Jing’s men burned them; Zhou dead piled up.
entries.literal: He tried every method of assault from the first month to the fourth and could not take the city. That year the heat was fierce; rain fell for ten days. Zhou camps stood in water several feet deep; the Huai and Fei surged. The catapult barges and Bamboo Dragons drifted to the south bank and were burned by Jing’s troops; many Zhou soldiers died.

entries.zh: 世宗東趨濠梁，以李重進為廬、壽都招討使。
entries.en: Shizong marched east to Hao Bridge and made Li Chongjin overall commander of Lu and Shou.
entries.literal: Shizong marched east to Hao Bridge and made Li Chongjin overall commander of Lu and Shou.

entries.zh: 景亦遣其元帥齊王景達等列砦紫金山下，為夾道以屬城中。
entries.en: Jing sent his commander-in-chief Prince Qi Jingda to camp below Purple Gold Mountain and build a covered road into the city.
entries.literal: Jing also sent his commander-in-chief, Prince Qi Jingda, and others to camp below Purple Gold Mountain and build a covered road linking the city.

entries.zh: 而重進與張永德兩軍相疑不協，仁贍屢請出戰，景達不許，由是憤惋成疾。
entries.en: Chongjin and Zhang Yongde distrusted each other and would not cooperate. Renzhan begged again and again to sally; Jingda refused—and resentment curdled into sickness.
entries.literal: Chongjin and Zhang Yongde’s two armies distrusted each other and would not cooperate. Renzhan repeatedly asked to sally forth; Jingda refused—so resentment and grief turned to illness.

entries.zh: 明年正月，世宗復至淮上，盡破紫金山砦，壞其夾道，景兵大敗，諸將往往見擒，而景之守將廣陵馮延魯、光州張紹、舒州周祚、泰州方訥、泗州範再遇等，或走或降，皆不能守，雖景君臣亦皆震懾，奉表稱臣，願割土地、輸貢賦，以效誠款，而仁贍獨堅守，不可下。
entries.en: First month of the next year Shizong returned to the Huai, smashed the Purple Gold Mountain camps, broke the covered road, and routed Jing’s army. Generals fell one after another; Feng Yanlu of Guangling, Zhang Shao of Guang, Zhou Zuo of Shu, Fang Ne of Tai, Fan Zaiyu of Si—commanders fled or surrendered and could not hold. Jing king and court shook, sent tribute, ceded land, bowed as subjects—Renzhan alone held and would not yield.
entries.literal: In the first month of the next year Shizong returned to the Huai, broke all the Purple Gold Mountain camps, destroyed the covered road, and routed Jing’s army badly. Generals were taken one after another; Jing’s defending commanders—Guangling’s Feng Yanlu, Guang Prefecture’s Zhang Shao, Shu Prefecture’s Zhou Zuo, Tai Prefecture’s Fang Ne, Si Prefecture’s Fan Zaiyu, and others—fled or surrendered and could not hold their posts. Though Jing, king and ministers alike, were shaken and submitted memorials calling themselves subjects, offering to cede land and pay tribute in proof of loyalty, Renzhan alone held firm and could not be taken.

entries.zh: 世宗使景所遣使者孫晟等至城下示之，仁贍子崇諫幸其父病，謀與諸將出降，仁贍立命斬之，監軍使周廷構哭於中門救之，不得，於是士卒皆感泣，願以死守。
entries.en: Shizong paraded Jing’s envoy Sun Sheng below the walls. Renzhan’s son Chongjian, seeing his father ill, plotted surrender with the generals. Renzhan ordered him killed on the spot. Supervisor Zhou Tinggou wept at the middle gate in vain; the soldiers wept and swore to die with the city.
entries.literal: Shizong had Jing’s envoy Sun Sheng and others come below the walls to show them. Renzhan’s son Chongjian, taking advantage of his father’s illness, plotted with the generals to surrender. Renzhan immediately ordered him executed. Supervisor Zhou Tinggou wept at the middle gate to save him but could not; the soldiers all wept and vowed to die defending the city.

entries.zh: 三月，仁贍病甚，已不知人，其副使孫羽詐為仁贍書，以城降。
entries.en: Third month: Renzhan was dying and no longer knew anyone. His deputy Sun Yu forged a letter in his name and surrendered the city.
entries.literal: In the third month Renzhan’s illness was grave; he no longer knew men. His deputy Sun Yu forged a letter in Renzhan’s name and surrendered the city.

entries.zh: 世宗命舁仁贍至帳前，嘆嗟久之，賜以玉帶、御馬，復使入城養疾，是日卒。
entries.en: Shizong had Renzhan carried to his tent, sighed a long while, gave him a jade belt and an imperial horse, and sent him back into the city to recover. He died that day.
entries.literal: Shizong had Renzhan carried before his tent, sighed long, granted him a jade belt and an imperial horse, and sent him back into the city to recover from illness. That day he died.

entries.zh: 制曰：「劉仁贍盡忠所事，抗節無虧，前代名臣，幾人可比！
entries.en: An edict ran: "Liu Renzhan gave his lord full loyalty and held his integrity without stain. Of the famed ministers of old, how many can match him!
entries.literal: An edict said: "Liu Renzhan gave full loyalty to his lord and held his integrity without stain. Of famous ministers in former ages, how many can compare!

entries.zh: 予之南伐，得爾為多。」
entries.en: In my southern campaign, winning you meant more than winning cities.”
entries.literal: In my southern campaign, gaining you counted for much.”

entries.zh: 乃拜仁贍檢校太尉兼中書令、天平軍節度使。
entries.en: He then made Renzhan Acting Grand Commandant and Concurrent Director of the Secretariat, and Military Governor of the Tianping Army.
entries.literal: He then appointed Renzhan Acting Grand Commandant and Concurrent Director of the Secretariat and Military Governor of the Tianping Army.

entries.zh: 仁贍不能受命而卒，年五十八。
entries.en: Renzhan died before he could take up the post. He was fifty-eight.
entries.literal: Renzhan could not accept the appointment before he died, at the age of fifty-eight.

entries.zh: 世宗遣使吊祭，喪事官給，追封彭城郡王，以其子崇贊為懷州刺史，賜莊宅各一區。
entries.en: Shizong sent envoys to mourn him and pay for the funeral from the treasury. He was posthumously made Prince of Pengcheng; his son Chongzan was named prefect of Huaizhou, and father and son each received an estate.
entries.literal: Shizong sent envoys to offer condolences and sacrifices; funeral expenses were supplied by the state. He was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Pengcheng. His son Chongzan was made prefect of Huaizhou, and each was granted an estate.

entries.zh: 李景聞仁贍卒，亦贈太師。
entries.en: When Li Jing heard Renzhan was dead, he too posthumously made him Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: When Li Jing heard that Renzhan had died, he too posthumously honored him as Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 壽州故治壽春，世宗以其難克，遂徙城下蔡，而復其軍曰忠正軍，曰：「吾以旌仁贍之節也。」
entries.en: Shou Prefecture had once been governed from Shouchun. Shizong, finding the place hard to take, moved the seat to Xiachai and restored the army’s name to the Loyal Upright Army, saying, “I do this to honor Renzhan’s integrity.”
entries.literal: Shou Prefecture had formerly been administered from Shouchun. Because Shizong found it hard to capture, he moved the seat to Xiachai and restored the army’s name to the Loyal Upright Army, saying: “I do this to honor Renzhan’s integrity.”

entries.zh: 嗚呼，天下惡梁久矣！
entries.en: Alas—the world has hated Liang for ages!
entries.literal: Alas, the world has hated Liang for a long time!

entries.zh: 然士之不幸而生其時者，不為之臣可也，其食人之祿者，必死人之事，如彥章者，可謂得其死哉！
entries.en: Yet for scholars born into that age, refusing office would have been enough; but whoever ate a lord’s salary owed that lord his death. Yanzhang may truly be said to have died as he ought.
entries.literal: Yet for gentlemen unlucky enough to be born in that age, not serving as its ministers would have been enough; but those who ate another man’s salary were bound to die for that man’s cause. A man like Yanzhang may truly be said to have died as he ought!

entries.zh: 仁贍既殺其子以自明矣，豈有垂死而變節者乎？
entries.en: Renzhan had already killed his own son to prove his loyalty—how could he have turned traitor at the point of death?
entries.literal: Renzhan had already killed his son to prove his loyalty—how could he have changed his colors on his deathbed?

entries.zh: 今《周世宗實錄》載仁贍降書，蓋其副使孫羽等所為也。
entries.en: The Veritable Records of Shizong credit Renzhan with a surrender letter—but that was forged by his deputy Sun Yu and the rest.
entries.literal: Now the Veritable Records of Emperor Shizong of Zhou record a surrender letter from Renzhan—but that was the work of his deputy Sun Yu and the others.

entries.zh: 當世宗時，王環為蜀守秦州，攻之久不下，其力屈而降，世宗頗嗟其忠，然止於為大將軍。
entries.en: Under Shizong, Wang Huan held Qin Prefecture for Shu. The siege wore on without result; when his strength gave out he surrendered. Shizong sighed at his loyalty, yet made him only a Grand General.
entries.literal: In Shizong’s time Wang Huan held Qin Prefecture for Shu. The siege dragged on without success; when his strength was spent he surrendered. Shizong sighed over his loyalty, yet made him only a Grand General.

entries.zh: 視世宗待二人之薄厚而考其制書，乃知仁贍非降者也。
entries.en: Weigh how differently Shizong treated the two men and read the edicts he wrote, and you will see Renzhan never surrendered.
entries.literal: Compare how thinly or richly Shizong treated the two men and read the edicts he issued, and you will know Renzhan did not surrender.

entries.zh: 自古忠臣義士之難得也！
entries.en: Since antiquity, loyal ministers and righteous men have been rare indeed!
entries.literal: From antiquity, loyal ministers and righteous men have been hard to find!

entries.zh: 五代之亂，三人者，或出於軍卒，或出於偽國之臣，可勝嘆哉！
entries.en: In the chaos of the Five Dynasties these three—some raised from the ranks, some drawn from the courts of usurper states—how much is there to sigh over!
entries.literal: In the chaos of the Five Dynasties these three men—some rising from the ranks of common soldiers, some from the courts of false states—how much is there to sigh over!

entries.zh: 可勝嘆哉！
entries.en: How much is there to sigh over!
entries.literal: How much is there to sigh over!

entries.zh: 語曰：「世亂識忠臣。」
entries.en: The proverb says: "In chaos, loyal ministers stand revealed."
entries.literal: The saying goes: "In a chaotic age one knows loyal ministers."

entries.zh: 誠哉！
entries.en: How true that is!
entries.literal: How true!

entries.zh: 五代之際，不可以為無人，吾得全節之士三人焉，作《死節傳》。
entries.en: The Five Dynasties were not without men of worth. I have found three who died with their integrity intact—and so I write this "Biography of Martyrs to Virtue."
entries.literal: In the age of the Five Dynasties one cannot say there were no men of worth. I have found three who kept their integrity whole, and compose this "Biography of Martyrs to Virtue."

entries.zh: 張源德者，不知其世家，或曰本晉人也。
entries.en: Zhang Yuande’s lineage is unknown; some say he was originally from Jin.
entries.literal: Zhang Yuande—his lineage is unknown; some say he was originally a man of Jin.

entries.zh: 少事晉，無所稱。
entries.en: In youth he served Jin without distinction.
entries.literal: In youth he served Jin, with nothing to his credit.

entries.zh: 從李罕之以潞州叛晉降梁，罕之遣源德見梁太祖。
entries.en: He followed Li Hanzhi when Hanzhi rebelled at Luzhou and surrendered to Liang; Hanzhi sent Yuande to Emperor Taizu of Liang.
entries.literal: He followed Li Hanzhi when Hanzhi rebelled against Jin at Luzhou and submitted to Liang; Hanzhi sent Yuande to see Emperor Taizu of Liang.

entries.zh: 太祖時，源德自金吾衛將軍為蔡州刺史。
entries.en: Under Taizu, Yuande rose from General of the Imperial Insignia Guard to prefect of Cai.
entries.literal: Under Taizu, Yuande rose from General of the Imperial Insignia Guard to prefect of Cai.

entries.zh: 梁貞明三年，魏博節度使楊師厚卒，末帝分魏、相等六州為兩鎮，懼魏軍不從，乃遣劉鄩將兵萬人，屯於魏以虞變。
entries.en: In Liang’s third Zhenming year, Weibo governor Yang Shihou died; the Last Emperor split Wei and five other prefectures into two commands, fearing mutiny, and sent Liu Yan with ten thousand men to camp at Wei.
entries.literal: In the third year of Zhenming of Liang, Yang Shihou, military governor of Weibo, died; the Last Emperor split the six prefectures of Wei and Xiang into two commands, fearing the Wei army would not obey, and sent Liu Yan with ten thousand men to camp at Wei to guard against trouble.

entries.zh: 魏軍果叛，迫其節度使賀德倫以魏、博二州降晉。
entries.en: The Wei army rebelled, forcing Governor He Delun to surrender Wei and Bo to Jin.
entries.literal: The Wei army did rebel, forcing their governor He Delun to surrender Wei and Bo to Jin.

entries.zh: 當是時，源德為鄩守貝州。
entries.en: At that time Yuande, under Liu Yan, held Bei Prefecture.
entries.literal: At that time Yuande was Liu Yan’s deputy defending Bei Prefecture.

entries.zh: 晉王入魏，諸將欲先擊貝州，晉王曰：「貝城小而堅，攻之難卒下。
entries.en: When the Prince of Jin entered Wei, his generals wanted to attack Bei first; he said, “Bei is small but strong—hard to seize quickly.
entries.literal: When the Prince of Jin entered Wei, the generals wished to strike Bei first; the Prince of Jin said, “Bei’s walls are small but strong—hard to take at once.

entries.zh: 且源德雖恃劉鄩之兵，然與滄州相首尾，今德州居其中而無備，不如先取之，則滄、貝之勢分而易圖也。」
entries.en: Yuande relies on Liu Yan, but he and Cangzhou back each other; Dezhou lies between, undefended—take it first, and Cang and Bei will be split and easier to crack."
entries.literal: Though Yuande relies on Liu Yan’s troops, he and Cangzhou support each other; Dezhou lies between them unguarded—better take it first, then Cang and Bei will be divided and easier to deal with."

entries.zh: 乃先襲破德州，然後以兵五千攻源德，源德堅守不下，晉軍塹而圍之。
entries.en: They stormed Dezhou first, then attacked Yuande with five thousand men; he held out, and the Jin army trenched and besieged him.
entries.literal: They first stormed and took Dezhou, then attacked Yuande with five thousand men; Yuande held firm and would not yield, and the Jin army dug trenches and besieged him.

entries.zh: 已而劉鄩大敗於故元城，南走黎陽，晉軍攻破洺州，而衛州刺史來昭、邢州節度使閻寶皆以城降晉，磁州刺史靳昭、相州張筠、滄州戴思遠皆棄城走。
entries.en: Soon Liu Yan was crushed at Old Yuancheng and fled to Liyang; Jin took Luozhou; Lai Zhao of Weizhou and Yan Bao of Xingzhou surrendered; Jin Zhao, Zhang Yun, and Dai Siyuan fled their posts.
entries.literal: Before long Liu Yan was routed at Old Yuancheng and fled south to Liyang; the Jin army took Luozhou, while Lai Zhao of Weizhou and Yan Bao of Xingzhou both surrendered their cities to Jin; Jin Zhao of Cizhou, Zhang Yun of Xiangzhou, and Dai Siyuan of Cangzhou all abandoned their posts and fled.

entries.zh: 當此時，晉已先下全燕，而鎮、定皆附於晉，自河以北、山以東，四面千里，六鎮數十州之地皆歸晉，獨貝一州，圍之逾年不可下。
entries.en: Jin had taken all Yan; Zhen and Ding submitted; for a thousand li north of the river and east of the mountains, six commands and dozens of prefectures fell to Jin—only Bei remained, besieged over a year without falling.
entries.literal: By then Jin had already taken all of Yan; Zhen and Ding both submitted; north of the Yellow River and east of the mountains, a thousand li on four sides—the lands of six commands and dozens of prefectures—all went to Jin; Bei alone was besieged more than a year and could not be taken.

entries.zh: 源德守既堅，而貝人聞晉已盡有河北，城中食且盡，乃勸源德出降，源德不從，遂見殺。
entries.en: Yuande held firm, but Bei’s people heard Jin held all Hebei; food ran low; they urged surrender; he refused and was killed.
entries.literal: Yuande’s defense was staunch, but the people of Bei heard Jin already held all Hebei; food in the city was nearly gone; they urged Yuande to surrender; he refused and was killed.

entries.zh: 夏魯奇，字邦傑，青州人也。
entries.en: Xia Luqi, courtesy name Bangjie, was from Qingzhou.
entries.literal: Xia Luqi, courtesy name Bangjie, was a man of Qingzhou.

entries.zh: 唐莊宗時，賜姓名曰李紹奇，其後莊宗賜姓名者，皆復其故。
entries.en: Zhuangzong granted him the surname Li and the name Shaoqi; later all such granted names were restored.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Zhuangzong of Tang he was granted the surname Li and the name Shaoqi; afterward all whom Zhuangzong had given surnames reverted to their former ones.

entries.zh: 魯奇初事梁為宣武軍校，後奔於晉，為衛護指揮使。
entries.en: Luqi first served Liang in the Xuanwu Army, then fled to Jin as commander of the Palace Guard.
entries.literal: Luqi first served Liang as an officer of the Xuanwu Army, then fled to Jin and became commander of the Palace Guard.

entries.zh: 從周德威攻劉守光於幽州，守光將單廷珪、元行欽以驍勇自負，魯奇每與二將鬥，輒不能解，兩軍皆釋兵而觀之。
entries.en: With Zhou Dewei he besieged Liu Shouguang at Youzhou; Shouguang’s generals Shan Tinggui and Yuan Xingqin boasted of valor; Luqi duelled each in turn without decision, both armies watching.
entries.literal: Following Zhou Dewei he attacked Liu Shouguang at Youzhou; Shouguang’s generals Shan Tinggui and Yuan Xingqin prided themselves on valor; Luqi fought each in turn and neither could prevail; both armies laid down weapons to watch.

entries.zh: 晉已下魏博，梁將劉鄩軍於洹水，莊宗以百騎覘敵，遇鄩伏兵，圍之數重，幾不得脫，魯奇力戰，手殺百餘人，身被二十餘創，與莊宗決圍而出。
entries.en: After Jin took Weibo, Liu Yan camped on the Huan; Zhuangzong scouted with a hundred horsemen, walked into an ambush, and was nearly trapped; Luqi fought hand to hand, slew a hundred men, took twenty wounds, and broke out with him.
entries.literal: After Jin took Weibo, Liang’s Liu Yan camped on the Huan; Zhuangzong rode out with a hundred men to scout and met Yan’s ambush, encircled many times deep and nearly unable to escape; Luqi fought fiercely, killing more than a hundred with his own hand, taking twenty-odd wounds, and broke out with Zhuangzong.

entries.zh: 莊宗益奇之，以為磁州刺史。
entries.en: Zhuangzong prized him and made him prefect of Ci.
entries.literal: Zhuangzong admired him all the more and made him prefect of Ci.

entries.zh: 從戰中都，擒王彥章，莊宗壯之，賜絹千疋，拜鄭州防禦使。
entries.en: At Zhongdu he captured Wang Yanzhang; Zhuangzong rewarded him with a thousand bolts of silk and made him Defender of Zhengzhou.
entries.literal: In the campaign at Zhongdu he captured Wang Yanzhang; Zhuangzong praised him and granted a thousand bolts of silk, appointing him Defender of Zhengzhou.

entries.zh: 遷河陽節度使，為政有惠愛。
entries.en: He became governor of Heyang, ruling with kindness.
entries.literal: He was transferred to military governor of Heyang, governing with kindness.

entries.zh: 徙鎮忠武，河陽之人遮留不得行，父老詣京師乞留，明宗遣中使往諭之，魯奇乃得去。
entries.en: Transferred to Zhongwu; Heyang’s people blocked his road; elders petitioned the capital; Mingzong sent an envoy to reason with them before Luqi could go.
entries.literal: Moved to Zhongwu; the people of Heyang blocked his departure and would not let him go; elders went to the capital to beg he stay; Mingzong sent a palace envoy to explain, and only then could Luqi leave.

entries.zh: 唐師伐荊南，以魯奇為招討副使，無功而還。
entries.en: On Tang’s Jingnan campaign he served as deputy pacification commissioner and returned without success.
entries.literal: When Tang campaigned against Jingnan, Luqi was deputy pacification commissioner; he returned without achievement.

entries.zh: 徙鎮武信，東川董璋反，攻遂州，魯奇閉城拒之，旬月救兵不至，城中食盡，魯奇自刎死，年四十九。
entries.en: Transferred to Wuxin; when Dong Zhang rebelled and attacked Suizhou, Luqi held the city; relief failed for ten days; food ran out; he killed himself at forty-nine.
entries.literal: Transferred to Wuxin; Dong Zhang of Dongchuan rebelled and attacked Suizhou; Luqi shut the city and resisted; for ten days no relief came; food ran out; Luqi cut his throat and died, aged forty-nine.

entries.zh: 明宗時，以久次為匡國軍節度使，徙鎮雄武。
entries.en: Under Mingzong, after long service he governed Kuangguo, then Xiongwu.
entries.literal: Under Mingzong, after long service he became military governor of Kuangguo, then moved to Xiongwu.

entries.zh: 是時，吐蕃數為寇，而秦州無亭障，思同列四十餘柵以禦之。
entries.en: Tibetans raided often; Qinzhou had no outposts; Sitong built forty-odd stockades.
entries.literal: Tibetans raided often and Qinzhou had no outposts; Sitong set up more than forty stockades to guard against them.

entries.zh: 居五年，來朝，明宗問以邊事，思同指畫山川，陳其利害。
entries.en: After five years he came to court; Mingzong asked about the border; Sitong traced the mountains and explained every advantage and risk.
entries.literal: After five years he came to court; Mingzong asked about the frontier; Sitong traced the mountains and rivers and laid out advantages and harms.

entries.zh: 思同去，明宗顧左右曰：「人言思同不管事，能若是邪？」
entries.en: As Sitong left, Mingzong told his attendants, “They say Sitong cannot govern—yet see this!"
entries.literal: When Sitong left, Mingzong said to those around him, “Men say Sitong is no administrator—can he do such as this?"

entries.zh: 於是始知其材，以為右武衛上將軍、京兆尹、西京留守。
entries.en: Then he recognized Sitong’s ability and made him General-in-Chief of the Right Martial Guard, metropolitan prefect, and western capital regent.
entries.literal: Then he knew Sitong’s talent and made him General-in-Chief of the Right Martial Guard, metropolitan prefect of Jingzhao, and western capital regent.

entries.zh: 石敬瑭討董璋，思同為先鋒指揮使，兵入劍門，而後軍不繼，思同與璋戰，不勝而卻。
entries.en: When Shi Jingtang attacked Dong Zhang, Sitong led the vanguard into Jianmen; the rear failed to follow; he fought Zhang, lost, and withdrew.
entries.literal: When Shi Jingtang campaigned against Dong Zhang, Sitong was vanguard commander; the army entered Jianmen, but the rear did not follow; Sitong fought Zhang, could not win, and withdrew.

entries.zh: 敬瑭兵罷，思同徙鎮山南西道，已而復為京兆尹、西京留守。
entries.en: When Jingtang’s campaign ended, Sitong governed Shannan West Circuit, then again became metropolitan prefect and western capital regent.
entries.literal: When Jingtang’s army was dismissed, Sitong was moved to govern Shannan West Circuit, then again became metropolitan prefect and western capital regent.

entries.zh: 張敬達，字志通，代州人也，小字生鐵。
entries.en: Zhang Jingda, courtesy name Zhitong, was from Daizhou; his childhood name was Raw Iron.
entries.literal: Zhang Jingda, courtesy name Zhitong, was a man of Daizhou; his childhood name was Raw Iron.

entries.zh: 少以騎射事唐莊宗為廳直軍使。
entries.en: Young and skilled in archery, he served Zhuangzong as commissioner of the Hall Direct Army.
entries.literal: In youth, skilled in mounted archery, he served Emperor Zhuangzong of Tang as commissioner of the Hall Direct Army.

entries.zh: 明宗時，為河東馬步軍都指揮使，領欽州刺史，累遷彰國、大同軍節度使，徙鎮武信、晉昌。
entries.en: Under Mingzong he commanded Hedong horse and foot and governed Qin, rose to governor of Zhangguo and Datong, then Wuxin and Jinchang.
entries.literal: Under Mingzong he was overall commander of horse and foot in Hedong and prefect of Qin, rising to military governor of Zhangguo and Datong, then moved to Wuxin and Jinchang.

entries.zh: 清泰二年，契丹數犯邊，廢帝以河東節度使石敬瑭兼大同、彰國、振武、威塞等軍蕃漢馬步軍都總管，屯於忻州，屯兵聚噪遮敬瑭呼「萬歲」，敬瑭斬三十餘人以止之。
entries.en: In Qingtai’s second year Khitan raids multiplied; the Deposed Emperor made Shi Jingtang overall commander of the northern armies at Xinzhou; his troops mutinied, blocked him, and shouted “Long live!”; he beheaded thirty men to quell them.
entries.literal: In the second year of Qingtai the Khitans raided the border repeatedly; the Deposed Emperor made Hedong governor Shi Jingtang overall commander of Tangut and Han horse and foot of Datong, Zhangguo, Zhenwu, Weisai, and other armies, camped at Xinzhou; the camp mutinied, blocked Jingtang, and shouted “Long live!”; Jingtang beheaded more than thirty to stop it.

entries.zh: 廢帝疑敬瑭有異志，乃以敬達為北面副總管，以分其兵。
entries.en: The Deposed Emperor suspected Jingtang and made Jingda deputy northern commander to split his force.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor suspected Jingtang of disloyalty and made Jingda deputy northern commander to divide his troops.

entries.zh: 明年夏，徙敬瑭鎮天平，遂以敬達為大同、彰國、振武、威塞等軍蕃漢馬步軍都部署，敬瑭因此遂反。
entries.en: Next summer Jingtang was moved to Tianping; Jingda took his armies—and Jingtang rebelled.
entries.literal: The next summer Jingtang was moved to govern Tianping, and Jingda was made overall commander of those armies; Jingtang therefore rebelled.

entries.zh: 即以敬達為太原四面招討使。
entries.en: Jingda was at once made four-sided pacification commissioner of Taiyuan.
entries.literal: Jingda was at once made four-sided pacification commissioner of Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 六月，兵圍太原，敬達為長城連柵，雲梯飛炮以攻之，所為城柵將成，輒有大風雨水暴至以壞之。
entries.en: In the sixth month he besieged Taiyuan with linked ramparts, ladders, and catapults—yet whenever the works neared completion, storms smashed them.
entries.literal: In the sixth month troops besieged Taiyuan; Jingda built linked ramparts and stormed with scaling ladders and flying catapults; whenever the works were nearly done, great winds and rain would burst forth and destroy them.

entries.zh: 敬瑭求救於契丹。
entries.en: Jingtang sought Khitan aid.
entries.literal: Jingtang sought rescue from the Khitans.

entries.zh: 九月，契丹耶律德光自雁門入，旌旗相屬五十餘里。
entries.en: In the ninth month Yelü Deguang entered through Yanmen; his banners stretched fifty li.
entries.literal: In the ninth month Yelü Deguang of the Khitans entered through Yanmen; banners and flags stretched more than fifty li.

entries.zh: 德光先遣人告敬瑭曰：「吾欲今日破敵可乎？」
entries.en: Deguang first asked Jingtang, “Shall I break the enemy today?"
entries.literal: Deguang first sent word to Jingtang: “Shall I break the enemy today?"

entries.zh: 敬瑭報曰：「大兵遠來，而賊勢方盛，要在成功，不必速也。」
entries.en: Jingtang replied, “You have marched far; the foe is strong—success matters, not haste.”
entries.literal: Jingtang replied: “Your great army has come far, and the foe’s power is at its height—the point is success, not speed.”

entries.zh: 使者未復命，而兵已交。
entries.en: Before the envoy returned, battle had begun.
entries.literal: Before the envoy could return, the armies had already joined battle.

entries.zh: 敬達陣於西山，契丹以羸騎三千，革鞭木鐙，人馬皆不甲胄，以趨唐軍。
entries.en: Jingda formed on the western hills; the Khitans sent three thousand unarmored horses with leather whips and wooden stirrups to charge the Tang line.
entries.literal: Jingda formed battle on the western hills; the Khitans sent three thousand weak horses with leather whips and wooden stirrups, men and horses all without armor, charging the Tang army.

entries.zh: 唐軍爭馳之，契丹兵走。
entries.en: The Tang army gave chase; the Khitans fled.
entries.literal: The Tang army raced after them; the Khitan troops fled.

entries.zh: 追至汾曲，伏發，斷唐軍為二，其在北者皆死，死者萬餘人。
entries.en: At Fen Qu an ambush sprang; the Tang line was cut in two; everyone north of the trap died—more than ten thousand.
entries.literal: Pursuit reached Fen Qu; ambush sprang; the Tang army was cut in two; all in the north died—more than ten thousand dead.

entries.zh: 敬達收軍柵晉安，契丹圍之。
entries.en: Jingda fell back to Jin’an; the Khitans besieged him.
entries.literal: Jingda gathered his troops and fortified at Jin’an; the Khitans besieged them.

entries.zh: 廢帝遣趙延壽、範延光等救之。
entries.en: The Deposed Emperor sent Zhao Yanshou, Fan Yanguang, and others to relieve him.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor sent Zhao Yanshou, Fan Yanguang, and others to rescue him.

entries.zh: 延壽屯團柏谷，延光屯遼州，相去皆百餘里。
entries.en: Yanshou camped at Tuanbai Valley, Yanguang at Liaozhou—more than a hundred li apart.
entries.literal: Yanshou camped at Tuanbai Valley, Yanguang at Liaozhou—each more than a hundred li away.

entries.zh: 契丹兵圍敬達者，自晉安寨南，長百餘里，闊五十里，敬達軍中望之，但見穹廬連屬如岡阜，四面亙以毛索，掛鈴為警，縱犬往來。
entries.en: The Khitan ring around Jin’an ran a hundred li south of the stockade and fifty li wide; inside Jingda’s camp yurts rose like hills; raw ropes and bells guarded every side; dogs patrolled the lines.
entries.literal: The Khitans surrounding Jingda stretched from south of the Jin’an stockade for more than a hundred li, fifty li wide; in Jingda’s camp one saw only yurts linked like hillocks; on four sides they ran raw ropes, hung bells for alarm, and let dogs run to and fro.

entries.zh: 敬達軍中有夜出者，輒為契丹所得，由是閉壁不敢復出。
entries.en: Night sorties from Jingda’s camp were captured; thereafter the walls stayed shut.
entries.literal: Anyone who went out by night from Jingda’s army was taken by the Khitans; thereafter they shut the walls and dared not go out again.

entries.zh: 延壽等皆有二心，無救敬達意。
entries.en: Yanshou and the rest were half-hearted and had no will to save him.
entries.literal: Yanshou and the rest all had divided hearts and no will to save Jingda.

entries.zh: 敬達猶有兵五萬人、馬萬匹，久之食盡，削木篩糞以飼其馬，馬死者食之，已而馬盡。
entries.en: Jingda still had fifty thousand men and ten thousand horses; food ran out; they shaved wood and sifted dung for the horses, then ate the dead horses—until there were no horses left.
entries.literal: Jingda still had fifty thousand men and ten thousand horses; in time food ran out; they shaved wood and sifted dung to feed the horses; when horses died they ate them; soon the horses were gone.

entries.zh: 副招討使楊光遠勸敬達降晉，敬達自以不忍背唐，而救兵且至，光遠促之不已，敬達曰：「諸公何相迫邪！
entries.en: Deputy commissioner Yang Guangyuan urged surrender to Jin; Jingda could not betray Tang and believed relief was near; Guangyuan pressed him; Jingda said, “Why do you hound me so!
entries.literal: Deputy pacification commissioner Yang Guangyuan urged Jingda to surrender to Jin; Jingda himself could not bear to betray Tang, and relief was due; Guangyuan pressed without cease; Jingda said, “Gentlemen, why do you press me so!

entries.zh: 何不殺我而降？」
entries.en: Why not kill me and surrender?"
entries.literal: Why not kill me and surrender?"

entries.zh: 光遠即斬敬達降。
entries.en: Guangyuan beheaded Jingda and surrendered.
entries.literal: Guangyuan at once beheaded Jingda and surrendered.

entries.zh: 契丹耶律德光聞敬達死，哀其忠，遣人收葬之。
entries.en: Deguang mourned Jingda’s loyalty and sent men to bury him.
entries.literal: When Yelü Deguang heard Jingda was dead he mourned his loyalty and sent men to gather and bury him.

entries.zh: 應順元年二月，潞王從珂反鳳翔，馳檄四鄰，言奸臣幸先帝疾病，賊殺秦王而立幼嗣，侵弱宗室，動搖藩方，陳己所以興兵討亂之狀。
entries.en: In Yingshun’s first year, second month, Prince of Lu Congke rebelled at Fengxiang and circulated proclamations accusing treacherous ministers of murdering the Prince of Qin during the late emperor’s illness, enthroning a child, weakening the clan, and shaking the realm—and stating why he had taken arms.
entries.literal: In the second month of the first year of Yingshun, Prince of Lu Congke rebelled at Fengxiang and sent proclamations to the four quarters, saying treacherous ministers had taken advantage of the late emperor’s illness to murder the Prince of Qin and set up a child heir, weakening the imperial clan and shaking the provinces, and stating why he had raised troops to punish disorder.

entries.zh: 因遣伶奴安十十以五弦謁思同，欲因其歡以通意。
entries.en: He sent the actor An Shishi with a five-string lute to visit Sitong, hoping pleasure would win him over.
entries.literal: He sent the actor An Shishi with a five-string lute to visit Sitong, hoping to win him through pleasure.

entries.zh: 是時，諸鎮皆懷向背，所得潞王書檄，雖以上聞，而不絕其使。
entries.en: Every command wavered; they reported Congke’s letters to court yet kept his envoys coming.
entries.literal: At that time every command wavered; though they reported the Prince of Lu’s letters upward, they did not cut off his envoys.

entries.zh: 獨思同執十十及從珂所使推官郝詡等送京師。
entries.en: Only Sitong seized Shishi and Congke’s staff officer Hao Xu and sent them to the capital.
entries.literal: Only Sitong seized Shishi and Congke’s staff officer Hao Xu and the rest and sent them to the capital.

entries.zh: 湣帝嘉其忠，即以思同為西面行營馬步軍都部署。
entries.en: The Deposed Emperor praised his loyalty and made him overall western campaign commander.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor praised his loyalty and at once made Sitong overall commander of horse and foot for the western campaign.

entries.zh: 三月，會諸鎮兵圍鳳翔，破東西關城。
entries.en: In the third month allied commands besieged Fengxiang and took the east and west gate cities.
entries.literal: In the third month the commands united to besiege Fengxiang and broke the eastern and western gate cities.

entries.zh: 從珂兵弱而守甚堅，外兵傷死者眾，從珂登城呼外兵而泣曰：「吾從先帝二十年，大小數百戰，甲不解體，金瘡滿身，士卒固嘗從我矣。
entries.en: Congke was weak but held firm; besiegers died in droves; he mounted the wall weeping: “Twenty years I followed the late emperor, hundreds of battles, armor never off, scars over my body—you marched with me!
entries.literal: Congke’s force was weak but his defense staunch; outside troops died in great numbers; Congke mounted the wall and called to the outside army in tears: “I followed the late emperor twenty years, fought hundreds of battles great and small, never doffed my armor, my body covered in scars—soldiers, you have marched with me!

entries.zh: 今先帝新棄天下，而朝廷信用奸人，離間骨肉，我實何罪而見伐乎？」
entries.en: The late emperor has just died, and the court’s wicked men sunder kin—what crime is mine that you attack me?"
entries.literal: The late emperor has just left the world, and the court trusts wicked men who sunder flesh and blood—what crime is mine that I should be attacked?"

entries.zh: 因慟哭。
entries.en: Then he sobbed aloud.
entries.literal: Then he wailed bitterly.

entries.zh: 士卒聞者，皆悲憐之。
entries.en: The soldiers who heard were moved to pity.
entries.literal: Soldiers who heard were all moved to pity.

entries.zh: 興元張虔釗攻城西，督戰甚急，士卒苦之，反兵攻虔釗，虔釗走。
entries.en: Zhang Qianzhao of Xingyuan stormed the west wall so hard the men mutinied and drove him off.
entries.literal: Zhang Qianzhao of Xingyuan assaulted the west of the city and pressed the fight fiercely; the troops suffered and turned on Qianzhao, who fled.

entries.zh: 羽林指揮使楊思權呼曰：「潞王，吾主也！」
entries.en: Yulin commander Yang Siquan shouted, “The Prince of Lu is our lord!"
entries.literal: Yulin commander Yang Siquan shouted, “The Prince of Lu is our lord!"

entries.zh: 乃引軍自西門入降從珂。
entries.en: He led his men through the west gate to surrender to Congke.
entries.literal: He then led his troops in through the west gate to surrender to Congke.

entries.zh: 而思同未知，猶督戰。
entries.en: Sitong had not yet heard, yet still pressed the attack.
entries.literal: Sitong did not yet know, but still urged the fight on.

entries.zh: 嚴衛指揮使尹暉麾其眾曰：「城西軍入城受賞矣！
entries.en: Yanwei commander Yin Hui called to his men, “The western army is in the city taking rewards!
entries.literal: Yanwei commander Yin Hui waved his troops and said, “The western army has entered the city for rewards!

entries.zh: 何用戰邪？」
entries.en: Why fight?"
entries.literal: Why fight?"

entries.zh: 士卒解甲棄仗，聲聞數里，遂皆入城降。
entries.en: Men threw off armor; the clamor carried for li; all entered the city and surrendered.
entries.literal: Soldiers cast off armor and weapons; the sound carried for li; then all entered the city and surrendered.

entries.zh: 諸鎮之兵皆潰。
entries.en: Every allied army broke and fled.
entries.literal: The armies of every command broke and fled.

entries.zh: 思同挺身走，至長安，西京副留守劉遂雍閉門不納，乃走潼關。
entries.en: Sitong fled to Chang’an; Deputy Regent Liu Suiyong shut the gates; he fled toward Tong Pass.
entries.literal: Sitong fled alone to Chang’an; Liu Suiyong, deputy regent of the western capital, shut the gates and would not admit him, and he fled toward Tong Pass.

entries.zh: 從珂引兵東，至昭應，前鋒追執思同。
entries.en: Congke marched east; at Zhaoying his vanguard captured Sitong.
entries.literal: Congke marched east; at Zhaoying his vanguard overtook and seized Sitong.

entries.zh: 從珂責曰：「罪可逃乎？」
entries.en: Congke reproached him: “Did you think your crime could escape?"
entries.literal: Congke reproached him: “Could your crime escape?"

entries.zh: 思同曰：「非不知從王而得生，恐終死不能見先帝於地下。」
entries.en: Sitong said, “I knew following you meant life—but I feared I could never face the late emperor in the grave.”
entries.literal: Sitong said, “It is not that I did not know following the prince would let me live—I feared that in the end I could not face the late emperor underground.”

entries.zh: 從珂愧其言，乃殺之。
entries.en: Congke was shamed by his words and had him killed.
entries.literal: Congke was shamed by his words and killed him.

entries.zh: 漢高祖即位，贈侍中。
entries.en: When Gaozu of Han took the throne, Sitong was posthumously made Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: When Gaozu of Han took the throne, Sitong was posthumously made Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 王清，字去瑕，洺州曲周人也。
entries.en: Wang Qing, courtesy name Quxia, was from Quzhou in Luozhou.
entries.literal: Wang Qing, courtesy name Quxia, was a man of Quzhou in Luozhou.

entries.zh: 初事唐為寧衛指揮使。
entries.en: He first served Tang as commander of the Ningwei Guard.
entries.literal: He first served Tang as commander of the Ningwei Guard.

entries.zh: 後事晉為奉國都虞候。
entries.en: Later he served Jin as chief adjutant of the Fengguo Army.
entries.literal: Later he served Jin as chief adjutant of the Fengguo Army.

entries.zh: 安從進叛襄州，從高行周攻之，逾年不能下，清謂行周曰：「從進閉孤城以自守，其勢豈得久邪？」
entries.en: When An Congjin rebelled at Xiangzhou, Gao Xingzhou besieged him a year without success; Qing said, “He holds one city—how long can that last?"
entries.literal: When An Congjin rebelled at Xiangzhou, Gao Xingzhou besieged him more than a year without taking the city; Qing said to Xingzhou, “Congjin holds a lone city—how long can he last?"

entries.zh: 因請先登，遂攻破之。
entries.en: He asked to lead the assault and took the city.
entries.literal: He asked to lead the assault and broke the city.

entries.zh: 開運二年冬，從杜重威戰陽城，清以力戰功為步軍之最，加檢校司徒。
entries.en: In Kaiyun’s second winter he fought with Du Chongwei at Yangcheng; for valor he was judged best among the infantry and made Acting Minister of Works.
entries.literal: In the winter of the second year of Kaiyun he followed Du Chongwei at the battle of Yangcheng; for fierce fighting he was judged foremost among the infantry and made Acting Minister of Works.

entries.zh: 是冬，重威軍中渡橋南，虜軍其北以相拒，而虜以精騎並西山出晉軍後，南擊欒城，斷晉餉道。
entries.en: That winter Chongwei camped south of Zhongdu Bridge, the Khitans north; Khitan elite cavalry swept behind the Jin line along the western hills, struck Luancheng, and cut Jin’s supplies.
entries.literal: That winter Chongwei’s army was south of the Zhongdu Bridge and the barbarians north, facing each other; the barbarians sent elite cavalry along the western hills behind the Jin army and struck south at Luancheng, cutting Jin’s supply route.

entries.zh: 清謂重威曰：「晉軍危矣！
entries.en: Qing told Chongwei, “The Jin army is doomed!
entries.literal: Qing said to Chongwei, “The Jin army is in peril!

entries.zh: 今去鎮州五里，而守死於此，營孤食盡，將若之何？
entries.en: Zhenzhou is five li away, yet we sit here to die, cut off and starving—what now?
entries.literal: Zhenzhou is only five li away, yet we sit here waiting to die, camp isolated and food gone—what is to be done?

entries.zh: 請以步兵二千為先鋒，奪橋開路，公率諸軍繼進以入鎮州，可以守也。」
entries.en: Give me two thousand foot to seize the bridge; you follow with the main army into Zhenzhou—we can hold."
entries.literal: Let me take two thousand foot as vanguard, seize the bridge and open the road; you lead the main army after and enter Zhenzhou—we can hold it."

entries.zh: 重威許之，遣與宋彥筠俱前，清與虜戰，敗之，奪其橋。
entries.en: Chongwei agreed and sent him with Song Yanyun; Qing beat the Khitans and took the bridge.
entries.literal: Chongwei agreed and sent him forward with Song Yanyun; Qing fought the barbarians, defeated them, and took the bridge.

entries.zh: 是時，重威已有二誌，猶豫不肯進，彥筠亦退走，清曰：「吾獨死於此矣！」
entries.en: Chongwei already wavered and would not advance; Yanyun retreated; Qing said, “Then I die here alone!"
entries.literal: By then Chongwei already had two minds and hesitated to advance; Yanyun also retreated; Qing said, “I die here alone!"

entries.zh: 因力戰而死。
entries.en: He fought on and died.
entries.literal: He fought on with all his strength and died.

entries.zh: 年五十三。
entries.en: He was fifty-three.
entries.literal: He was fifty-three.

entries.zh: 漢高祖立，贈清太傅。
entries.en: When Gaozu of Han took the throne, Qing was posthumously made Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: When Gaozu of Han took the throne, Qing was posthumously made Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 周世宗征淮，李景懼，始遣泗州牙將王知朗至徐州，奉書以求和，世宗不答。
entries.en: When Shizong campaigned on the Huai, Jing in fear sent Wang Zhilang to Xuzhou to sue for peace; Shizong ignored him.
entries.literal: When Shizong of Zhou campaigned on the Huai, Jing feared and first sent Sizhou aide Wang Zhilang to Xuzhou with a letter seeking peace; Shizong did not answer.

entries.zh: 又遣翰林學士鐘謨、文理院學士李德明奉表稱臣，不答。
entries.en: He sent Zhong Mo and Li Deming with a memorial of submission; still no answer.
entries.literal: He again sent Academician Zhong Mo and Institute scholar Li Deming with a memorial calling himself subject; no answer.

entries.zh: 乃遣禮部尚書王崇質副晟奉表，謨與晟等皆言景願割壽、濠、泗、楚、光、海六州之地，歲貢百萬以佐軍。
entries.en: Then he sent Minister of Rites Wang Chongzhi as deputy to Cheng with a memorial; Mo, Cheng, and the rest offered six Huai prefectures and a million a year in tribute.
entries.literal: Then he sent Minister of Rites Wang Chongzhi as Cheng’s deputy with a memorial; Mo, Cheng, and the rest all said Jing would cede the six prefectures of Shou, Hao, Si, Chu, Guang, and Hai and pay a million a year to support the army.

entries.zh: 而世宗已取滁、揚、濠、泗諸州，欲盡取淮南乃止，因留使者不遣，而攻壽州益急。
entries.en: Shizong had already taken Chu, Yang, Hao, and Si and wanted all Huainan; he detained the envoys and tightened the siege of Shouzhou.
entries.literal: But Shizong had already taken Chu, Yang, Hao, and Si and wished to take all Huainan before stopping; he detained the envoys and pressed the siege of Shouzhou harder.

entries.zh: 謨等見世宗英武非景敵，而師甚盛，壽春且危，乃曰：「願陛下寬臣五日之誅，容臣還取景表，盡獻淮北諸州。」
entries.en: Mo and the rest saw Shizong’s might and Shouchun’s peril; they said, “Grant us five days to return with Jing’s offer of all north Huai prefectures."
entries.literal: Mo and the others saw that Jing was no match for Shizong's martial prowess, that the army was overwhelmingly strong, and that Shouchun was near peril; they said, “We beg Your Majesty to grant us five days' reprieve, so that we may return and bring Jing's memorial offering all the prefectures north of the Huai.”

entries.zh: 世宗許之，遣供奉官安弘道押德明、崇質南還，而謨與晟皆見留。
entries.en: Shizong agreed, sent An Hongdao south with Deming and Chongzhi, and kept Mo and Cheng.
entries.literal: Shizong agreed and sent Palace Attendant An Hongdao to escort Deming and Chongzhi south, while Mo and Cheng were detained.

entries.zh: 德明等既還，景悔，不肯割地。
entries.en: When Deming returned, Jing repented and refused to cede land.
entries.literal: When Deming and the rest returned, Jing repented and would not cede land.

entries.zh: 世宗亦以暑雨班師，留李重進、張永德等分攻廬、壽，周兵所得揚、泰諸州，皆不能守，景兵復振。
entries.en: Shizong withdrew for summer rain, leaving Chongjin and Yongde to attack Lu and Shou; Zhou lost Yang and Tai; Jing’s army revived.
entries.literal: Shizong also withdrew for summer rains; he left Li Chongjin and Zhang Yongde to attack Lu and Shou separately; the Yang and Tai prefectures Zhou had taken could not be held; Jing’s army revived.

entries.zh: 重進與永德兩軍相疑，有隙，永德上書言重進反，世宗不聽。
entries.en: Chongjin and Yongde mistrusted each other; Yongde accused Chongjin of rebellion; Shizong disbelieved.
entries.literal: Chongjin and Yongde distrusted each other and had a rift; Yongde memorialized that Chongjin had rebelled; Shizong did not believe it.

entries.zh: 景知二將之相疑也，乃以蠟丸書遺重進，勸其反。
entries.en: Jing knew they were at odds and sent Chongjin a wax-sealed letter urging rebellion.
entries.literal: Jing knew the two generals were at odds and sent a wax-sealed letter urging Chongjin to rebel.

entries.zh: 初，晟之奉使也，語崇質曰：「吾行必不免，然吾終不負永陵一抷土也。」
entries.en: When Cheng first went as envoy he told Chongzhi, “I shall surely not return—but I will never betray Yongling’s soil."
entries.literal: When Cheng first went on embassy he told Chongzhi, “My journey will surely not spare me—but I will never betray a handful of soil from Yongling."

entries.zh: 永陵者，墓也。
entries.en: Yongling means the royal tomb.
entries.literal: Yongling means the tomb.

entries.zh: 及崇質還，而晟與鐘謨俱至京師，館於都亭驛，待之甚厚，每朝會入閣，使班東省官後，召見必飲以醇酒。
entries.en: When Chongzhi returned, Cheng and Mo reached the capital, lodged at the Capital Pavilion, were honored at court, ranked after eastern officials, and were plied with wine at every audience.
entries.literal: When Chongzhi returned, Cheng and Zhong Mo both reached the capital and lodged at the Capital Pavilion; they were treated very generously; at each court session they ranked after the eastern-province officials; when summoned they were always given strong wine.

entries.zh: 已而周兵數敗，盡失所得諸州，世宗憂之，召晟問江南事，晟不對，世宗怒，未有以發。
entries.en: Soon Zhou armies lost repeatedly; Shizong worried and asked Cheng about the south; Cheng was silent; Shizong raged but had no cause.
entries.literal: Before long Zhou armies suffered repeated defeats and lost all the prefectures they had taken; Shizong worried and summoned Cheng to ask about affairs south of the Yangzi; Cheng would not answer; Shizong grew angry but had no pretext.

entries.zh: 會重進以景蠟丸書來上，多斥周過惡以為言，由是發怒曰：「晟來使我，言景畏吾神武，願得北面稱臣，保無二心，安得此指斥之言乎？」
entries.en: When Chongjin sent up Jing’s wax letter full of Zhou’s crimes, Shizong exploded: “Cheng told me Jing feared my might and would submit—how is this abuse?"
entries.literal: When Chongjin sent up Jing’s wax letter, full of Zhou’s faults and wickedness, Shizong flared: “Cheng came as my envoy and said Jing feared my divine might and wished to submit north and keep faith—how comes this abuse?"

entries.zh: 亟召待衛軍虞候韓通收晟下獄，及其從者二百餘人皆殺之。
entries.en: He summoned Han Tong, imprisoned Cheng, and killed him and two hundred followers.
entries.literal: He at once summoned Guard Army commissioner Han Tong, seized Cheng and put him in prison, and killed him and more than two hundred followers.

entries.zh: 晟臨死，世宗猶遣近臣問之，晟終不對，神色怡然，正其衣冠南望而拜曰：「臣惟以死報國爾！」
entries.en: At execution Shizong still sent an attendant to question him; Cheng was calm, straightened his robes, bowed south, and said, “I repay the state with death alone!"
entries.literal: At the point of death Shizong still sent a close attendant to question him; Cheng never answered, his expression calm; he straightened his robes, bowed south, and said, “I have only death to repay the state!"

entries.zh: 乃就刑。
entries.en: Then he was executed.
entries.literal: Then he went to the block.

entries.zh: 晟既死，鐘謨亦貶耀州司馬。
entries.en: After Cheng died, Mo was demoted to military adjutant of Yao.
entries.literal: After Cheng died, Zhong Mo was demoted to military adjutant of Yao.

entries.zh: 其後，世宗怒解，憐晟忠，悔殺之，召拜鐘謨衛尉少卿。
entries.en: Later Shizong’s anger cooled; he pitied Cheng and regretted the killing; he recalled Mo as Vice Director of the Imperial Guard.
entries.literal: Later Shizong’s anger eased; he pitied Cheng’s loyalty and regretted killing him; he recalled and made Zhong Mo Vice Director of the Imperial Guard.

entries.zh: 景已割江北，遂遣謨還，而景聞晟死，亦贈魯國公。
entries.en: Jing had ceded land north of the Yangzi and sent Mo back; hearing Cheng was dead, he too posthumously made him Duke of Lu.
entries.literal: Jing had already ceded north of the Yangzi and sent Mo back; when Jing heard Cheng was dead he too posthumously made him Duke of Lu.

entries.zh: 嗚呼甚哉！
entries.en: Alas—how extreme!
entries.literal: Alas, how extreme!

entries.zh: 自開平訖於顯德，終始五十三年，而天下五代。
entries.en: From Kaiping to Xiande, fifty-three years passed—and through them the realm saw five dynasties.
entries.literal: From the Kaiping era through Xiande, fifty-three years in all—and through that span the realm knew five dynasties.

entries.zh: 士之不幸而生其時，欲全其節而不二者，固鮮矣。
entries.en: Few were the scholars born into that age who could keep their integrity intact and never serve a second lord.
entries.literal: Scholars unlucky enough to be born in that age who wished to keep their integrity whole and serve no second master were indeed few.

entries.zh: 於此之時，責士以死與必去，則天下為無士矣。
entries.en: In such an age, demanding that every gentleman die or quit office would have left the realm without gentlemen at all.
entries.literal: At such a time, if one demanded that every gentleman die or certainly depart, the realm would have had no gentlemen left.

entries.zh: 然其習俗，遂以茍生不去為當然。
entries.en: Yet custom came to treat clinging to life and never leaving office as only natural.
entries.literal: Yet custom came to treat clinging to life and not leaving as the natural thing.

entries.zh: 至於儒者，以仁義忠信為學，享人之祿，任人之國者，不顧其存亡，皆恬然以茍生為得，非徒不知愧，而反以其得為榮者，可勝數哉！
entries.en: Confucians trained in benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and faith—men who ate another’s salary and governed another’s state—often ignored their state’s survival, calmly treating shameful survival as success; not only unashamed, they took it as glory. Their number was beyond counting!
entries.literal: As for Confucians, who took benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and faith as their study—men who enjoyed others’ salaries and bore charge of others’ states—many ignored whether those states lived or died, all calmly taking a shameful survival as gain; not only did they feel no shame, but took that gain as glory. Who could count them!

entries.zh: 故吾於死事之臣，有所取焉。
entries.en: That is why I find something worth honoring in ministers who died for their lord’s cause.
entries.literal: Therefore in ministers who died for their lords’ cause I find something worth taking.

entries.zh: 君子之於人也，樂成其美而不求其備，況死者人之所難乎？
entries.en: A gentleman delights in another’s virtues and does not demand perfection—especially when death is what men find hardest.
entries.literal: The gentleman toward others delights in completing their excellence and does not demand their perfection—how much more when death is what men find hardest?

entries.zh: 吾於五代，得全節之士三人而已。
entries.en: In the Five Dynasties I find only three men who kept their integrity intact throughout.
entries.literal: In the Five Dynasties I find only three men who kept their integrity whole.

entries.zh: 其初無卓然之節，而終以死人之事者，得十有五人焉，而戰沒者不得與也。
entries.en: Fifteen men lacked outstanding integrity at first yet died for another’s cause in the end; those killed in battle are not counted here.
entries.literal: Those who at first lacked outstanding integrity but in the end died for another’s cause number fifteen; those who died in battle are not counted among them.

entries.zh: 然吾取王清、史彥超者，其有旨哉！
entries.en: Yet that I include Wang Qing and Shi Yanchao—was there not a reason?
entries.literal: Yet that I take Wang Qing and Shi Yanchao—was there not a point to it?

entries.zh: 其有旨哉！
entries.en: There was a reason!
entries.literal: Was there not a point to it!

entries.zh: 作《死事傳》。
entries.en: Hence I wrote the “Biographies of Martyrs to Service.”
entries.literal: I composed the “Biographies of Martyrs to Service.”

entries.zh: 嗚呼，五代之亂極矣，《傳》所謂「天地閉，賢人隱」之時歟！
entries.en: Alas—the Five Dynasties’ chaos reached its height. Was this not the age the Records call “Heaven and Earth shut, worthy men in hiding”?
entries.literal: Alas, the disorder of the Five Dynasties reached its extreme—is this not the time the “Records” calls “Heaven and Earth shut, worthy men in hiding”?

entries.zh: 當此之時，臣弒其君，子弒其父，而搢紳之士安其祿而立其朝，充然無復廉恥之色者皆是也。
entries.en: Ministers murdered lords, sons murdered fathers, yet officials took salary and stood in court without a trace of shame.
entries.literal: In that age ministers murdered their lords and sons murdered their fathers, while gentry and officials took their salaries and stood in court, all replete and without the color of shame.

entries.zh: 吾以謂自古忠臣義士多出於亂世，而怪當時可道者何少也，豈果無其人哉？
entries.en: Loyal ministers and righteous men usually rise in chaotic ages—yet how few in that time were worth naming. Were there truly none?
entries.literal: I hold that loyal ministers and righteous men have always come forth in ages of disorder—yet I marvel that so few in that time were worth speaking of; was it truly that there were no such men?

entries.zh: 雖曰干戈興，學校廢，而禮義衰，風俗隳壞，至於如此，然自古天下未嘗無人也，吾意必有潔身自負之士，嫉世遠去而不可見者。
entries.en: War rose, schools fell, ritual decayed, custom collapsed—yet the world has never lacked men. Surely some of clean conduct scorned the age and withdrew beyond sight.
entries.literal: Though it is said arms were raised, schools abandoned, ritual and righteousness declined, and custom ruined to such a point—yet the world has never been without men; I believe there were men of clean conduct who scorned the age, went far off, and could not be seen.

entries.zh: 自古材賢有韞於中而不見於外，或窮居陋巷，委身草莽，雖顏子之行，不遇仲尼而名不彰，況世變多故，而君子道消之時乎！
entries.en: Talent often hides within and never shows without—men in poor lanes, lost in the wild. Even Yan Hui’s virtue needed Confucius to be known; how much more when the gentleman’s Way was fading in constant turmoil!
entries.literal: From antiquity talent and worth have been stored within and not shown without, or dwelt in poor lanes and cast themselves on the wild—though Yan Hui’s conduct, without meeting Confucius, would not have won fame; how much more in an age of many changes when the gentleman’s Way was in decline!

entries.zh: 吾又以謂必有負材能，修節義，而沈淪於下，泯沒而無聞者。
entries.en: Surely too were men of talent and integrity who sank below and died unheard.
entries.literal: I also hold that there were men of talent and ability who cultivated integrity and righteousness yet sank below and were drowned without a hearing.

entries.zh: 求之傳記，而亂世崩離，文字殘缺，不可復得，然僅得者四五人而已。
entries.en: Records of that collapse are broken; little can be recovered. I find only four or five men.
entries.literal: Seeking in records, in disorder and collapse the writing is broken and cannot be recovered; yet of those barely found there are only four or five.

entries.zh: 鄭遨，字雲叟，滑州白馬人也。
entries.en: Zheng Ao, courtesy name Yunsong, was from Baima in Huazhou.
entries.literal: Zheng Ao, courtesy name Yunsong, was a man of Baima in Huazhou.

entries.zh: 唐明宗祖廟諱遨，故世行其字。
entries.en: Mingzong’s ancestral taboo forbade the character ao, so the world used his courtesy name.
entries.literal: Emperor Mingzong of Tang’s ancestral temple tabooed the character ao, so the world used his courtesy name.

entries.zh: 遨少好學，敏於文辭。
entries.en: In youth he loved learning and wrote with ease.
entries.literal: Ao in youth loved study and was quick at literary composition.

entries.zh: 唐昭宗時，舉進士不中，見天下已亂，有拂衣遠去之意，欲攜其妻、子與俱隱，其妻不從，遨及入少室山為道士。
entries.en: Under Zhaozong he failed the jinshi; seeing chaos, he wished to flee with wife and children—his wife refused; he entered Mount Shaoshi as a Daoist.
entries.literal: Under Emperor Zhaozong of Tang he entered the jinshi examinations and failed; seeing the realm already in disorder, he had the will to shake off his robes and go far off, wishing to take wife and children into hiding together—his wife would not follow; Ao thereupon entered Mount Shaoshi as a Daoist priest.

entries.zh: 其妻數以書勸遨還家，輒投之於火，後聞其妻、子卒，一慟而止。
entries.en: His wife wrote again and again; he burned each letter; when he heard she and the children were dead, he grieved once and stopped.
entries.literal: His wife several times wrote urging Ao to return home; he always threw the letters into the fire; later hearing his wife and children had died, he mourned once and stopped.

entries.zh: 遨與李振故善，振後事梁貴顯，欲以祿遨，遨不顧，後振得罪南竄，遨徒步千里往省之，由是聞者益高其行。
entries.en: He had been close to Li Zhen; when Zhen rose high in Liang and offered him office, Ao refused; when Zhen was disgraced and fled south, Ao walked a thousand li to see him—and his fame grew.
entries.literal: Ao had been friendly with Li Zhen; Zhen later served Liang in high honor and wished to give Ao an office—Ao paid no heed; later Zhen was punished and fled south; Ao walked a thousand li on foot to visit him, and hearers all the more exalted his conduct.

entries.zh: 其後，遨聞華山有五粒松，脂淪入地，千歲化為藥，能去三屍，因徙居華陰，欲求之。
entries.en: He heard Mount Hua’s five-kernel pines oozed resin that, buried a thousand years, became medicine to expel the three corpses; he moved to Huayin to seek it.
entries.literal: Later Ao heard that on Mount Hua there were five-kernel pines whose resin sank into the earth and after a thousand years became medicine that could expel the three corpses; he moved to Huayin to seek it.

entries.zh: 與道士李道殷、羅隱之友善，世目以為三高士。
entries.en: He befriended the Daoist Li Daoyin and Luo Yinzhi; the age called them the Three High Recluses.
entries.literal: He was friendly with the Daoist Li Daoyin and Luo Yinzhi; the age called them the Three High Recluses.

entries.zh: 遨種田，隱之賣藥以自給，道殷有釣魚術，鉤而不餌，又能化石為金，遨嘗驗其信然，而不之求也。
entries.en: Ao farmed; Yin sold herbs; Daoyin fished with hook but no bait and could turn stone to gold—Ao proved it true yet never asked.
entries.literal: Ao farmed; Yin sold medicine to support themselves; Daoyin had an art of fishing—hook without bait—and could also turn stone to gold; Ao once tested him and found it true, yet did not ask for it.

entries.zh: 節度使劉遂凝數以寶貨遺之，遨一不受。
entries.en: Governor Liu Suining sent treasures repeatedly; Ao refused every gift.
entries.literal: Military governor Liu Suining several times sent him treasures; Ao never accepted one.

entries.zh: 唐明宗時以左拾遺、晉高祖時以諫議大夫召之，皆不起，即賜號為逍遙先生。
entries.en: Mingzong summoned him as Left Reminder, Gaozu as Grand Master of Remonstrance—he refused both and was named Master Free Wanderer.
entries.literal: Under Mingzong of Tang he was summoned as Left Reminder; under Gaozu of Jin as Censor; he rose for neither; they at once granted him the title Master Free Wanderer.

entries.zh: 天福四年卒，年七十四。
entries.en: He died in the fourth Tianfu year, aged seventy-four.
entries.literal: In the fourth year of Tianfu he died, aged seventy-four.

entries.zh: 與遨同時張薦明者，燕人也。
entries.en: His contemporary Zhang Jianming was from Yan.
entries.literal: Zhang Jianming of the same time was a man of Yan.

entries.zh: 少以儒學遊河朔，後去為道士，通老子、莊周之說。
entries.en: Young he studied Confucianism in Hebei; later he became a Daoist versed in Laozi and Zhuangzi.
entries.literal: In youth he traveled the Hebei region as a Confucian scholar; later he left that and became a Daoist, penetrating the teachings of Laozi and Zhuang Zhou.

entries.zh: 高祖召見，問「道家可以治國乎？」
entries.en: Gaozu summoned him and asked, “Can Daoism govern the state?”
entries.literal: Gaozu summoned him and asked, “Can the Daoist teaching govern the state?”

entries.zh: 對曰：「道也者，妙萬物而為言，得其極者，屍居衽席之間可以治天地也。」
entries.en: He replied, “The Dao accounts for all things in speech; at its utmost one governs Heaven and Earth while lying between mat and coverlet.”
entries.literal: He replied: “The Dao is that which subtly accounts for the ten thousand things in speech; one who attains its utmost can govern Heaven and Earth while remaining still between mat and coverlet.”

entries.zh: 高祖大其言，延入內殿講《道德經》，拜以為師。
entries.en: Gaozu prized his words, drew him into the inner hall to lecture on the Daodejing, and honored him as teacher.
entries.literal: Gaozu magnified his words, drew him into the inner hall to lecture on the “Classic of the Way and Its Power,” and honored him as teacher.

entries.zh: 薦明聞宮中奉時鼓，曰：「陛下聞鼓乎？
entries.en: Hearing the palace drum for the seasons, Jianming said, “Does Your Majesty hear the drum?
entries.literal: Jianming heard the palace observe the seasonal drum and said, “Your Majesty hears the drum?

entries.zh: 其聲一而已。
entries.en: Its sound is one.
entries.literal: Its sound is one only.

entries.zh: 五音十二律，鼓無一焉，然和之者鼓也。
entries.en: Of five tones and twelve pipes the drum holds not one—yet harmony depends on the drum.
entries.literal: Among the five tones and twelve pitch pipes the drum has not one—yet what harmonizes them is the drum.

entries.zh: 夫一，萬事之本也，能守一者可以治天下。」
entries.en: The One is the root of all things; whoever keeps the One can govern the realm.”
entries.literal: The One is the root of the ten thousand affairs; one who can keep the One can govern the realm.”

entries.zh: 高祖善之，賜號通玄先生，後不知其所終。
entries.en: Gaozu approved and named him Master Penetrating Mystery; later his end is unknown.
entries.literal: Gaozu approved and granted him the title Master Penetrating Mystery; later his end is unknown.

entries.zh: 昂父亦好學，平生不喜佛說，父死，昂於柩前誦《尚書》，曰：「此吾先人之所欲聞也。」
entries.en: His father too loved learning and disliked Buddhist teachings; at the bier Ang recited the Documents, saying, “This is what my father wished to hear.”
entries.literal: Ang’s father also loved study and in life disliked Buddhist teachings; when the father died, Ang before the bier recited the “Documents,” saying: “This is what my forebear wished to hear.”

entries.zh: 禁其家不可以佛事汙吾先人。
entries.en: He forbade Buddhist rites that would defile his father.
entries.literal: He forbade his household to defile the forebear with Buddhist rites.

entries.zh: 晉高祖時，詔天下求孝悌之士，戶部尚書王權、宗正卿石光贊、國子祭酒田敏、兵部侍郎王延等相與詣東上閤門，上昂行義可以應詔。
entries.en: Under Gaozu of Jin, the court sought filial and dutiful men across the realm. Wang Quan, Minister of Revenue; Shi Guangzan, Director of the Imperial Clan Court; Tian Min, Director of the National University; Wang Yan, Vice Minister of War; and others went together to the Eastern Upper Gate and recommended Ang’s conduct as meeting the edict.
entries.literal: Under Gaozu of Jin, an edict sought filial and brotherly men throughout the realm. Minister of Revenue Wang Quan, Director of the Imperial Clan Court Shi Guangzan, Director of the National University Tian Min, Vice Minister of War Wang Yan, and others together went to the Eastern Upper Gate of the Secretariat and memorialized that Ang’s conduct and righteousness qualified him to answer the edict.

entries.zh: 詔昂至京師，召見便殿，以為宗正丞。
entries.en: Ang was summoned to the capital, received in the side hall, and made Vice Director of the Imperial Clan Court.
entries.literal: An edict summoned Ang to the capital; he was received in the side hall and appointed Vice Director of the Imperial Clan Court.

entries.zh: 遷少卿。
entries.en: He was promoted to Vice Minister of the Imperial Clan Court.
entries.literal: He was promoted to Vice Director.

entries.zh: 出帝即位，晉政日壞，昂數上疏極諫，不聽，乃稱疾東歸，以壽終于家。
entries.en: When the Deposed Emperor came to the throne, Jin governance grew worse day by day. Ang repeatedly submitted sharp memorials, was ignored, pleaded illness, returned east, and died at home in old age.
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor ascended, Jin government daily worsened; Ang several times submitted memorials in utmost remonstrance, was not heeded, then pleaded illness and returned east, dying of old age at home.

entries.zh: 昂既去，而晉室大亂。
entries.en: After Ang left, the Jin court fell into great disorder.
entries.literal: Once Ang had gone, the Jin house fell into great disorder.

entries.zh: 李自倫者，深州人也。
entries.en: Li Zilun was from Shenzhou.
entries.literal: Li Zilun was a man of Shenzhou.

entries.zh: 天福四年正月，尚書戶部奏：「深州司功參軍李自倫六世同居，奉敕準格。
entries.en: In Tianfu’s fourth year, first month, the Ministry of Revenue reported: “Li Zilun of Shenzhou, six generations under one roof—per statute and edict.
entries.literal: In the first month of the fourth year of Tianfu the Ministry of Revenue memorialized: “Li Zilun, Assistant for Merit of Shenzhou, six generations dwelling together—per imperial order and statute.

entries.zh: 按格，孝義旌表，必先加按驗，孝者復其終身，義門仍加旌表。
entries.en: By statute, filial piety must be verified first; the filial are exempt for life, and righteous households receive further honors.
entries.literal: According to the statute, to honor filial piety one must first add investigation and verification; the filial are restored for life, and gates of righteousness receive further commendation.

entries.zh: 得本州審到鄉老程言等稱，自倫高祖訓，訓生粲，粲生則，則生忠，忠生自倫，自倫生光厚，六世同居不妄。」
entries.en: The prefecture verified through elders Cheng Yan and others: from great-grandfather Xun through Can, Ze, Zhong, Zilun, to Guanghou—six generations, no falsehood.”
entries.literal: The prefecture verified through village elders Cheng Yan and others, who said: from Zilun’s great-grandfather Xun, Xun begot Can, Can begot Ze, Ze begot Zhong, Zhong begot Zilun, Zilun begot Guanghou—six generations dwelling together without falsehood.”

entries.zh: 敕以所居飛鳧鄉為孝義鄉，匡聖裏為仁和裏，準式旌表門閭。
entries.en: An edict renamed their village Village of Filial Piety, their lane Lane of Humaneness, and honored their gate by statute.
entries.literal: An edict named their dwelling Feiniao Village as Village of Filial Piety, Kuangsheng Lane as Lane of Humaneness, and honored their gate by the prescribed form.

entries.zh: 九月丙子，戶部復奏：「前登州義門王仲昭六世同居，其旌表有聽事、步欄，前列屏，樹烏頭正門，閥閱一丈二尺，烏頭二柱端冒以瓦桶，築雙闕一丈，在烏頭之南三丈七尺，夾樹槐柳，十有五步，請如之。」
entries.en: In the ninth month the Ministry reported: “Wang Zhongzhao of Dengzhou, another six-generation household, whose gate had hall, screen, black-headed pillars, memorial tablet, twin towers, and planted trees—and asked that Zilun’s gate match.”
